We start from the robot arm that we already know as a chain of rigid links. In chapter 27 we wrote its equations of motion and assumed that each link only turns and moves while its shape stays the same. Here we give that assumption up. We also use the beam (chapters 5 and 12), which tells how a strip bends, and its vibration (chapter 13), which tells how fast it oscillates.

Let us look at the words of the title. A link (člen) is one piece of a chain, in an arm the part between two joints, where the arm can turn. A flexible link (podajni člen) is one that gives way under a load instead of staying straight. Flexibility is therefore not a fault of one particular robot. Every link is made of a material that gives way, and the only question is whether the giving way is small enough to neglect.

Why this matters we show on a steel strip 1 m long that a motor turns at one end. If we pull its free end with a force of 10 N, the end bends by \(23{,}6\) mm. The freely vibrating strip oscillates about five times a second, and a motion of the arm takes about \(0{,}2\) s, which is one oscillation of the strip. In so fast a motion the link bends and vibrates. This counts for light robots with a long reach and for robots that must stop quickly and accurately, because the end of the arm still vibrates when the motor has stopped.

The chapter promises four things. First we show when the bending must be taken into account and why the tools of the chapter on deformation alone cannot describe it. Then we choose a description of motion that follows both the turning of the link and its bending, and with it we write the energy and the equations of motion of a link turned by a motor. Next we look at what steady turning does to the stiffness of the link. Finally we turn the equations into the form used for finite elements and into a small number of vibration modes (načini nihanja), with which a computer can solve them quickly. What the book cannot prove we cite with a source and say so.

28.1 Why robot links bend

A robot arm is a chain of links (členi) joined by joints (sklepi) and driven by motors. The word link means one piece of a chain, and in the arm it is one stretch between two joints. Until now we treated each such piece as a rigid body (chapter 8, definition 8.38): the distances between its points do not change. In this chapter the link also bends while it turns. Such a link is called a flexible link (podajni člen), because under load it yields, it gives way, instead of staying straight. For a link on a hub the chapter will write equations of motion whose unknowns are the angle of rotation and the elastic coordinates, compute frequencies that the rigid model cannot predict, and show what steady rotation does to its stiffness. This first section answers two questions: when must we take the bending into account at all, and why can we not describe it with the tools of the chapter on deformation that we have used so far.

Take the link that we follow through the whole chapter: a steel strip of length \(L = 1\) m, \(b = 40\) mm wide perpendicular to the plane of motion and \(h = 6\) mm thick in the plane of motion, with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ as the steel of chapter 5. The strip is rigidly fixed at one end to the hub (pest), which for it is a clamp. The hub is the part to which the link is fixed and which the motor turns. The same name is used for the part of a wheel into which the axle is fixed. The hub turns about a vertical axis, the plane of motion is horizontal, and so the weight acts in the direction of \(b\), where the strip is stiff. This example is our own choice and not taken from a source, because no book in the library treats a robot link with numbers. We shall therefore vary the inertia of the hub later, so that the conclusions do not depend on our choice.

The model is the beam model of chapter 5 with three simplifications, which we name at once. First: the motion is planar, and a spatial link (SHABANA, section 6.6, PDF pp. 303-308) is only named. Second: the link is an Euler-Bernoulli beam (definition 5.14), cross sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis. Third: the axis does not lengthen. This is a simplification and not a fact. The axial stiffness \(EA/L\) of the strip is \(4{,}704 \cdot 10^7\) N/m, the bending stiffness of the tip \(3EI/L^3\) is \(423{,}4\) N/m, and the ratio is \(1{,}11 \cdot 10^5\). A force of \(10 \cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 423{,}4 = 4{,}23\) N bends the tip by 10 mm. If the same force acted along the axis, it would lengthen it by only \(4{,}23/(4{,}704 \cdot 10^{7}) \approx 9 \cdot 10^{-8}\) m, which is below \(10^{-7}\) of the length. The own weight in the direction of \(b\), with \(I = h\,b^3/12 = 32\,000\) mm⁴ (lemma 5.27, roles of the sides exchanged), lowers the tip by \(0{,}366\) mm by theorem 5.56, item 2. This deflection is perpendicular to the plane of motion, so the planar model does not contain it.

28.1.1 How much the link bends

First look at a link at rest, loaded. Let us draw it in the upper half of figure 28.1.

The hub is a circle with the axis as a dot pointing towards us. The link starts at it. The coordinate axes \(x\) and \(y\) at the bottom left give the directions: \(x\) runs along the link from the hub to the tip, \(y\) is perpendicular to it in the plane of motion, and the deflection \(v\) is the displacement of a point of the link in the direction \(y\). The dashed line is the axis of the link before loading, and the orange curve is the same axis after it. A rope pulls the tip of the link in the plane of motion with the force \(F = 10\) N. The force starts at the point of the tip and points down in the figure, because it pulls. The deflection \(v(L)\) is the distance between the dashed and the orange position of the tip, drawn with bars at both ends.

How large is the deflection? For a cantilever clamped at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L\), theorem 5.56, item 1, equation (5.54), gives \(v(L) = -F L^3/(3EI)\). The bending stiffness of definition 5.36 is \(EI = 196 \cdot 10^9 \cdot 720 \cdot 10^{-12} = 141{,}12\) N m². The second moment of area \(I = b\,h^3/12 = 40 \cdot 6^3/12 = 720\) mm⁴ is by lemma 5.27, because \(h\) lies in the plane of bending. So

\[|v(L)| = \frac{10\ \text{N} \cdot (1\ \text{m})^3}{3 \cdot 141{,}12\ \text{N m}^2} = 23{,}62\ \text{mm} . \tag{28.1}\]

This is \(2{,}4\,\%\) of the length. The slope of the tip is by the same equation \(|v'(L)| = F L^2/(2EI) = 0{,}0354\) rad, at which the sine and the tangent of the angle differ from the angle by less than \(0{,}1\,\%\), so the small-displacement model of chapter 5 is accurate enough here.

28.1.2 When the static calculation is not enough

But the arm does not move slowly. How fast must a load change for the static calculation to fail? The link has a natural frequency. By theorem 13.37 \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = x_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\omega_0\) with \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{EI/(\rho A L^4)}\) and \(x_1 = 1{,}8751\). With \(\rho A = 7800 \cdot 240 \cdot 10^{-6} = 1{,}872\) kg/m we get \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{141{,}12/1{,}872} = 8{,}682\) 1/s and

\[\omega_1 = 1{,}8751^2 \cdot 8{,}682 = 30{,}53\ \text{rad/s} , \qquad f_1 = \frac{\omega_1}{2\pi} = 4{,}86\ \text{Hz} , \qquad T_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_1} = 0{,}206\ \text{s} . \tag{28.2}\]

A freely vibrating link would oscillate almost five times a second. A movement of the arm that lasts about \(0{,}2\) s is therefore as long as one oscillation of the link.

What does this mean for the response? Take a force that rises linearly from zero to a final value \(Q_0\) in the time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) and then stays constant. For a system with one degree of freedom without damping and with natural frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), lemma 9.70 gives the largest value of the response

\[q_{\max} = \frac{Q_0}{k}\Big(1 + \frac{|\sin\theta|}{\theta}\Big) , \qquad \theta = \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,t_{\mathrm{r}}}{2} , \tag{28.3}\]

where \(Q_0/k\) is the static value. For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\) we have \(\theta \to 0\) and the expression tends to \(2\), as for a step (theorem 9.69). Inserting \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \omega_1 = 30{,}53\) rad/s gives the ratio of the largest response to the static value: \(1{,}98\) for \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}02\) s, \(1{,}91\) for \(0{,}05\) s, \(1{,}65\) for \(0{,}1\) s and \(1{,}00\) for \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = T_1 = 0{,}206\) s, and again \(1{,}22\) for \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}29\) s. At \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = T_1\) the overshoot is zero only because \(\sin\theta = \sin\pi = 0\), for a longer \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) it rises again. A reliable bound comes from \(|\sin\theta| \le 1\): the response exceeds the static value by at most \(1/\theta\) of that value, so by less than \(10\,\%\) for \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0{,}66\) s (\(\theta \ge 10\)) and by less than \(5\,\%\) for \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 1{,}31\) s (\(\theta \ge 20\)). The static calculation therefore holds when the load rises over at least a few oscillations of the link, for \(10\,\%\) accuracy over at least \(3{,}2\) oscillations. When it rises in less than one oscillation, the largest response is up to twice the static one. The values hold for the part of the response in the first mode. That each mode of the link really is a system with one degree of freedom under a load proportional to the acceleration of the hub we shall prove in section 28.6, and the higher modes add less (numbers in section 28.9).

28.1.3 The load that the hub produces

A load on the link can also arise without an external force, only because the hub accelerates. Let us draw it in the lower half of figure 28.1. The hub turns with the angular acceleration \(\alpha = 10\) rad/s², drawn as the curved arrow, counterclockwise. First we take the link as straight, as if it were rigid, and compute which forces its points need for this acceleration.

  1. A point of the link at distance \(s\) from the axis has by lemma 8.40, with \(\vek o = \vek 0\) and \(\vek r_0 = (s, 0)\), the position \(s\,(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)\). We differentiate it twice in time (definition 8.69): the acceleration is \(s\,\big(\ddot\theta\,(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta) - \dot\theta^2\,(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)\big)\). At the instant when \(\dot\theta = 0\) it is perpendicular to the link and has magnitude \(s\,\alpha\).
  2. The part of the link from \(x\) to the end has the mass \(\rho A\,(L - x)\), and each of its points has the acceleration \(s\,\alpha\) upwards. In this calculation this part moves as a rigid body, so by theorem 8.74 (first equation of (8.62)) the resultant of the forces on it is the integral of the density times the acceleration, \(\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L \rho A\,\alpha\,s\,\mathrm{d}s = \rho A\,\alpha\,(L^2 - x^2)/2\), upwards. It is supplied by the rest of the link through the cross section \(x\), and the part from \(x\) to the end acts back with the same force downwards. The shear force (force of the larger \(x\) on the smaller) is therefore \(V(x) = -\rho A\,\alpha\,(L^2 - x^2)/2\) and its derivative is \(V' = \rho A\,\alpha\,x\). By the relation \(V' = -q\) (corollary 5.11) this is the same as if a distributed load \(q(x) = -\rho A\,\alpha\,x\) acted on the link, downwards. These are the arrows of the load. They end on the link, because they push, and they are proportional to \(x\), so the dashed line above joins them into a triangle.
  3. The moment with which the hub acts on the link (arrow \(M_0\)) is, by the second equation of (8.62) for the whole link as a rigid body, the moment of all these forces about the axis, \(M_0 = \int_0^L s \cdot \rho A\,\alpha\,s\,\mathrm{d}s = \rho A\,\alpha\,L^3/3\). The moment of inertia of the link about the axis is by definition 8.73 \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = \int_0^L \rho A\,s^2\,\mathrm{d}s = \rho A\,L^3/3 = 0{,}624\) kg m², so \(M_0 = J_{\mathrm{link}}\,\alpha = 6{,}24\) N m. This is the moment that the hub must give to a rigid link.
\[M_0 = \frac{\rho A\,\alpha\,L^3}{3} = 1{,}872 \cdot 10 \cdot \frac{1}{3}\ \text{N m} = 6{,}24\ \text{N m} . \tag{28.4}\]

Now this moment acts on the link as bending. By theorem 5.35 \(M = EI\,v''\) and by theorem 5.15 the strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v''\) (equation (5.17) with \(u' = 0\)). At the root it is largest at the edge of the strip, \(y = h/2 = 3\) mm:

\[|\varepsilon_{\max}| = \frac{M_0\,h/2}{EI} = \frac{6{,}24 \cdot 0{,}003}{141{,}12} = 1{,}327 \cdot 10^{-4} . \tag{28.5}\]

By theorem 5.35 the stress at the root is \(M_0\,(h/2)/I = 26{,}0\) MPa. We get the deflection from the deflection curve equation \(EI\,v'''' = q\) (theorem 5.42) with the load \(q = -\rho A\,\alpha\,x\), downwards. The boundary conditions are the clamp, \(v(0) = v'(0) = 0\), and the free end, \(v''(L) = v'''(L) = 0\) (zero moment and shear force). Four integrations give the deflection curve

\[v(x) = -\frac{\rho A\,\alpha}{120\,EI}\,\big(x^5 - 10\,L^2 x^3 + 20\,L^3 x^2\big) , \qquad v(L) = -\frac{11\,\rho A\,\alpha\,L^5}{120\,EI} = -12{,}16\ \text{mm} , \tag{28.6}\]

which we check. At \(x = 0\) both \(v\) and \(v'\) are zero, because the bracket has no terms with \(x^0\) and \(x^1\). The derivatives are \(v'' = -\dfrac{\rho A\alpha}{120\,EI}\,(20\,x^3 - 60\,L^2 x + 40\,L^3)\) and \(v''' = -\dfrac{\rho A\alpha}{120\,EI}\,(60\,x^2 - 60\,L^2)\). At \(x = L\) both are zero, and at \(x = 0\) we have \(EI\,v''(0) = -\rho A\,\alpha\,L^3/3 = -M_0\) from equation (28.4). The fourth derivative is \(EI\,v'''' = -\rho A\,\alpha\,x = q\). The deflection is \(1{,}2\,\%\) of the length.

The calculation was simplified: we computed the load with a straight and rigid link. We left out two things. The first is the acceleration of the bending \(\ddot v\). The deflection \(12{,}16\) mm is the static response to a load that has acted for a long time. If the acceleration of the hub is switched on faster than one oscillation of the link, by section 28.1.2 the deflection can nearly double, to about \(24\) mm. The second is the rotation of the tip. The real link bends and its tip turns by the slope \(v'(L) = \rho A\alpha L^4/(8EI) = 0{,}0166\) rad, \(0{,}95^\circ\). By this angle the acceleration of the tip is turned relative to the bent axis of the link. The load therefore gets an axial component of \(\sin 0{,}0166 \approx 1{,}7\,\%\) of the transverse load, while the transverse load decreases only by \(1 - \cos 0{,}0166 = 1{,}4 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of its value. This suffices for the estimate in this section. The feedback of the bending on the motion will be the main subject of sections 28.4 to 28.6.

The meaning of the two numbers: a deflection of 12 mm and a strain of \(1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-4}\) are small, as the beam model requires (definition 5.14). The angle through which the hub turns the link, however, can be large: a robot arm turns by tens of degrees and more in one move, and in this chapter we also compute with \(30^\circ\). The link therefore performs two motions at once. It turns a lot as a whole and bends a little. Let us see what this does to the description of displacements from the chapter on deformation, which measures displacements from the position before loading in fixed axes.

28.1.4 The false stretch of a rotation

To begin with, take without bending a square \(OABC\) with side \(L\) and the point \(O\) on the axis of the hub, which the hub turns through the angle \(\theta\) as a rigid body. Let us draw it in figure 28.2, with \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

The dashed square is the position before the motion and the orange one the same plate after the turn. The angle \(\theta\) is the angle between \(OA\) and \(OA'\). Every point with position vector \(\vek r\) from \(O\) goes to \(\mat R(\theta)\,\vek r\) (lemma 8.40), so its displacement is \(\vek u = (\mat R(\theta) - \mat I)\,\vek r\), where \(\mat I\) is the \(2 \times 2\) identity matrix. In the figure this is the arrow from \(A\) to \(A'\) and from \(C\) to \(C'\). The plate has not deformed, every segment has the same length after the turn. What does the small strain tensor say about this displacement?

Lemma 28.1 False stretch of a rotation (lažni raztezek zasuka)

Let \(\theta\) be an angle and \(\mat R(\theta)\) the rotation matrix in the plane \(xy\) (lemma 8.40). A rigid rotation about the point \(O\) is the displacement field \(\vek u = (\mat R(\theta) - \mat I)\,\vek r\) in the plane \(xy\), with \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(\vek r\) the position vector from \(O\). We write the matrices \(\mat H\), \(\ten\varepsilon\) and \(\mat E\) only with their elements in the plane \(xy\), the other elements are zero, and \(\mat I\) is the \(2 \times 2\) identity matrix. Then:

  1. the displacement gradient is \(\mat H = \mat R(\theta) - \mat I\) at every point,
  2. the small strain tensor (definition 1.115) is in the plane \(\ten\varepsilon = (\cos\theta - 1)\,\mat I\), so the small strain tensor assigns to a fibre in every direction \(\vek n\) in the plane the strain \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \cos\theta - 1\),
  3. the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (definition 1.112) is \(\mat E = \mat 0\).
Proof

We must show three items: the gradient is the matrix that writes the field, and then we compute both tensors from it.

  1. The components of the field are \(u_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (R_{\mathrm{ij}} - \delta_{\mathrm{ij}})\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with constant \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}} - \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (the partial derivative of a linear function is its coefficient). Hence \(\mat H = \mat R - \mat I\) (definition 1.109).
  2. By definition 1.115, \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T) = \tfrac12(\mat R + \mat R^\T) - \mat I\). For \(\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\) we have \(\mat R + \mat R^\T = 2\cos\theta\,\mat I\) (the off-diagonal elements cancel), so \(\ten\varepsilon = (\cos\theta - 1)\,\mat I\). With the small strain tensor the strain of a fibre in direction \(\vek n\) is approximated by \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) (theorem 1.114 and corollary 1.122), and this is \((\cos\theta - 1)\,\vek n^\T\vek n = \cos\theta - 1\), because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector.
  3. By definition 1.110, \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H = \mat R\). By definition 1.112, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat R^\T\mat R - \mat I)\). The rotation matrix is orthogonal, \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\) (lemma 2.40), which we also see directly from the elements \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) (lemma 8.10, item 1) on the diagonal and \(-\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0\) off it. Hence \(\mat E = \mat 0\).

Source: The lemma keeps the promise of chapter 1 at figure 1.465 and theorem 1.134. The proof is not from the sources.

What does this mean in the figure? The small strain tensor claims that every fibre has shortened by \(1 - \cos\theta\). At \(\theta = 30^\circ\) we have \(\cos\theta - 1 = -0{,}134\). According to the tensor the fibre \(OA'\) would have the length \((1 + \varepsilon)\,L = 0{,}866\,L\), while the true length is \(L\): we did not squeeze the plate, we only turned it. The same calculation in numbers for \(\theta = 30^\circ\): \(\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}134 & -0{,}5 \\ 0{,}5 & -0{,}134 \end{bmatrix}\), its symmetric part is \(-0{,}134\,\mat I\), as the lemma says, and the Green-Lagrange tensor is \(\mat 0\). Hooke's law (chapter 3) would assign to a fibre in uniaxial stress from this strain the stress \(E \cdot 0{,}134 = 26{,}3\) GPa, which is a thousand times the stress of \(26\) MPa from the true bending that we computed above.

At which angle is the false strain larger than the true one? For the true strain at the root \(\varepsilon = 1{,}327 \cdot 10^{-4}\) from equation (28.5) the following corollary answers.

Corollary 28.2 Angle at which the false strain dominates (meja zasuka, pri kateri lažna deformacija prevlada)

Let \(0 < \varepsilon < 2\) and \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\). The false strain \(|\cos\theta - 1| = 1 - \cos\theta\) of lemma 28.1 is less than or equal to \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(\theta \le \theta_\varepsilon\), where \(\theta_\varepsilon \in (0, \pi)\) is the unique angle with \(\cos\theta_\varepsilon = 1 - \varepsilon\).

Proof

We must show that the angle \(\theta_\varepsilon\) exists and that the comparison \(1 - \cos\theta \le \varepsilon\) means exactly \(\theta \le \theta_\varepsilon\).

  1. The condition \(1 - \cos\theta \le \varepsilon\) is equivalent to \(\cos\theta \ge 1 - \varepsilon\).
  2. The cosine is differentiable (theorem 8.12), so by lemma 1.79 it is continuous, and by lemma 8.10 strictly decreasing on \([0, \pi]\), with \(\cos 0 = 1\) and \(\cos\pi = -1\) (items 2 and 3). Since \(-1 < 1 - \varepsilon < 1\), by the intermediate value theorem 2.57 there is \(\theta_\varepsilon \in (0, \pi)\) with \(\cos\theta_\varepsilon = 1 - \varepsilon\), and it is unique by strict monotonicity.
  3. Since the cosine is strictly decreasing on \([0, \pi]\), \(\cos\theta \ge \cos\theta_\varepsilon\) holds exactly for \(\theta \le \theta_\varepsilon\).

Source: The corollary is ours. The proof is not from the sources.

For \(\varepsilon = 1{,}327 \cdot 10^{-4}\) we get \(\theta_\varepsilon = 0{,}01629\) rad \(= 0{,}933^\circ\). For a turn by more than \(0{,}93^\circ\) the false strain is therefore larger than the true one, and at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) it is three orders of magnitude larger. The values for a few angles are:

\(\theta\) \(0{,}01\) rad \(0{,}1\) rad \(30^\circ\) \(90^\circ\)
\(\cos\theta - 1\) \(-5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-5}\) \(-5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-3}\) \(-0{,}134\) \(-1\)

At \(90^\circ\) the small strain tensor would claim that all fibres have length zero.

Does this contradict theorem 1.134, which says that a field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) with an antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) has a zero small strain tensor? It does not, and this very example shows where the theorem holds. We split the rotation matrix into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts,

\[\mat R - \mat I = (\cos\theta - 1)\,\mat I + \sin\theta\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{28.7}\]

where the first term is not antisymmetric if \(\theta \ne 0\). The matrix \(\mat R - \mat I\) is therefore not of the form \(\mat W\) of the theorem, so the theorem cannot be applied to a finite rotation. The theorem stays true, only its hypothesis is not met here. For a small angle the first term is small: at \(\theta = 0{,}01\) it is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-5}\), which is \(\theta^2/2\) at the digits shown. For the square plate of chapter 1 (figure 1.465) the angle was \(s = 0{,}001\) and the error \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and there the theorem was good enough. For our link the true strain is \(10^{-4}\), so the error \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-5}\) at \(0{,}57^\circ\) is already more than a third of the true strain, and at \(30^\circ\) it is a thousand times larger.

The consequence for the link is this. We must not measure the displacement of a turned link in fixed axes and compute small strains from it, because the false stretch would swamp the true strain, which is three orders of magnitude smaller. If instead we split the displacement into a large rotation, described by an angle and a position (lemma 8.40), and a small elastic displacement, measured in axes that turn with the link, the gradient of this displacement will be small and the strain will make sense, as we shall prove in the next section. The source also uses this idea: it describes the position and orientation of a chosen point of the body with one group of coordinates and the deformation relative to it with another (SHABANA, PDF pp. 199-200). Rods, beams, plates and shells have an infinite number of degrees of freedom (SHABANA, PDF p. 200), so we write the deformation with a finite number of coordinates by the Ritz method (definition 6.32, SHABANA, PDF p. 201). The axes that turn with the link and the coordinates in them are defined in section 28.2.

28.2 The floating frame of reference

Section 28.1 showed that the displacement of a turned link must not be measured in fixed axes and used to compute small strains. At a turn of \(30°\) the false stretch is \(\cos\theta - 1 = -0{,}134\), while the true strain of the link is about \(10^{-4}\). We must therefore describe the turn and the bending each with its own numbers: the turn with a position and an angle, the bending with another set of numbers. Where does a point of the link stand when the hub turns and the link bends at the same time? We build the answer on figure 28.3, piece by piece, as on a blackboard.

First we draw the fixed axes \(x\) and \(y\) with origin \(O\). In them we measured the position of a rigid body in the plane in chapter 8, and by lemma 8.40 it is determined by three numbers: the position of one point of the body and an angle. For the point we choose the place where the link is fixed to the hub and give it the position \(\vek o\), shown by the arrow from \(O\). At this point we draw two new axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\). The axis \(\bar x\) is turned against the axis \(x\) by the angle \(\theta\), measured from the direction of the axis \(x\), which is dashed in the figure, and the axis \(\bar y\) is a quarter turn further on. Because the hub turns, \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) change with time. The link is clamped to the hub, so in these axes it is unloaded always in the same place: straight and along the axis \(\bar x\). The reason is the rigid motion of lemma 8.40: a point of a rigid body has the position \(\vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\bar{\vek r}_0\), and the two numbers \(\bar{\vek r}_0\) do not change during the motion. The point labelled \(x\) on the axis of the unloaded link therefore always has, in the turned axes, the position \(\bar{\vek r}_0 = (x, 0)\), measured in the figure from \(\vek o\) along \(\bar x\). We call these numbers the components in the frame, because they are measured in the axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).

Under load the link bends and its axis is the blue curve. The point \(x\) of the axis moves to the point \(P\), and its displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is again measured in the turned axes. For our link this displacement is perpendicular to \(\bar x\) and equal to the deflection \(v(x)\). The point is therefore at \(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \bar{\vek u}\) in the turned axes, and in the fixed axes we get its position \(\vek r\) if we turn this sum by \(\theta\) and add \(\vek o\),

\[\vek r = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\big(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \bar{\vek u}\big) . \tag{28.8}\]

This is the rule of lemma 8.40 with the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) in the brackets, and for \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\) it is that lemma.

Definition 28.3 Floating frame of reference of a link (plavajoči koordinatni sistem člena)

Let a link move in the plane \(xy\) (lemma 8.40). The floating frame of reference, the frame for short (plavajoči koordinatni sistem, okvir), is a rectangular coordinate system with origin at the point with position \(\vek o(t) \in \mathbb R^2\) and with axes in the directions \(\mat R(\theta)\,(1, 0)^\T\) and \(\mat R(\theta)\,(0, 1)^\T\), where \(\theta(t)\) is an angle in radians and \(\mat R(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\). The functions \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) are twice continuously differentiable, \(\vek o(0) = \vek 0\) and \(\theta(0) = 0\). The components of a point in the frame (komponente točke v okviru) are the numbers \(\bar{\vek w} \in \mathbb R^2\) for which the position of the point is \(\vek r = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\bar{\vek w}\). The components in the frame of a vector \(\vek w\) (a difference of positions) are \(\bar{\vek w} = \mat R(\theta)^\T\,\vek w\).

Source: SHABANA, PDF p. 202 (body reference in floating frame of reference), PDF p. 203 (the planar case \(\vek r = \vek R + \mat A\,\bar{\vek u}\)). Notation after chapter 8: \(\vek o\) as in lemma 8.40, angle \(\theta\) instead of \(\varphi\).

The frame is called floating because its origin is not necessarily tied to the same material point of the body: it "floats" with the motion of the body and follows only the requirements that we fix below (SHABANA, PDF p. 202). In our link \(\vek o\) will be the hub, which is a material point, but in other frames (\(\bar x\) along the chord of the link) it would not be. The motion of the frame is therefore not the rigid motion of the link: for the same link we can choose different frames (figure 28.4), and the formulation does not separate rigid motion from deformation (SHABANA, PDF p. 202).

Definition 28.4 Reference and elastic coordinates of a link (referenčne in elastične koordinate člena)

Let the link in the unloaded state have its axis as the segment \([0, L]\) on the axis \(\bar x\) of the frame of definition 28.3, and let the point of the axis labelled \(x\) have the components \(\bar{\vek r}_0 = (x, 0)^\T\). Let \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}} \colon [0, L] \to \mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable and linearly independent functions (definition 6.32, trial functions) and \(\mat\Psi(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \psi_1(x) & \cdots & \psi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) \end{bmatrix}\) a matrix of size \(2 \times n\). The elastic coordinates (elastične koordinate) \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}(t) \in \mathbb R^n\) determine the displacement of the point \(x\) in the frame,

\[\bar{\vek u}(x, t) = \mat\Psi(x)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}(t) , \qquad v(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{k} = 1}^{n} \psi_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) , \tag{28.9}\]

and the reference coordinates (referenčne koordinate) are the three numbers \(\vek q_{\mathrm{r}} = (o_{\mathrm{x}}, o_{\mathrm{y}}, \theta)^\T\) of definition 28.3. The position of the point \(x\) of the axis is

\[\vek r(x, t) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\Big(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi(x)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\Big) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ v(x, t) \end{bmatrix} , \tag{28.10}\]

and the coordinates of the link are \((\vek q_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\), together \(3 + n\) numbers. A point at a distance \(y\) from the axis (in the plane of motion) has, in the Euler-Bernoulli model (theorem 5.15), the displacement \(\bar{\vek u} = (-y\,v'(x),\ v(x))^\T\).

Source: SHABANA, PDF p. 202 (equation 5.4, reference coordinates), PDF p. 203 (equations 5.6 and 5.7), PDF p. 204 (equations 5.8 and 5.9). SHABANA has a shape matrix \(\mat S\) with an axial and a transverse part, we take only the transverse part (idealization, section 28.1).

Why these names? The reference coordinates tell where the frame stands, the frame to which (refer) everything else is related. The elastic coordinates measure how the link bends relative to the frame, that is the elastic part of the motion. The subscript \(_{\mathrm{d}}\) comes from the word deformation, because in chapter 7 the subscript \(\mathrm f\) already has the meaning "free". The angle \(\theta\) is the angle \(\varphi\) of lemma 8.40, because \(\varphi\) in chapter 12 means the rotation of a node. This chapter does not use the shear rotation \(\theta\) of chapter 5. The matrix \(\mat\Psi\) is the shape matrix of SHABANA (there \(\mat S\)), the \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the trial functions of the Ritz method from chapter 6, and the matrix \(\mat S\) in this book is the second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor and the geometric stiffness matrix.

There are three idealizations and we name them. First: the motion is planar. Second: the displacement of the axis is only transverse, the first component of the vector \(\bar{\vek u}\) of the axis is zero. Under deflection the axis of a real beam keeps its length \(L\), but its projection on the axis \(\bar x\) shortens to the length \(\ell < L\). We estimate the shortening \(\Delta = L - \ell\) as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.133, which does not use the values of \(v\) at the ends: from \(L = \int_0^\ell\sqrt{1 + v'^2}\,\mathrm dx\) and \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} \le 1 + p^2/2\) it follows that \(\Delta \le \tfrac12\int_0^\ell v'^2\,\mathrm dx \le \tfrac12\int_0^L v'^2\,\mathrm dx\), since \(\ell < L\) and \(v'^2 \ge 0\). For the first mode with a tip deflection of \(10\) mm this bound is \(0{,}058\) mm, that is \(5{,}8 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of the length. This shortening will not disappear, it will return in section 28.7, where it becomes essential because of the rotation. Third: the frame and the shapes \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are chosen so that the position is unique. This requires the next subsection.

28.2.1 Does the position have one decomposition

The triple \((\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) is a triple of numbers, while the position of the link is a curve \(\vek r(x)\). The equations of motion have as many unknowns as there are numbers in the triple. If the position did not change when the triple changes in some direction, the equations would have more unknowns than motions: to this direction would belong a zero velocity of all points, and the mass matrix would be singular. First we ask: does the position \(\vek r(x)\) determine the triple through equation (28.10) at all? The mass matrix is checked in section 28.4.

The answer depends on how we measure \(v\). Let us look at two ways and a bad example, shown in figure 28.4.

In the first way the axis \(\bar x\) lies on the tangent of the link where the link is clamped in the hub. The bent link moves away from the axis \(\bar x\), and the displacement \(v\) is its distance from the axis. The conditions are therefore \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\), and exactly these two conditions are satisfied by all the cantilever modes of theorem 13.37. In the second way the axis \(\bar x\) is the chord that joins both ends, so \(v(0) = v(L) = 0\). The link has the distance \(v\) from the chord. We leave the length of the axis equal to \(L\), as in the first way, because the shortening \(\Delta\) of the projection, which we estimated above, is of second order.

The conditions \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\) in the first way and \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v(L) = 0\) in the second are similar: each pair removes the displacement and the rotation of the hub from the field \(v\). When the position in general determines the triple is stated by the next definition.

Definition 28.5 Reference conditions of a link (referenčna pogoja člena)

Let \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} q_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the transverse elastic field of the link (definition 28.4). The reference conditions (referenčna pogoja) are two equations \(\ell_1(v) = 0\) and \(\ell_2(v) = 0\), where each \(\ell_{\mathrm{j}}(v)\) is the value \(v(s_{\mathrm{j}})\) or the slope \(v'(s_{\mathrm{j}})\) of the field at a point \(s_{\mathrm{j}} \in [0, L]\), and the matrix

\[\mat C = \begin{bmatrix} \ell_1(1) & \ell_1(x) \\ \ell_2(1) & \ell_2(x) \end{bmatrix} \tag{28.11}\]

is invertible. Here \(1\) and \(x\) are the fields \(v(x) = 1\) and \(v(x) = x\), that is a displacement of the hub and a rotation, which we call the rigid fields of first order (toga polja).

Source: SHABANA §6.2, PDF pp. 286 to 287: the conditions determine the nature of the frame, their number must be at least equal to the number of rigid modes in the field. The matrix \(\mat C\) is not from the source, the condition on its invertibility writes this requirement down.

The matrix \(\mat C\) tells whether one of the fields \(a + b\,x\) satisfies both conditions: if \(\mat C\) is invertible, only \(a = b = 0\) does. For the clamped frame the conditions are \(v(0)\) and \(v'(0)\) and the matrix is the identity. For the chord frame the conditions are \(v(0)\) and \(v(L)\), and the matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & L \end{bmatrix}\) with determinant \(L \ne 0\).

Lemma 28.6 Unique decomposition of the position of a link (enolična razstavitev lege člena)

Let \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) be as in definition 28.4.

  1. Let \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\) for every \(k\) (clamped frame). If the position of the axis is \(\vek r(x) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,(x,\ v(x))^\T\) with \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} q_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), then \(\vek o = \vek r(0)\) and \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^\T = \vek r'(0)\). The angle \(\theta\) is determined by the position up to a multiple of \(2\pi\), and exactly under continuity in time and \(\theta(0) = 0\) (definition 28.3), and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is uniquely determined by the position. The conditions \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\) are reference conditions and every choice of \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) satisfies them.
  2. Let \(\ell_1\), \(\ell_2\) be reference conditions and \(v\) an arbitrary field. Then there is exactly one pair of numbers \((a, b)\) for which the field \(v - a - b\,x\) satisfies both conditions.
Proof

We must show that the position determines \(\vek o\), \(\theta\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (point 1) and that the solution of the system of two equations is unique (point 2).

  1. At \(x = 0\) we have \(v(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} q_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = 0\), so by equation (28.10) \(\vek r(0) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,(0, 0)^\T = \vek o\).
  2. The vector \(\vek o\) and the matrix \(\mat R(\theta)\) do not depend on \(x\), so \(\vek r'(x) = \mat R(\theta)\,(1,\ v'(x))^\T\). At \(x = 0\) we have \(v'(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} q_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), so \(\vek r'(0) = \mat R(\theta)\,(1, 0)^\T = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^\T\). Two numbers with equal cosine and sine differ by a multiple of \(2\pi\): by point 3 of definition 8.9 we shift them by multiples of \(2\pi\) into \((-\pi, \pi]\), there the sign of the sine separates \([0, \pi]\) from \((-\pi, 0)\), and the cosine is strictly decreasing on \([0, \pi]\) and even (lemma 8.10, points 3 and 4), so the shifted numbers are equal. Now let \(\theta\) and \(\tilde\theta\) be continuous functions of time with the same vector \((\cos, \sin)^\T = \vek r'(0)\) at every time and with \(\theta(0) = \tilde\theta(0) = 0\). The function \(g = (\theta - \tilde\theta)/(2\pi)\) is continuous and has only integer values. If it had different values at times \(t_1 < t_2\), then by theorem 2.57 it would also take a non-integer value between them on \([t_1, t_2]\). So \(g\) is constant, and \(g(0) = 0\) gives \(\tilde\theta = \theta\).
  3. From equation (28.10) it follows that \((x,\ v(x))^\T = \mat R(\theta)^\T\,(\vek r(x) - \vek o)\) (\(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\) because \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\)), so \(v(x)\) follows from the position and the already known \(\vek o\), \(\theta\). If two choices of coordinates give the same \(v\), then \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} (q_{\mathrm{k}} - q_{\mathrm{k}}')\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\), and by linear independence \(q_{\mathrm{k}} = q_{\mathrm{k}}'\) for every \(k\).
  4. Point 2: the sought numbers \((a, b)\) must satisfy \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(v) - a\,\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(1) - b\,\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(x) = 0\) for \(i = 1, 2\) (the conditions are linear). This is the system \(\mat C\,(a, b)^\T = (\ell_1(v), \ell_2(v))^\T\), which for an invertible matrix \(\mat C\) has exactly one solution.

Source: The proof is not from the source. SHABANA, PDF pp. 286 to 287 says that reference conditions remove the rigid modes that the field contains.

Point 1 matters for us: the cantilever modes of theorem 13.37 satisfy \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), so for them the frame is determined exactly by the hub, \(\vek o\) is the hub and \(\theta\) the direction of the link axis at the hub. Point 2 holds for any other pair of conditions. For the chord frame \(a = v(0)\) and \(b = (v(L) - v(0))/L\), and the field \(v - a - b\,x\) is indeed zero at both ends. Point 2 is a statement about fields. It has a geometric meaning only to first order: a frame turned by a small angle \(b\) changes the transverse displacement by \(b\,x\) and the first component of the point by \(x\,(1 - \cos b) \approx x\,b^2/2\), which for \(b = 0{,}01\) is \(5 \cdot 10^{-5}\,x\).

Let us also test the bad example: a single shape \(\psi_1 = x/L\), which satisfies only \(v(0) = 0\) and not \(v'(0) = 0\) (figure 28.4, third part). With the axis \(\bar x\) of frame A the straight link at \(q_1 = q\) is turned by \(\beta\) with \(\tan\beta = q/L\). Its offset \(q\) at the end is measured from \(\bar x\). The same link can also be described with frame B with the axis \(\bar x'\), turned by \(2\beta\) against the first, and with \(q' = -q\): in this frame the link has the offset \(-q\). The computation for an arbitrary point \(x\):

\[\mat R(\theta)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ q\,x/L \end{bmatrix} = x\sqrt{1 + (q/L)^2}\ \mat R(\theta + \beta)\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat R(\theta + 2\beta)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ -q\,x/L \end{bmatrix} = x\sqrt{1 + (q/L)^2}\ \mat R(\theta + \beta)\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{28.12}\]

because \((1, q/L) = \sqrt{1 + (q/L)^2}\,(\cos\beta, \sin\beta)\) and \(\mat R(2\beta)\,(\cos\beta, -\sin\beta)^\T = (\cos\beta, \sin\beta)^\T\). The same position therefore has two triples, \((\theta, q)\) and \((\theta + 2\beta, -q)\). For \(q = 10\) mm and \(L = 1\) m we have \(2\beta = 2\arctan 0{,}01 = 0{,}0199993\) rad \(= 1{,}146°\), and the computer finds in the two descriptions points that differ by less than \(2 \cdot 10^{-16}\) m. The reason is that \(\psi_1 = x/L\) contains a rigid rotation. Point 1 of the lemma does not hold, because \(\psi_1'(0) = 1/L \ne 0\). The condition \(v(0) = 0\) alone is not a pair of reference conditions, because the matrix \(\mat C\) has one row \((1, 0)\), and the field \(x\) satisfies this condition. In section 28.4 the same example will give a singular mass matrix at \(q = 0\), where the two triples merge into one.

This field has one more fault. In the frame where \(v = q\,x/L\) and \(\bar{\vek u} = (0, q\,x/L)\), the displacement gradient has a single non-zero entry \(\partial\bar u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = q/L\), so by lemma 1.113 \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12(q/L)^2\). The axis really lengthens: a piece of the axis of length \(h\) has the length \(h\sqrt{1 + (q/L)^2}\) in the position, and the stretch \(\sqrt{1 + (q/L)^2} - 1\) differs from \(\tfrac12(q/L)^2\) by less than \(2 \cdot 10^{-9}\). For \(q/L = 0{,}01\) this is \(5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) or \(0{,}05\) mm at the end. In size this is the false stretch \(\cos\theta - 1 = -5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) at \(\theta = 0{,}01\) rad from lemma 28.1, only the sign is opposite: a rotation written as an elastic displacement gives a false deformation.

28.2.2 Strain in the floating frame

Section 28.1 promised that the rotation would no longer fake the deformation. The theorem that follows fulfils this: the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (definition 1.112), computed from the displacement in the frame, does not depend on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\).

Theorem 28.7 Strain in the floating frame of reference (deformacija v plavajočem koordinatnem sistemu)

Let the body be planar (the displacement in the direction \(z\) is zero, all quantities are independent of \(z\)), let a point of the body have in the unloaded state the position \(\vek X = (X_1, X_2, 0)^\T\) and at time \(t\) the position \(\vek r = \vek o + \mat Q(\theta)\,(\vek X + \bar{\vek u}(\vek X, t))\) with \(\mat Q(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \mat R(\theta) & \vek 0 \\ \vek 0^\T & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and a continuously differentiable field \(\bar{\vek u}\) (components in the frame, third component zero). Let \(\bar{\mat H} = \partial\bar{\vek u}/\partial\vek X\) be its gradient and \(\det(\mat I + \bar{\mat H}) > 0\). Let \(\ten\sigma\) be the matrix of stresses after loading at the point and \(\bar{\ten\sigma} = \mat Q^\T\ten\sigma\,\mat Q\). Then:

  1. the deformation gradient is \(\mat F = \mat Q(\theta)\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})\),
  2. the Green-Lagrange strain tensor is \(\mat E = \tfrac12\big(\bar{\mat H} + \bar{\mat H}^\T + \bar{\mat H}^\T\bar{\mat H}\big)\) and does not depend on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\),
  3. if \(\mat I + \bar{\mat H} = \bar{\mat R}\,\bar{\mat U}\) is the polar decomposition, then the polar decomposition of the gradient is \(\mat F = (\mat Q\,\bar{\mat R})\,\bar{\mat U}\), so the stretch \(\bar{\mat U}\) does not depend on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\),
  4. the second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor is \(\mat S = \bar J\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-1}\,\bar{\ten\sigma}\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-\T}\) with \(\bar J = \det(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})\), so we compute it from the components of the stress in the frame,
  5. if \(|\bar H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m \le \tfrac16\), then \(|E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac32\,m^2\) and \(|\bar U_{\mathrm{ij}} - I_{\mathrm{ij}} - \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 18\,m^2\) for \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \tfrac12(\bar{\mat H} + \bar{\mat H}^\T)\),
  6. the small strain tensor in the fixed axes for the same motion is \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) with \(\mat H = \mat F - \mat I\), and for \(\bar{\mat H} = \mat 0\) it is \(\ten\varepsilon = (\cos\theta - 1)\,\mathrm{diag}(1, 1, 0)\).
Proof

We must show six statements. The gradient is obtained by differentiating the position with respect to \(\vek X\), the other statements follow from definitions and theorems of chapters 1 and 2.

  1. The vector \(\vek o\) and the matrix \(\mat Q\) are functions of time, not of the point, so \(\partial\vek r/\partial\vek X = \mat Q\,(\mat I + \partial\bar{\vek u}/\partial\vek X) = \mat Q\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})\). This is the deformation gradient, since \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) with \(\mat H\) the gradient of the displacement \(\vek r - \vek X\) (definition 1.110).
  2. The matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal, \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) (definition 8.38, equation (2.40)). By definition 1.112, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I) = \tfrac12\big((\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^\T\mat Q^\T\mat Q\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H}) - \mat I\big) = \tfrac12\big(\bar{\mat H} + \bar{\mat H}^\T + \bar{\mat H}^\T\bar{\mat H}\big)\). The result contains neither \(\vek o\) nor \(\theta\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat I + \bar{\mat H}\) has a positive determinant, so by theorem 2.85 it splits into \(\bar{\mat R}\,\bar{\mat U}\). The product \(\mat Q\,\bar{\mat R}\) is an orthogonal matrix with determinant \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\) (a product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal), and \(\bar{\mat U}\) is symmetric with positive eigenvalues. By the uniqueness in theorem 2.85 this is the polar decomposition of the matrix \(\mat F\).
  4. Because \(\det\mat Q = 1\) we have \(\det\mat F = \bar J\). The inverse is \(\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-1}\mat Q^\T\), so \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat Q\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-\T}\). Substituting in equation (2.83) gives \(\mat S = \bar J\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-1}\,(\mat Q^\T\ten\sigma\,\mat Q)\,(\mat I + \bar{\mat H})^{-\T}\).
  5. For \(\mat Q = \mat I\) and \(\vek o = \vek 0\) the gradient \(\bar{\mat H}\) is the gradient of the displacements of the body, so corollary 1.122 (first estimate) and lemma 2.86 hold with \(\bar{\mat H}\) in place of \(\mat H\).
  6. For \(\bar{\mat H} = \mat 0\) we have \(\mat H = \mat Q - \mat I\) and \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat Q + \mat Q^\T) - \mat I\). Along the diagonal this is \(\cos\theta - 1\) in the first two places and \(1 - 1 = 0\) in the third, off the diagonal it is \(-\sin\theta + \sin\theta = 0\).

Source: SHABANA §5.1 and §5.2, PDF pp. 203 to 204 (position as \(\vek R + \mat A\,\bar{\vek u}\)). The relation to the strain in the frame by the theorems of chapters 1 and 2, the proof is not from the source.

The theorem says what the frame gives us: \(\mat E\) and \(\bar{\mat U}\) do not know the rotation. If the link is only turned (\(\bar{\mat H} = \mat 0\)), then \(\mat E = \mat 0\) and \(\bar{\mat U} = \mat I\), while in the fixed axes the small strain tensor is, by point 6, \(\mathrm{diag}(-0{,}134, -0{,}134, 0)\) at \(30°\), which lemma 28.1 shows. The reason is that the rotation in the frame hides in \(\mat Q\), which drops out of \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\).

Let us test the theorem on our link, first cantilever mode, \(L = 1\) m, \(h = 6\) mm, \(y = \pm 3\) mm. With the Euler-Bernoulli field (definition 28.4) we have \(\bar{\mat H} = \begin{bmatrix} -y\,v'' & -v' \\ v' & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v'' + \tfrac12\big(y^2v''^2 + v'^2\big)\), and the first term is \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For a tip deflection of \(10\) mm the maximal values are \(\max|v'| = 1{,}38 \cdot 10^{-2}\) and \(y\max|v''| = 1{,}05 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so \(m = 1{,}38 \cdot 10^{-2}\) and \(\tfrac32 m^2 = 2{,}8 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The estimate of point 5 is therefore larger than the bending strain itself, \(1{,}05 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and nothing follows from it. The expansion \(\mat E - \bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \tfrac12\bar{\mat H}^\T\bar{\mat H}\) is enough, however: on the axis \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12 v'^2 \le 9{,}5 \cdot 10^{-5}\), which is \(90\) % of the bending strain at \(10\) mm and \(9\) % at \(1\) mm (\(9{,}5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) against \(1{,}05 \cdot 10^{-5}\)). This is not a true strain: under deflection the axis of a real beam keeps its length and only its projection on \(\bar x\) shortens (the second idealization above), whereas the field \((0, v)\) lengthens the axis. In section 28.5 we shall therefore take \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v''\) for the energy, which is linear in \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (lemma 5.76), and drop \(\tfrac12 v'^2\). The same term will return as \(\tfrac12\int N v'^2\,\mathrm dx\) in section 28.7, where it is essential at steady rotation.

A bad example for the theorem is a rotation written as an elastic field: in the frame let \(v = b\,x\) and take the Euler-Bernoulli field \(\bar{\vek u} = (-b\,y,\ b\,x)\) (definition 28.4). The gradient \(\bar{\mat H} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -b \\ b & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) is antisymmetric, so \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat 0\) and the motion is to first order a rotation. Nevertheless \(\mat E = \tfrac12\bar{\mat H}^\T\bar{\mat H} = \tfrac12 b^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, 1)\), so \(\mat E \ne \mat 0\). On the axis \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12 b^2\), the same as in the bad example above with \(b = q/L\). The theorem does not prevent this, because it claims only that \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) do not influence \(\mat E\). It says nothing about a rotation written into \(\bar{\vek u}\). The frame must therefore prevent a rotation from entering the elastic coordinates, and the reference conditions of lemma 28.6 achieve this.

28.3 Kinematics of the link

In section 28.2 we wrote the position of every point of a flexible link with three parts: the origin \(\vek o\) of the floating frame, the angle \(\theta\) of its direction, and the elastic coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) that carry the bending. Now we ask how fast such a point moves and what accelerates it. We need the answer three times. The kinetic energy of the link (next section) is a square of the velocity. Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88) turn it into accelerations by differentiating in time, so the equations of motion will contain the same terms as here. And whoever reads the equations of motion has to know which term belongs to which kind of motion.

We use two examples. The first is the beam of SHABANA, examples 5.1 and 5.2 (PDF pp. 204-211), because it gives numbers that we can compare with the source. The second is our running link of section 28.1: a steel strip of length \(L = 1\) m and cross-section \(40 \times 6\) mm, driven on a hub by a torque (link A). The model is planar: the link moves in the plane \(xy\). A spatial position would need three angles or four rotation parameters, which the book does not prove (SHABANA, section 5.1, PDF pp. 207-208, and section 6.6, PDF pp. 303-308, only cited here). Link A is an Euler-Bernoulli beam (definition 5.14) with transverse elastic displacement only, and its axis does not lengthen in the elastic coordinates. This is an idealization, and we name it because we will correct it in the section on constant spin.

The symbols have several meanings, so we separate them from the others in the book at first meeting. We write \(\theta\) for the angle of the floating frame. Chapter 8 writes the angle of position in equation (8.26) with \(\varphi\) and uses \(\theta\) in the kinematics of planar motion of a rigid body, as in this section. Chapter 5 writes \(\theta\) for the rotation of the cross-section of a Timoshenko beam, which we do not use in this chapter. The quarter turn is the matrix

\[\mat J = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat J\,\vek y = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} \times \vek y \ \text{ for every vector } \vek y \text{ in the plane,} \tag{28.13}\]

which is not a moment of inertia. We write the moments of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) (hub) and \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\) (link) so that they cannot be confused. The subscript \(d\) of \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) means "deformation". We do not use the letter \(f\), because in chapter 7 it marks the free unknowns (\(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\)).

The position of a point of the link from section 28.2 (definition 28.4) is written as

\[\vek r = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\bar{\vek p} , \qquad \bar{\vek p} = \bar{\vek r}_0 + \bar{\vek u} = \bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} . \tag{28.14}\]

Here \(\vek r\) is the position of the point in the fixed axes, \(\vek o\) the origin of the floating frame, \(\mat R(\theta)\) the rotation of equation (8.26), \(\bar{\vek r}_0\) the position of this point in the undeformed link in the axes of the floating frame (attached to the point, so independent of time), \(\mat\Psi\) the \(2 \times n\) matrix of shape functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) (which are the trial functions of Ritz's method, definition 6.32), and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}(t)\) the column of \(n\) elastic coordinates. The vector \(\bar{\vek p}\) is the position of the point in the deformed link, measured in the axes of the floating frame, and \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is its elastic displacement of equation (28.9). The position gets its own letter \(p\) (for position) so that we do not confuse it with the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\). A bar over a letter always means "in the axes of the floating frame".

We build figure 28.5 together. First the fixed axes \(x\) and \(y\), in which we measure the position. At the point \(\vek o\) the floating frame stands and its axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) are turned by \(\theta = 30^\circ\) against the fixed ones. We attached the frame to the link so that the axis \(\bar x\) points along the axis of the link at the clamp, which is the condition of section 28.2. We draw the link twice: dashed the undeformed one, which lies on the axis \(\bar x\) and has length \(l = 0{,}5\) m, and solid the deformed one, described by the shape \(\psi_2(\xi) = 3\xi^2 - 2\xi^3\) with \(\xi = x/l\). The point \(A\) at the end of the link is given by the vector \(\bar{\vek p}\) from \(\vek o\) to \(A\) in the deformed link. For example 5.1,

\[\mat\Psi(\xi) = \begin{bmatrix} \xi & 0 \\ 0 & 3\xi^2 - 2\xi^3 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}001 \\ 0{,}01 \end{bmatrix}\ \text{m} , \qquad \bar{\vek p}_{\mathrm{A}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \mat\Psi(1)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}501 \\ 0{,}010 \end{bmatrix}\ \text{m} ,\]

and by equation (28.14) the point \(A\) lies at \(\vek r_{\mathrm{A}} = (1{,}4289;\ 0{,}7592)\) m, which agrees with the source (SHABANA, PDF p. 206). The first shape function describes the extension and the second the bending, so \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) has two coordinates in example 5.1. Definition 28.4 has the first row of the matrix \(\mat\Psi\) equal to zero, while this example has an axial part. The two lemmas below hold for every \(2 \times n\) matrix \(\mat\Psi(x)\), also with an axial part.

Now we ask how fast \(A\) moves. In equation (28.14) three things change in time. The point \(\vek o\) moves, the angle \(\theta\) grows, and the elastic coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) change. We build an expectation from the mechanics of a rigid body. If the link were frozen in its present shape, lemma 8.78 would apply: the velocity is \(\dot{\vek o}\) plus a turn about \(\vek o\) with the rate \(\dot\theta\), which is a vector perpendicular to \(\vek r - \vek o\) of length \(\dot\theta\,|\bar{\vek p}|\). In addition the point travels along the link, because the bend changes. Do these two parts simply add? We show that they do.

Lemma 28.8 Velocity of a point of a flexible link (hitrost točke podajnega člena)

Let \(\vek o(t)\), \(\theta(t)\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}(t)\) be differentiable, \(\mat\Psi\) a matrix of shape functions that depends only on the place in the link, and \(\bar{\vek r}_0\) the position of the point in the undeformed link. For the point with the position (28.14),

\[\dot{\mat R} = \dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J , \qquad \dot{\vek r} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p} + \mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} . \tag{28.15}\]

The first two terms \(\dot{\vek o} + \dot\theta\,\mat J\,(\vek r - \vek o)\) are the velocity of the same point with the link frozen (lemma 8.78 with \(\vek\omega = \dot\theta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)), the third term is the velocity relative to the floating frame.

Proof

We have to show the derivative of the rotation and then the derivative of the sum (28.14).

  1. The elements of the matrix \(\mat R(\theta)\) are \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) with \(\theta = \theta(t)\). By theorem 8.12 and the rule for the derivative of a composite function, \(\dot{\mat R} = \dot\theta\begin{bmatrix} -\sin\theta & -\cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \end{bmatrix}\).
  2. The product is \(\mat R\,\mat J = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\theta & -\cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \end{bmatrix}\), which is the matrix of step 1. So \(\dot{\mat R} = \dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\). The same computation in the other order gives \(\mat J\,\mat R = \mat R\,\mat J\).
  3. By the product rule (lemma 1.81, applied to every element), (28.14) gives \(\dot{\vek r} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot{\mat R}\,\bar{\vek p} + \mat R\,\dot{\bar{\vek p}}\).
  4. The vector \(\bar{\vek r}_0\) and the matrix \(\mat\Psi\) do not depend on time, so \(\dot{\bar{\vek p}} = \mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  5. We insert step 2 and step 4 into step 3 and obtain (28.15). By step 2, \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p} = \dot\theta\,\mat J\,\mat R\,\bar{\vek p} = \dot\theta\,\mat J\,(\vek r - \vek o)\), which is \(\vek\omega \times (\vek r - \vek o)\) with \(\vek\omega = \dot\theta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) by equation (28.13). For \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) the equation therefore agrees with lemma 8.78.

Source: SHABANA (5.13)-(5.19) and the explanation of the terms on PDF p. 207, where the central term is written as \(\mat B\,\dot{\vek\theta}\) with \(\mat B = (\partial\mat A/\partial\theta)\,\bar{\vek u}\) (the source writes \(\bar{\vek u}\) for our position \(\bar{\vek p}\)). The notation with the matrix \(\mat J\) and the proof in five steps are not from the source.

Every term of (28.15) has its own meaning. The velocity of the point \(\vek o\) is the speed with which the floating frame moves as a whole. The turning term \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) is perpendicular to \(\bar{\vek p}\) (because \(\mat J\) turns a vector by a quarter turn) and of length \(\dot\theta\,|\bar{\vek p}|\), like a point on a wheel at the distance \(|\bar{\vek p}|\) from the axle. We call it the turning term because it comes from the turning of the frame. The elastic term \(\mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the velocity seen by an observer standing on the floating frame, carried into the fixed axes by \(\mat R\), and it vanishes when the bend does not change. The sum of these three arrows in figure 28.5 is the velocity we are after.

Example 28.9 Velocity of the tip of the SHABANA beam (hitrost konca nosilca iz SHABANA)

By example 5.2 (SHABANA, PDF pp. 209-210) the beam of figure 28.5 has \(\dot{\vek o} = (0{,}1;\ 1{,}0)\) m/s, \(\dot\theta = 5\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = (2;\ 3)\) m/s. At \(\theta = 30^\circ\) and \(\bar{\vek p}_{\mathrm{A}} = (0{,}501;\ 0{,}010)\) m we have \(\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}_{\mathrm{A}} = (-0{,}25916;\ 0{,}42888)\) m and \(\mat R\,\mat\Psi(1)\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = (0{,}2321;\ 3{,}5981)\) m/s. Equation (28.15) gives

\[\dot{\vek r}_{\mathrm{A}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}1 \\ 1{,}0 \end{bmatrix} + 5\begin{bmatrix} -0{,}25916 \\ 0{,}42888 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}2321 \\ 3{,}5981 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}9638 \\ 6{,}7425 \end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{m/s} .\]

The source gives \((-0{,}96380;\ 6{,}74235)\) m/s (PDF p. 210). The source computes with \(\cos 30^\circ = 0{,}8660\) (the matrix \(\mat A\mat S\) on PDF p. 210). With this value we get \((-0{,}96380;\ 6{,}74233)\) m/s, so the first component of the source exactly and the second to within two units in the fifth place. We also checked numerically that the time derivative of the position \(\vek r_{\mathrm{A}}(t)\) at these values is \((-0{,}96375;\ 6{,}74247)\) m/s (script num-03.py). The turning term has length \(2{,}5\) m/s, the elastic term \(3{,}6\) m/s because the large velocity \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) drives it, and the velocity of the point \(\vek o\) \(1{,}0\) m/s. None of the three may be left out.

In our link A the ratio is different, and that is the reason why the turning term must not be forgotten. Let \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\dot\theta = 2\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(\dot{\vek o} = \vek 0\) (the hub stays in its place), and let the first mode (section 13.6, \(\psi_1(L) = 1\)) show the end displaced by \(q_{\mathrm{d}} = 10\) mm, moving away at \(0{,}1\) m/s. The position of the end in the axes of the floating frame is \(\bar{\vek p} = (1;\ 0{,}010)\) m. In the axes of the floating frame the turning term has the components \(2\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p} = (-0{,}020;\ 2{,}000)\) m/s, the elastic term \((0;\ 0{,}100)\) m/s, together \((-0{,}020;\ 2{,}100)\) m/s, and in the fixed axes \((-1{,}067;\ 1{,}809)\) m/s. The turning contributes twenty times more than the bending. The first component \(-0{,}020\) m/s is the turning term acting on the sideways offset: \(\dot\theta\,\mat J\,(0;\ q_{\mathrm{d}}) = (-\dot\theta\,q_{\mathrm{d}};\ 0)\), which is \(2 \cdot 0{,}010\) m/s towards the hub.

What would happen if we made the mistake that is the easiest to imagine at first sight? The observer on the floating frame sees the point move with the velocity \(\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\). So we would conclude that the velocity in the fixed axes is simply \(\dot{\vek o} + \mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), which is equation (28.15) without the turning term. We try it on the rigid turning of the link about the point \(\vek o\), which stands still (\(\dot{\vek o} = \vek 0\)), with \(\dot\theta = 1\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). At the instant drawn the link makes the angle \(30^\circ\) with the fixed axis \(x\). The link does not bend, \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\), so the computation from the components alone gives zero everywhere: every point of the link would stand still although the link turns. The correct speed of a point is \(\dot\theta\) times the distance of the point from the axle (lemma 8.78), and points perpendicular to the link: for the end \(A\) of figure 28.5 this is \(|\dot\theta\,\bar{\vek p}_{\mathrm{A}}| = 0{,}5011\) m/s, which is \(|\bar{\vek p}_{\mathrm{A}}|\). The error is that the floating frame, in which the observer stands, turns together with the point, so \(\mat R\) is not a constant when we differentiate. Without the turning term, example 5.2 would lose the vector \((-1{,}296;\ 2{,}144)\) m/s of length \(2{,}505\) m/s, which is \(37\,\%\) of the true velocity \(6{,}811\) m/s.

We get the acceleration with the second derivative. In doing so every part gets its name and its reason.

Lemma 28.10 Acceleration of a point of a flexible link (pospešek točke podajnega člena)

Let \(\vek o\), \(\theta\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) be twice differentiable, the rest as in lemma 28.8. Then

\[\ddot{\vek r} = \ddot{\vek o} + \ddot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p} - \dot\theta^2\,\mat R\,\bar{\vek p} + 2\,\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} . \tag{28.16}\]
Proof

We differentiate (28.15) term by term, each by the product rule (lemma 1.81).

  1. The derivative of \(\dot{\vek o}\) is \(\ddot{\vek o}\).
  2. The derivative of the term \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) has three parts: \(\ddot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) from the derivative of the rate, \(\dot\theta\,\dot{\mat R}\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) from the derivative of the rotation and \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\dot{\bar{\vek p}}\) from the derivative of the vector.
  3. By lemma 28.8 \(\dot{\mat R} = \dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\), and \(\mat J^2 = -\mat I\) (the product \(\mat J\mat J\) of (28.13) is \(-\mat I\)). So the second part of step 2 is \(\dot\theta^2\,\mat R\,\mat J^2\,\bar{\vek p} = -\dot\theta^2\,\mat R\,\bar{\vek p}\).
  4. By lemma 28.8 \(\dot{\bar{\vek p}} = \mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), so the third part of step 2 equals \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  5. The derivative of the term \(\mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) is \(\dot{\mat R}\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  6. We add: the terms \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) of steps 4 and 5 are equal and give \(2\,\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\). This is (28.16).

Source: SHABANA (5.37)-(5.38) (PDF p. 209), where the same acceleration is written with the vector products \(\vek\omega \times (\vek\omega \times \vek u)\), \(\vek\alpha \times \vek u\) and \(2\,\vek\omega \times (\mat A\dot{\bar{\vek p}})\). The notation with the matrix \(\mat J\) and the proof are not from the source.

We name the terms of equation (28.16) and give their reasons on figure 28.7. It shows the deformed link with the origin \(\vek o\) and the end \(A\) in the same position as for the velocity, and the arrows are the parts of the acceleration of the end, drawn as a chain that starts at \(A\). The translational part \(\ddot{\vek o}\) is the acceleration of the point \(\vek o\) with which the floating frame moves as a whole, and it does not depend on the shape of the link. The tangential part \(\ddot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) is the turning with an accelerating angle: it is perpendicular to \(\bar{\vek p}\), so tangent to the circle that the point would describe about \(\vek o\) if the link were frozen, hence the name tangential, and of length \(\ddot\theta\,|\bar{\vek p}|\). The centripetal part \(-\dot\theta^2\,\mat R\,\bar{\vek p}\) points from the point \(A\) to \(\vek o\) along the line \(A\vek o\), which means it points to the centre (Latin "seeking the centre"), and has length \(\dot\theta^2\,|\bar{\vek p}|\), like a point on a wheel that needs an acceleration towards the axle to stay on its circle. This part exists also at uniform turning, when \(\ddot\theta = 0\).

The Coriolis part \(2\,\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the one that a rigid body does not have. It is made of two equal contributions, from steps 4 and 5 of the proof. The first arises because the vector \(\bar{\vek p}\) changes with the velocity \(\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), so the turning part \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\) of the velocity is no longer constant. The second arises because the elastic velocity \(\mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) turns together with the floating frame at the rate \(\dot\theta\). The factor \(2\) is therefore the sum of two equal contributions and not a convention. The name Coriolis part is the usual name of this term in the sources (SHABANA, PDF p. 209, SPONG). Why it is called so, the sources of the book do not say, and we write no history here. The part is zero if the hub stands still (\(\dot\theta = 0\)) or if the link does not bend (\(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\)), so a rigid-link argument does not notice it. It is perpendicular to the elastic velocity, because \(\mat J\) turns the vector by a quarter turn. The relative part \(\mat R\,\mat\Psi\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the acceleration seen by the observer on the floating frame. We call it relative because it is measured against the frame. The sum of all parts is \(\ddot{\vek r}\).

Example 28.11 Acceleration of the tip of the SHABANA beam (pospešek konca nosilca iz SHABANA)

Example 5.2 (PDF pp. 209-211) with \(\dot{\vek o}\) and \(\dot\theta\) as above, \(\ddot{\vek o} = (2;\ 0)\) m/s\(^2\), \(\ddot\theta = 0\) and \(\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = (10;\ 20)\) m/s\(^2\). The parts of equation (28.16) in m/s\(^2\) are: translational \((2;\ 0)\), tangential \((0;\ 0)\), centripetal \((-10{,}722;\ -6{,}479)\), Coriolis \((-35{,}981;\ 2{,}321)\), relative \((-1{,}340;\ 22{,}321)\). The sum is \((-46{,}042;\ 18{,}162)\) m/s\(^2\) and the source gives \((-46{,}042;\ 18{,}161)\) (PDF p. 211). The source separates also the sum of the translational and relative parts, \((0{,}66;\ 22{,}32)\), and the rest \((-46{,}702;\ -4{,}159)\), which is the sum of the centripetal and Coriolis parts, in our computation \((-46{,}703;\ -4{,}158)\). The numerical second derivative of \(\vek r_{\mathrm{A}}(t)\) at these values gives the same result. The Coriolis part, \(36{,}1\) m/s\(^2\), is here the largest of all, and for a rigid link we would leave it out.

In link A the shares are as follows. At \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\dot\theta = 2\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\), \(\ddot\theta = 10\ \mathrm{s}^{-2}\) (the hub acceleration of section 28.1), \(q_{\mathrm{d}} = 10\) mm, \(\dot q_{\mathrm{d}} = 0{,}1\) m/s and \(\ddot q_{\mathrm{d}} = 5\) m/s\(^2\), the components of the acceleration of the end in the axes of the floating frame, in m/s\(^2\), are: tangential \((-0{,}1;\ 10{,}0)\), centripetal \((-4{,}0;\ -0{,}04)\), Coriolis \((-0{,}4;\ 0)\), relative \((0;\ 5{,}0)\), together \((-4{,}5;\ 14{,}96)\). The Coriolis part points along the axis of the link towards the hub and is \(8\,\%\) of the relative part. Because it points along the axis, it would couple the transverse motion with an axial one, which the inextensible axis of link A does not know. We will leave this coupling out in the section on constant spin and name it there.

What remains is the question of how accurate the transverse field \(\bar{\vek u} = (0;\ \psi(x)\,q_{\mathrm{d}})\) is for link A. Its axis does not lengthen in bending, so it should shorten at the end: by steps 1 to 3 of the proof of lemma 8.133, which do not use the end values of \(v\), the shortening of the axis is approximately \(\tfrac12\int_0^\ell v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (an integral over the projection of the axis, \(\ell\) is its length) with a relative error of at most \(v'^2_{\max}/4\). For the end displaced by \(10\) mm in the first mode the slope of the end is \(0{,}0138\), the shortening \(0{,}058\) mm (that is \(5{,}8 \cdot 10^{-5}\,L\)) and the error of the estimate at most \(5 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The shortening changes the position of the end by \(0{,}058\) mm and the centripetal part \(4{,}0\) m/s\(^2\) by \(2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) m/s\(^2\), so in the kinematics it does not count. In the elastic energy under an axial force it does count: the work of the axial force \(\tfrac N2\int v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) is quadratic in \(q_{\mathrm{d}}\), of the same order as the bending energy. The section on constant spin deals with this.

We have closed the kinematics: the velocity (28.15) and the acceleration (28.16) of every point are expressed by the coordinates \(\vek o\), \(\theta\), \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and their derivatives. In the next section we square the velocity (28.15) and integrate over the link to get the kinetic energy and the mass matrix of the link. The term \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\,\mat J\,\bar{\vek p}\), which the wrong computation overlooked, will there tie the turning of the hub to the bending coordinates.

28.4 The mass matrix of the link

In section 28.3 we wrote the velocity of every point of the link, \(\dot{\vek r} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot\theta\,\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p} + \mat R\mat\Psi\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) (lemma 28.8). Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88), however, need the kinetic energy as a function of the coordinates and their derivatives on the way to the equations of motion. For a system of rigid bodies it is the quadratic form \(\tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}\) with a mass matrix (theorem 8.86). What matrix do we get for a link that both turns and bends? A comparison with the rigid body (theorem 8.82) predicts two things: the mass of the link does not change, but its inertia changes with the bend, and the turning of the frame is coupled to the elastic coordinates.

The model is the same as in the previous sections. We write it once more with its idealizations, because this section uses them.

  1. The link is a straight bar with the axis \(\bar x \in [0, L]\) in the undeformed state. Its mass is distributed along the axis with the mass per unit length \(\mu(\bar x) = \rho A\), which is continuous and positive (we simply write \(\mu\) and write the variable as \(x\)). We neglect the rotary inertia of the cross-sections. By lemma 13.27 the two parts of the kinetic energy are \(\tfrac12\int\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (the motion of the cross-sections) and \(\tfrac12\int\rho I\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (their turning). In a vibration in a mode with the shape \(\varphi(x)\) the ratio of the second to the first is \(\dfrac{I}{A}\,\dfrac{\int\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{h^2}{12}\,\dfrac{\int\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x}\), where \(h\) is the section height in the plane of motion. For the steel strip of example A (\(h = 6\) mm, \(L = 1\) m) the quotient of the integrals is \(4{,}648/L^2\) at the first mode of the cantilever and \(142{,}9/L^2\) at the fourth, and the ratio is \(1{,}4\cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(4{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\). So the idealization is good for low modes.
  2. The position of a point of the axis is \(\vek r = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) by definition 28.4 in the floating frame (plavajoči koordinatni sistem, definition 28.3), where \(\bar{\vek r}_0 = (x, 0)\) is the position of the point at \(x\) in the undeformed state, and the matrix \(\mat\Psi(x)\) with \(2\) rows and \(n\) columns is the collection of shapes, known from the trial functions of the Ritz method (definition 6.32). The coordinates of the link are therefore \(\vek o\) (two numbers), \(\theta\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (\(n\) numbers), \(n + 3\) in all. The subscript \(d\) stands for deformation, because \(f\) is used in chapter 7 for the free unknowns.
  3. The matrix \(\mat J = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) is the quarter turn of section 28.3. It is not a moment of inertia: we write the moments of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\) and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\).

For a general planar link \(\mat\Psi\) has the rows \(\mat\Psi_1\) (displacements along the axis of the frame) and \(\mat\Psi_2\) (displacements perpendicular to the axis), each with \(n\) functions. For an Euler-Bernoulli link with an inextensible axis (definition 5.14) we have \(\mat\Psi_1 = \vek 0\) and \(\mat\Psi_2 = \vek\psi^\T\), where \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) are continuous functions on \([0, L]\) and the displacement of the axis is \(v(x) = \vek\psi(x)^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). The axis stays along the frame at its own \(x\). This is an idealization: the bent axis is longer than \(L\) by \(\int_0^L\big(\sqrt{1 + v'^2} - 1\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is at most \(\tfrac12\int_0^L v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) by the inequality \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} - 1 \le p^2/2\) (step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.133). For a slope \(|v'| \le 0{,}03\) this is no more than \(4{,}5\cdot 10^{-4}\,L\). The correction is of second order and this section does not need it, but at fast spin it becomes important.

We build figure 28.8 as one would draw it on a board. First the axes of the frame: \(\bar x\) along the link and \(\bar y\) perpendicular to it, with the origin at the hub. On them we place the undeformed axis, the dashed line of length \(L\). The link is clamped in the hub, so the shape is clamped at \(x = 0\) too: \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\). These are the reference conditions of the clamped frame (definition 28.5). The bent link is the graph of the function \(v(x)\). We choose the point at \(x\) to see what velocity is assigned to it. The frame turns with the angular velocity \(\dot\theta\), so the point at the position vector \(\bar{\vek p}\) from the hub moves with the velocity \(\dot\theta\,\mat J\bar{\vek p}\), perpendicular to \(\bar{\vek p}\) (every point of a rigid body circles about the centre of rotation, section 28.3). This is the orange arrow, in the frame \((-\dot\theta\,v,\ \dot\theta\,x)\), and it is almost perpendicular to the axis. At the same time the point moves relative to the frame because of the bend: the blue arrow \(\psi(x)\,\dot q\) is perpendicular to the axis. Both velocities point the same way, so their sum is longer than either alone, and the square of the length of the sum is not the sum of the squares. The difference is the mixed product \(2\,\dot\theta\,x\,\psi(x)\,\dot q\). The sum of this mixed product over the points of the link is the coupling of turning and bending, which a rigid body does not have.

The square of the length of the velocity has six terms. With the notation \(\bar{\vek p} = \bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) they are

\[|\dot{\vek r}|^2 = |\dot{\vek o}|^2 + \dot\theta^2\,|\bar{\vek p}|^2 + |\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}|^2 + 2\,\dot\theta\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p} + 2\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} - 2\,\dot\theta\,\bar{\vek p}^\T\mat J\,\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} . \tag{28.17}\]

Each term is a product of velocities of coordinates, which do not depend on \(x\), and a function of \(x\) that we must integrate along the link with the weight \(\mu\). The right half of figure 28.8 shows three such functions for the shape \(\psi\) on the axis \(\xi = x/L\) from \(0\) to \(1\): \(x^2\) from the term with \(\dot\theta^2\), \(x\,\psi\) from the mixed term and \(\psi^2\) from the term with \(\dot q^2\). The area under the orange curve is the integral of the mixed term. All three areas are numbers that we compute once, because they do not depend on the coordinates. We collect all such integrals and name them.

Definition 28.12 Inertia shape integrals (vztrajnostni integrali oblike)

Let the link have the mass per unit length \(\mu(x) > 0\) on \([0, L]\), the undeformed position of the point \(\bar{\vek r}_0(x) = (x, 0)\) and the shape \(\mat\Psi(x)\), a matrix with two rows and \(n\) columns whose entries are continuous functions. The inertia shape integrals of the link are

\[\begin{aligned} m &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mathrm{d}x , & \vek s_0 &= \int_0^L \mu\,\bar{\vek r}_0\,\mathrm{d}x = (s, 0) , & J_{\mathrm{link}} &= \int_0^L \mu\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \\ \mat S &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mat\Psi\,\mathrm{d}x , & \vek c &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mat\Psi^\T\bar{\vek r}_0\,\mathrm{d}x , & \vek b &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mat\Psi^\T\mat J\,\bar{\vek r}_0\,\mathrm{d}x , \\ \mat Z &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mat\Psi^\T\mat J\mat\Psi\,\mathrm{d}x , & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} &= \int_0^L \mu\,\mat\Psi^\T\mat\Psi\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned} \tag{28.18}\]

where \(s = \int_0^L\mu\,x\,\mathrm{d}x\).
