The numbers are \(m\) (unit kg), \(s\) (kg m) and \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\) (kg m\(^2\)), \(\vek s_0\) is a vector with two components, \(\mat S\) is a \(2 \times n\) matrix, \(\vek c\) and \(\vek b\) are columns with \(n\) entries, \(\mat Z\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix (antisymmetric, \(\mat Z^\T = -\mat Z\), because \(\mat J^\T = -\mat J\)) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is a symmetric \(n \times n\) matrix. For a link with a transverse shape (\(\mat\Psi_1 = \vek 0\), \(\mat\Psi_2 = \vek\psi^\T\)) we have \(\vek c = \vek 0\), \(\mat Z = \mat 0\), the first row of \(\mat S\) is zero and the second is \(\int\mu\,\vek\psi^\T\mathrm{d}x\), and

\[\vek b = \int_0^L \mu\,x\,\vek\psi\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int_0^L \mu\,\vek\psi\vek\psi^\T\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{28.19}\]

Source: SHABANA (5.94) and (5.95) (PDF p. 219): the same set of integrals for a planar body, written with volume integrals. The notation with the right-angle matrix \(\mat J\) and with integrals along the link is ours, because the link has its mass on the axis.

The names have reasons. The integrals are called inertia integrals because they measure inertia: mass, moment of mass and moment of inertia. They are called shape integrals because besides the distribution of mass they contain the shape \(\mat\Psi\), so we cannot compute them until the shape is chosen. The vector \(\vek s_0\) is the moment of mass (moment mase): mass multiplied by the lever arm and summed along the link, just as the moment of a force is force times lever arm. The quantity \(s/m\) is the position of the centre of mass of the link on the axis, because the centre of mass is the average of the position with the weight of mass. The column \(\vek b\) tells how strongly the turning of the frame "drives" each shape: \(\mat J\,\bar{\vek r}_0 = (0, x)\) is the direction and size of the velocity that turning with unit angular velocity gives, and \(\mat\Psi^\T\) maps it onto each shape, which for a transverse shape is the orange integrand in figure 28.8. All three curves have the value \(1\) at \(\xi = 1\), because \(\psi(L) = 1\).

For the steel strip of example A (from section 28.1: \(L = 1\) m, \(\mu = 1{,}872\) kg/m) and the static shape \(\psi = (3\xi^2 - \xi^3)/2\), which is the deflection curve of a cantilever under a force at the free end, normalized to a unit end displacement (theorem 5.56), we have \(m = 1{,}872\) kg, \(s = 0{,}9360\) kg m, \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}6240\) kg m\(^2\), \(\vek b = \mu L^2\cdot 0{,}275 = 0{,}5148\) kg m, \(M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \mu L\cdot 0{,}2357 = 0{,}4413\) kg and \(\int\mu\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}7020\) kg. The unit of \(\vek b\) is kg m, because \(\psi\) has no unit and is multiplied by the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{d}}\) in metres.

Now we write the kinetic energy with them.

Theorem 28.13 Kinetic energy of a flexible link (kinetična energija člena)

Let the link be as in definition 28.12 with the coordinates \(\vek x = (\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) and let \(\mat R = \mat R(\theta)\). Then the kinetic energy of the link is \(T = \tfrac12\int_0^L \mu\,|\dot{\vek r}|^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek x}^\T\mat M(\theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\,\dot{\vek x}\) with the mass matrix (masna matrika)

\[\mat M = \begin{bmatrix} m\,\mat I & \mat R\mat J\,(\vek s_0 + \mat S\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}) & \mat R\mat S \\ \ast & m_{\theta\theta} & \vek b^\T - \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat Z \\ \ast & \ast & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{bmatrix} , \qquad m_{\theta\theta} = J_{\mathrm{link}} + 2\,\vek c^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} , \tag{28.20}\]

where the asterisks mean the transposed entries above the diagonal, so \(\mat M\) is symmetric. The matrix depends on \(\theta\) only in the first row of blocks, and on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) only in the first two.

Proof

We have to show that \(T\) is a quadratic form in the velocities of the coordinates with the coefficients of definition 28.12. We expand the square of the velocity and write every product with velocities that do not depend on \(x\).

  1. The velocity of the point is \(\dot{\vek r} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot\theta\,\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p} + \mat R\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) with \(\bar{\vek p} = \bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (lemma 28.8).
  2. The matrix satisfies \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\), because \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) (lemma 8.10), and \(\mat J^\T\mat J = \mat I\) by computation: \(\mat J^\T\mat J = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} = \mat I\). Hence \(|\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p}|^2 = |\bar{\vek p}|^2\) and \((\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p})^\T\mat R\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \bar{\vek p}^\T\mat J^\T\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = -\bar{\vek p}^\T\mat J\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), since \(\mat J^\T = -\mat J\). The square of the sum of three vectors with these equalities is (28.17).
  3. We multiply by \(\tfrac12\mu\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). The velocities \(\dot{\vek o}\), \(\dot\theta\), \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) and the coordinates \(\theta\), \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) do not depend on \(x\), so by linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39) we take them out. The term \(|\dot{\vek o}|^2\) gives \(\tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek o}|^2\), the term \(|\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}|^2 = \dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat\Psi^\T\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) gives \(\tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  4. The two mixed terms with \(\dot{\vek o}\): \(\dot\theta\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat J\int\mu\,\bar{\vek p}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\int\mu\,\mat\Psi\,\mathrm{d}x\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\). The first integral is \(\int\mu\,(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek s_0 + \mat S\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), the second is \(\mat S\). These are the first row of blocks in (28.20).
  5. The term with \(\dot\theta^2\): \(\tfrac12\dot\theta^2\int\mu\,|\bar{\vek p}|^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(|\bar{\vek p}|^2 = |\bar{\vek r}_0|^2 + 2\,\bar{\vek r}_0^\T\mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat\Psi^\T\mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). After integration this is \(\tfrac12\dot\theta^2\,m_{\theta\theta}\) with \(\int\mu\,|\bar{\vek r}_0|^2 = J_{\mathrm{link}}\) and \(\int\mu\,\bar{\vek r}_0^\T\mat\Psi = \vek c^\T\).
  6. The term with \(\dot\theta\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\): \(-\dot\theta\int\mu\,\bar{\vek p}^\T\mat J\mat\Psi\,\mathrm{d}x\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(\bar{\vek p}^\T\mat J\mat\Psi = \bar{\vek r}_0^\T\mat J\mat\Psi + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat\Psi^\T\mat J\mat\Psi\). Transposition (lemma 1.101) gives \(\bar{\vek r}_0^\T\mat J\mat\Psi = -(\mat\Psi^\T\mat J\bar{\vek r}_0)^\T\), because \(\mat J^\T = -\mat J\). After integration the term is \(\dot\theta\,(\vek b^\T - \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat Z)\,\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  7. The sum of steps 3 to 6 is a quadratic form in \(\dot{\vek x}\) with the blocks stated in (28.20), and with the same blocks below the diagonal if the mixed term \(\dot{\vek x}_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{ij}}\dot{\vek x}_{\mathrm{j}} + \dot{\vek x}_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{ij}}^\T\dot{\vek x}_{\mathrm{i}}\) is split into two equal halves. The symmetric matrix of a quadratic form is determined uniquely.

Source: SHABANA (5.39)-(5.47) (PDF pp. 211-213) for the definition and the block structure of the mass matrix of a body, (5.78)-(5.93) (PDF pp. 217-219) for the planar case. The notation with integrals along the link and with the quarter turn \(\mat J\), and the proof, are ours.

The matrix has three groups of blocks, and figure 28.9 separates them. The grid lines divide the matrix into blocks by the coordinates \(\vek o\), \(\theta\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). The two blue blocks \(m\,\mat I\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) are constant. The first is the mass of the link, the same as for a rigid body, the second is the matrix of masses of all the shapes, as a beam has it without any motion of the frame. The orange blocks, \(m_{\theta\theta}\) and the row \(\vek b^\T - \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat Z\), depend only on the elastic coordinates. The grey blocks in the first row of blocks depend on \(\theta\) too, because \(\mat R\) turns the contribution of the frame into the axes of the world. The lower block is the transpose of the upper one, and the headers show which velocities each column multiplies.

We test the theorem on an example of the book that we can compare with its numbers. Example 5.3 in SHABANA (PDF pp. 220 to 222) has a link with \(m = 1{,}236\) kg, \(l = 0{,}5\) m and the shape \(\mat\Psi = \begin{bmatrix}\xi & 0\\ 0 & 3\xi^2 - 2\xi^3\end{bmatrix}\) (\(\xi = x/l\)), at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = (0{,}001,\ 0{,}01)\). The inertia integrals from the definition are \(\vek s_0 = (0{,}309,\ 0)\) kg m, \(\mat S = 0{,}618\,\mat I\) kg, \(\vek c = (0{,}206,\ 0)\), \(\vek b = (0,\ 0{,}2163)\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \operatorname{diag}(0{,}412,\ 0{,}4591)\) kg. By (28.20) the blocks are \(\mat R\mat J(\vek s_0 + \mat S\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}) = (-0{,}1602,\ 0{,}2650)\) and \(\mat R\mat S = \begin{bmatrix}0{,}5352 & -0{,}309\\ 0{,}309 & 0{,}5352\end{bmatrix}\), which agrees in all digits with the example on PDF p. 222. The lower row of blocks \(\vek b^\T - \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat Z = (-0{,}004326,\ 0{,}2167)\) agrees with the printed \(-4{,}326\cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(0{,}2167\). For \(m_{\theta\theta}\) we get \(0{,}103 + 4{,}12\cdot 10^{-4} + 4{,}63\cdot 10^{-5} = 0{,}1035\) kg m\(^2\), and the book prints \(0{,}1031\). The difference is in the book itself: its term \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is \(2{,}316\cdot 10^{-5}\), half of the correct \(4{,}63\cdot 10^{-5}\), because in the computation the matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is multiplied by \(\tfrac12\) (PDF p. 222), in contrast to (5.88) on PDF p. 219 and to its matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(0{,}412,\ 0{,}4591)\) on the same page. The sum of the printed terms (\(0{,}103 + 4{,}12\cdot 10^{-4} + 2{,}3\cdot 10^{-5} = 0{,}1034\)) is not the printed value either. We also checked the theorem with an independent computation: the kinetic energy by numerical integration of \(\tfrac12\int\mu|\dot{\vek r}|^2\mathrm{d}x\) at random velocities is \(0{,}88455359\) J and equals \(\tfrac12\,\dot{\vek x}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek x}\) to the eighth digit.

At every test we ask what the theorem returns in a known case. The known case is the rigid link.

Corollary 28.14 Rigid link (togi člen)

Let \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) and \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). Then the kinetic energy of the link from theorem 28.13 is

\[T = \tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek o}|^2 + \dot\theta\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat J\,\vek s_0 + \tfrac12\,J_{\mathrm{link}}\,\dot\theta^2 , \tag{28.21}\]

and it equals \(\tfrac12\,m\,|\vek v_{\mathrm{G}}|^2 + \tfrac12\,J_{\mathrm{G}}\,\dot\theta^2\) for a rigid bar (theorem 8.82) with the centre of mass \(G\) at \(\vek o + \mat R\,\vek s_0/m\) and \(J_{\mathrm{G}} = J_{\mathrm{link}} - s^2/m\).

Proof

We have to show that (28.21) equals theorem 8.82. At \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) the matrix (28.20) becomes a matrix with three rows of blocks without the elastic ones.

  1. Theorem 28.13 with \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) gives \(T = \tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek o}|^2 + \dot\theta\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat J\vek s_0 + \tfrac12\,m_{\theta\theta}\dot\theta^2\) with \(m_{\theta\theta} = J_{\mathrm{link}}\). This is (28.21).
  2. The centre of mass is at \(\vek r_{\mathrm{G}} = \vek o + \mat R\vek s_0/m\) (the position of a point with the mass \(m\) whose moment of mass is \(\vek s_0\)). Its velocity is \(\dot{\vek r}_{\mathrm{G}} = \dot{\vek o} + \dot\theta\,\mat R\mat J\vek s_0/m\) (the time derivative with lemma 28.8 at \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\)).
  3. The square: \(\tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek r}_{\mathrm{G}}|^2 = \tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek o}|^2 + \dot\theta\,\dot{\vek o}^\T\mat R\mat J\vek s_0 + \tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2\,|\vek s_0|^2/m\), because \(|\mat R\mat J\vek s_0| = |\vek s_0|\) (step 2 of the previous proof).
  4. Steiner's theorem (lemma 8.83) gives \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = J_{\mathrm{G}} + m\,(s/m)^2\), so \(\tfrac12\,J_{\mathrm{link}}\,\dot\theta^2 = \tfrac12\,J_{\mathrm{G}}\,\dot\theta^2 + \tfrac12\,\dot\theta^2\,s^2/m\). With step 2, (28.21) equals \(\tfrac12\,m\,|\dot{\vek r}_{\mathrm{G}}|^2 + \tfrac12\,J_{\mathrm{G}}\,\dot\theta^2\).

Source: SHABANA (5.48)-(5.50) (PDF p. 213) for the rigid case. The proof is not from the source.

For example A: \(J_{\mathrm{G}} = m L^2/12 = 0{,}1560\) kg m\(^2\), \(s^2/m = 0{,}4680\) and the sum \(0{,}6240 = J_{\mathrm{link}}\), which is also the moment of inertia of a bar about its end. The more important case is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} \ne \vek 0\), and the next lemma treats it.

Lemma 28.15 Inertia of a link with a transverse shape (vztrajnost člena s prečno obliko)

Let the link have a transverse shape \(\mat\Psi = \begin{bmatrix}\vek 0\\ \vek\psi^\T\end{bmatrix}\) with linearly independent functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) (definition 6.22) and let \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) be arbitrary. Then in (28.20) we have \(\vek c = \vek 0\), \(\mat Z = \mat 0\), the second row of the matrix \(\mat S\) is \(\vek\sigma^\T\) with the column \(\vek\sigma = \int_0^L\mu\,\vek\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\) (the first row is zero), and

\[m_{\theta\theta} = J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = J_{\mathrm{link}} + \int_0^L \mu\,v^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ \ge\ J_{\mathrm{link}} , \qquad \vek b^\T - \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat Z = \vek b^\T . \tag{28.22}\]

The moment of inertia of the link about the hub is therefore larger than for a rigid link, and the difference is quadratic in the displacement. The column \(\vek b\) does not depend on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), and

\[\vek b^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\,\vek b \ \le\ J_{\mathrm{link}} , \tag{28.23}\]

with equality only if \(x = \vek a^\T\vek\psi(x)\) for some column \(\vek a\), that is, if the function \(x\) is a linear combination of the shapes.

Proof

We have to show the forms of the blocks and the inequality, which is the Cauchy-Schwarz one. We compute the integrals with the rows \(\mat\Psi_1 = \vek 0\) and \(\mat\Psi_2 = \vek\psi^\T\).

  1. With \(\mat\Psi_1 = \vek 0\) we have \(\vek c = \int\mu\,\mat\Psi^\T\bar{\vek r}_0\,\mathrm{d}x = \int\mu\,x\,\mat\Psi_1^\T\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek 0\) and \(\mat J\mat\Psi = \begin{bmatrix}-\mat\Psi_2\\ \mat\Psi_1\end{bmatrix}\), so \(\mat\Psi^\T\mat J\mat\Psi = -\mat\Psi_1^\T\mat\Psi_2 + \mat\Psi_2^\T\mat\Psi_1 = \mat 0\). Hence \(\mat Z = \mat 0\) and from (28.20) follow \(m_{\theta\theta}\) and the row \(\vek b^\T\) of (28.22). For \(\vek b\) we have \(\mat J\bar{\vek r}_0 = (0, x)\), so \(\vek b = \int\mu\,x\,\vek\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\) as in (28.19).
  2. With \(v = \vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) we have \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \int\mu\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\vek\psi\vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int\mu\,v^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\), since \(\mu > 0\) (lemma 3.39, item 4). This is (28.22).
  3. Let \(\vek a\) be an arbitrary column and \(f = x\), \(g = \vek\psi^\T\vek a\). The inner product \((f, g) = \int\mu\,f\,g\,\mathrm{d}x\) has the properties of lemma 6.19, so \((\vek a^\T\vek b)^2 = (f, g)^2 \le (f, f)\,(g, g) = J_{\mathrm{link}}\,\vek a^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek a\).
  4. By step 2 and the independence of the functions, the matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite: \(\vek a^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek a = \int\mu\,(\vek\psi^\T\vek a)^2 > 0\) for \(\vek a \ne \vek 0\), because otherwise the function \(\vek\psi^\T\vek a\) would be zero everywhere (as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 6.7), which independence excludes. So \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\) exists and \(\vek a = \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b\) is admissible. Step 3 gives \((\vek b^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b)^2 \le J_{\mathrm{link}}\,\vek b^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b\), and after dividing by \(\vek b^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b > 0\) (for \(\vek b \ne \vek 0\)) we get (28.23). Equality holds in step 3 only if \(f\) is a multiple of \(g\).

Source: SHABANA (5.84)-(5.89) (PDF pp. 218-219) for \(m_{\theta\theta}\) as a sum of three terms. The inequality (28.23) and its proof are not from the source.

For example A and the static shape, \(m_{\theta\theta} = 0{,}6240 + 0{,}4413\,q^2\) kg m\(^2\). At an end displacement \(q = 10\) mm the increase is \(4{,}4\cdot 10^{-5}\) kg m\(^2\), which is \(7{,}1\cdot 10^{-5}\) of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\), and at \(100\) mm it is \(7{,}1\cdot 10^{-3}\). For the first mode of the cantilever of example A (theorem 13.37), which is a different shape, this share at \(10\) mm is \(7{,}5\cdot 10^{-5}\). It is small enough that in dynamics staying at small displacements the moment of inertia of the link may be taken as constant, but only under the condition that the end displacement stays below about \(10\) % of the length, where the increase is below \(1\) %. The coupling \(\vek b\), however, is not small: \(b/\sqrt{J_{\mathrm{link}}M_{\mathrm{dd}}} = 0{,}981\), close to the upper bound \(1\) that inequality (28.23) gives for one shape. The rotation of the hub therefore strongly "drives" the elastic coordinate, and this is the main effect in the equations of motion. Here \(J_{\mathrm{link}} - b^2/M_{\mathrm{dd}} = 0{,}0234\) kg m\(^2\) (\(3{,}8\) % of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\)), the quantity that the bound (28.23) leaves.

Now we can check whether the matrix is positive definite. We expect it, because a moving mass has positive kinetic energy unless each of its points is at rest. The question is whether the rest of all points of the link really implies the rest of all coordinates, and the answer depends on the reference conditions.

Theorem 28.16 Positive definiteness of the mass matrix of a link (pozitivna definitnost masne matrike člena)

Let the link have a transverse shape with continuous functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'\) that are linearly independent, and let them satisfy the reference conditions of the clamped frame \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\) (definition 28.5). Then the mass matrix \(\mat M(\theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) of theorem 28.13 is positive definite (definition 6.27) for every \(\theta\) and every \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\).

Proof

We have to show that zero kinetic energy implies that all velocities of coordinates are zero. Let \(\dot{\vek x} = (\dot{\vek o}, \dot\theta, \dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}})\) and \(\dot{\vek x}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek x} = 0\).

  1. The matrix is symmetric (theorem 28.13) and \(\dot{\vek x}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek x} = \int_0^L\mu\,|\dot{\vek r}|^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\). At the value zero the continuous non-negative function \(\mu\,|\dot{\vek r}|^2\) is zero everywhere, otherwise its integral over a neighbourhood of a point where it is positive would have a positive lower bound (as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 6.7). Hence \(\dot{\vek r}(x) = \vek 0\) for every \(x\).
  2. At \(x = 0\) we have \(\bar{\vek p}(0) = (0, v(0)) = \vek 0\) and \(\mat\Psi(0) = \mat 0\), so \(\dot{\vek r}(0) = \dot{\vek o}\) (lemma 28.8). Hence \(\dot{\vek o} = \vek 0\).
  3. What remains is \(\dot\theta\,\mat R\mat J\bar{\vek p} + \mat R\mat\Psi\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). We multiply by \(\mat R^\T\) and insert \(\bar{\vek p} = (x, v)\), \(\mat J\bar{\vek p} = (-v, x)\): the second component is \(\dot\theta\,x + \vek\psi(x)^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L]\).
  4. We differentiate with respect to \(x\) at \(x = 0\): \(\dot\theta + \vek\psi'(0)^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \dot\theta = 0\), because \(\vek\psi'(0) = \vek 0\).
  5. Now \(\vek\psi(x)^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\) everywhere, and by linear independence (definition 6.22) \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). Hence \(\dot{\vek x} = \vek 0\).

Source: SHABANA section 6.2 (PDF pp. 286-287) for the reference conditions in finite elements, but the positive definiteness of the mass matrix is not proved in the source. The proof is not from the source.

Each of the conditions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\) is used in the proof in one step: the first in step 2 (the hub is a point of the frame), the second in step 4 (the direction of the axis at the hub is the direction of the frame). What happens if we leave one out? With \(\psi(0) = 0\) without the other condition the proof stops at step 4, and a case of this kind follows.

Let us first draw what this shape does. At \(\psi = x/L\) the link is a straight line from the hub to the point \((L, q)\), so the elastic displacement \(q\) is a displacement of the end perpendicular to the axis of the frame. We get nearly the same position in another way: we turn the frame by the angle \(\arctan(q/L)\) so that its axis lies in the direction of the left link, and there is no elastic displacement. Such a link has the same direction, but its length is \(L\), while the left one is \(L\sqrt{1 + q^2/L^2}\) long. At \(q = 0{,}01\) m the two lengths differ by \(5{,}0\cdot 10^{-5}\,L\), so we write the sign \(\approx\) between the two positions and not an equals sign. Two coordinates, \(\theta\) and \(q\), therefore describe the same position of the body to first order in \(q/L\). An exact pair, \((\theta, q)\) and \((\theta + 2\beta, -q)\) with \(\tan\beta = q/L\), we found in section 28.2.1. Because the turn of the frame and the elastic displacement move the points of the link in the same way to first order, the matrix for this case is bad.

Lemma 28.17 A shape without the slope condition: a singular mass matrix (oblika brez pogoja za naklon)

Let \(n = 1\), \(\psi = x/L\) and \(\mu\) constant, so that \(\psi(0) = 0\) but \(\psi'(0) = 1/L \ne 0\). Then \(\vek b = J_{\mathrm{link}}/L\) and \(M_{\mathrm{dd}} = J_{\mathrm{link}}/L^2\), the block of the mass matrix for the coordinates \((\theta, q)\) is

\[\begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{link}}\,(1 + q^2/L^2) & J_{\mathrm{link}}/L \\ J_{\mathrm{link}}/L & J_{\mathrm{link}}/L^2 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \det = \frac{J_{\mathrm{link}}^2\,q^2}{L^4} . \tag{28.24}\]

At \(q = 0\) the matrix is singular with the null vector \((\dot\theta, \dot q) = (1, -L)\), and for example A (\(J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}6240\) kg m\(^2\), \(L = 1\) m) its determinant at \(q = 0{,}01\) m equals \(3{,}9\cdot 10^{-5}\) and the smallest eigenvalue \(3{,}1\cdot 10^{-5}\) kg m\(^2\) against the largest \(1{,}248\) kg m\(^2\).

Proof

We have to show the blocks, the determinant and the null vector and connect them with the motion.

  1. The integrals: \(\vek b = \int\mu\,x\,(x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = J_{\mathrm{link}}/L\) and \(M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int\mu\,(x/L)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = J_{\mathrm{link}}/L^2\) (definition 28.12). By lemma 28.15 \(m_{\theta\theta} = J_{\mathrm{link}} + q^2M_{\mathrm{dd}}\). This is the matrix in (28.24).
  2. The determinant: \(J_{\mathrm{link}}(1 + q^2/L^2)\,J_{\mathrm{link}}/L^2 - J_{\mathrm{link}}^2/L^2 = J_{\mathrm{link}}^2\,q^2/L^4\).
  3. At \(q = 0\) the matrix is \(\tfrac{J_{\mathrm{link}}}{L^2}\begin{bmatrix}L^2 & L\\ L & 1\end{bmatrix}\) and multiplying by \((1, -L)\) gives \(\tfrac{J_{\mathrm{link}}}{L^2}\,(L^2 - L^2,\ L - L) = (0, 0)\).
  4. Physical meaning: at \(q = 0\) the velocity of the point is \(\dot{\vek r} = \mat R\,(\dot\theta\,\mat J\bar{\vek r}_0 + \psi\,\dot q\,\vek e_2) = \mat R\,x\,(\dot\theta + \dot q/L)\,\vek e_2\) (lemma 28.8), and it is zero for every \(x\) at \(\dot q = -L\,\dot\theta\).
  5. For example A: \(J_{\mathrm{link}}^2q^2/L^4 = 0{,}6240^2\cdot 10^{-4} = 3{,}9\cdot 10^{-5}\), the trace is \(1{,}248\) kg m\(^2\), so the smallest eigenvalue is approximately \(\det/\mathrm{trace} = 3{,}1\cdot 10^{-5}\) kg m\(^2\).

Source: Not from the source. SHABANA PDF pp. 280-281 mentions that the element field contains rigid motion, and p. 286 the conditions that remove it.

At \(q = 0\) the matrix is singular and at \(q = 10\) mm nearly singular: the ratio of the smallest and the largest eigenvalue is \(2{,}5\cdot 10^{-5}\), so a computation with eight digits would lose five digits. At the same time the elastic energy is zero, because \(\int EI\,\psi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for a straight shape (energy of a beam, lemma 5.76), and the coordinate \(q\) has no restoring force. This is one more reason why the reference conditions require \(\psi'(0) = 0\) as well: with it \(\theta\) and \(q\) are separated, which is the difference between rigid and elastic motion. Theorem 28.16 is therefore exactly as strong as we need, and not weaker.

What have we shown? The kinetic energy of the link is a quadratic form in the velocities of the coordinates \((\dot{\vek o}, \dot\theta, \dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}})\) (theorem 28.13), whose coefficients are eight integrals along the link, computed once (definition 28.12). For a rigid link it becomes the energy of a rigid body (corollary 28.14), and for a transverse shape it has a moment of inertia that grows quadratically with the bend and a coupling \(\vek b\) that does not depend on the bend (lemma 28.15). The matrix is positive definite if the shapes satisfy the reference conditions (theorem 28.16) and singular if a shape contains a rigid turn (lemma 28.17). In the next section we add the elastic energy and the generalized forces, and the matrix obtained enters Lagrange's equations.

28.5 Forces on the link

In section 28.6 the motion of the link will come from Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88) for each coordinate \((\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\). Their left side, the kinetic energy, was built in section 28.4. The right side is the generalized forces (definition 8.50). The name is so because such a force is not always a force in newtons: to a coordinate that is an angle belongs a moment in newton metres, and the coordinate itself is not always a length. Such a force is generalized because one notion covers force, moment and everything else that does work when a coordinate changes. Two questions must be answered. The first: what does the bent link itself pull back with, and does that depend on where in space the link is and how it is turned. The second: into which of the three groups of coordinates, the shift \(\vek o\), the rotation \(\theta\) or the bending \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), does each external load enter, that is, the force at the end of the link, the weight of the link and the motor moment.

We prepare the link. It is an Euler-Bernoulli beam (definition 5.14) of length \(L\) with constant bending stiffness \(EI\) and mass per length \(\rho A\), in the plane of motion. The planar case is the only one the book proves, because it has no rotations in space yet. The frame is chosen as in section 28.2. The link is fixed to the hub (pest), a rigid body that the motor turns about the point \(\vek o\). The hub has this name in the way of a wheel: it is the central part to which the rest is fixed, the spokes of a wheel, here the link. The link is clamped into the hub, so the root of the link turns as the hub does. The frame is the clamped one, which by definition 28.5 means \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\), and the transverse displacement of the axis, measured in the frame, is \(v(x) = \vek\psi(x)^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the shapes \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) of definition 28.4. The position of the point of the link with local coordinate \(x\) is by that definition

\[\vek r(x) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,\big(\bar{\vek r}_0(x) + \mat\Psi(x)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big) , \qquad \bar{\vek r}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} , \quad \mat\Psi = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \psi_1 & \cdots & \psi_{\mathrm{n}} \end{pmatrix} . \tag{28.25}\]

28.5.1 Elastic energy of the link

We begin with what the link pulls back with. We take the steel strip of section 28.1, \(L = 1\) m, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m\(^2\), \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, and bend it into the shape of the first cantilever mode (chapter 13), so that the tip is \(10\) mm off the straight line. We draw it twice (figure 28.11). On the left the hub is at the point \(\vek o\) with the frame axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) and rotation \(\theta = 0\), the straight dashed line is the undeformed link, the blue curve is the bent link, and the tip displacement \(q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is measured from the line to the tip. On the right is the same bent link in another position: its rotation \(\theta\) is \(40^\circ\), the hub is elsewhere, the frame axes are turned with the link and the displacement \(q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is measured perpendicular to the turned line. The shape relative to the frame is the same in both placements. The question is whether the energy is the same in both.

If we computed the energy in fixed axes from the small strain tensor, we would get different energies. Section 28.1 showed that for a rigid rotation by the angle \(\theta\) this tensor is \((\cos\theta - 1)\,\mat I\) (lemma 28.1). At \(\theta = 40^\circ\) that is a false stretch of \(-0{,}2340\). Multiplied by \(E = 196\) GPa it is a stress of \(45{,}9\) GPa that exists nowhere, while the bending of the link gives in the most strained fibre at the root a strain of only \(1{,}055 \cdot 10^{-4}\), which is \(2218\) times less. In the frame there is no false stretch. Theorem 28.7 says that the Green-Lagrange tensor of the link is computed from the displacement gradient \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) in the axes of the frame, and neither \(\vek o\) nor \(\theta\) is in it.

For the energy we must still say what the model takes for the displacement of the axis along the link. The model has three named simplifications.

  1. The Euler-Bernoulli model (definition 5.14): the cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis, the shear deformation and the rotation of the sections are neglected. The bound is in chapter 13: section 13.10 computes that at \(r/L = 0{,}0115\) the rotation of the sections lowers the first frequency of the beam by \(0{,}066\) %, our strip has \(r = h/\sqrt{12}\), so \(r/L = 0{,}0017\), and the error is smaller still.
  2. The axis does not change length: the axial stiffness \(EA/L\) is \(1{,}11 \cdot 10^5\) times the tip stiffness \(3EI/L^3\). When the tip moves away by \(q_{\mathrm{d}}\), an unstretched axis must come closer to the hub by the shortening of the axis \(\tfrac12\int_0^L v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 58{,}1\) \(\mu\)m, which is \(0{,}58\) % of the displacement (the estimate of step 2 of the proof of lemma 8.133, error at most \(v'^2_{\max}/4\)). The tip is free in the axial direction, so it can approach without work. If it were held at the length \(L\), the axis would stretch by that much and store the energy \(\tfrac12 (EA/L)\,s^2 = 0{,}0794\) J, which is \(3{,}64\) times the whole bending energy \(0{,}0218\) J. The axis therefore stays unstretched. This displacement we leave out of the position (28.25). It is \(6 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of the link length, and for the forces on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) that is also the relative error. For the forces on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) it is not that small. The shortening is quadratic in \(q\), so its derivative with respect to \(q\) is of first order, \(\partial u(L)/\partial q = -q\int_0^L\psi_1'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = -0{,}0116\) at \(10\) mm. An axial force component therefore changes the stiffness by about \(1\) %. With an axial force of \(-5\) N at the tip, the tip deflection by the beam-column formula is \(1{,}44\) % larger than the linear one. This term is the geometric stiffness. The model of this section leaves it out, section 28.7 brings it back, where an axial force pulls on it.
  3. Small slope: the curvature of the graph is \(v''(1 + v'^2)^{-3/2}\), and we write the energy with \(v''\). At the largest slope \(0{,}0138\) this error is \(2{,}8 \cdot 10^{-4}\) (relative), at the slope \(0{,}1\) it would be \(1{,}5\) %.

Under these assumptions the following holds.

Theorem 28.18 Elastic energy of a link (elastična energija člena)

Let the link be an Euler-Bernoulli beam of length \(L\) with constant stiffness \(EI\) in a floating frame with the reference conditions \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\) (definition 28.5), the transverse displacement \(v = \vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) with linearly independent \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} \in C^2[0, L]\) satisfying \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), and let the axis not change length, while its shortening is left out of the position (28.25) (simplification 2). Then:

  1. The strain energy of the link in the placement \((\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) is
    \[U = \tfrac12\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\,\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} , \qquad \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int_0^L EI\,\vek\psi''(x)\,\vek\psi''(x)^\T\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{28.26}\]
    independent of \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
  3. The generalized forces of the elastic forces, that is \(-\partial U/\partial(\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\), are \(\big(\vek 0,\ 0,\ -\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big)\).
Proof

We must show that \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) do not appear in the energy, that the energy is a quadratic form in \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and that this form is positive definite.

  1. By theorem 28.7 the Green-Lagrange tensor of a point of the link is a function of the displacement gradient \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) in the axes of the frame, and \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) are not in it. By definition 4.85 the energy is the integral of a density \(w\) that is a function of the strain. So \(U\) does not depend on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\).
  2. In the displacement field (5.16) we have \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = u' - y\,v''\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = v'\), so by theorem 28.7, item 2, the Green-Lagrange strain is \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v'' + \tfrac12\big((u' - y\,v'')^2 + v'^2\big)\). The axis does not change length, which means \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at \(y = 0\), that is \(u' + \tfrac12(u'^2 + v'^2) = 0\). Subtracting this leaves \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v''(1 + u') + \tfrac12 y^2 v''^2\). For the strip of the example \(|u'| < 10^{-4}\) and \(\tfrac12|y\,v''| < 6 \cdot 10^{-5}\), so \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v''\) with a relative error below \(2 \cdot 10^{-4}\). This is the strain of the field (5.16) with \(u' = 0\), and lemma 5.76 with \(u' = 0\) gives \(U = \tfrac12\int_0^L EI\,(v'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. For \(v = \vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) we have \(v'' = \vek\psi''^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \((v'')^2 = \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\,\vek\psi''\vek\psi''^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). Since \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) depends only on time, by the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39) we take it out of the integral and obtain (28.26). The integrands \(EI\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}''\psi_{\mathrm{k}}''\) are continuous, so the integrals exist.
  4. The matrix is symmetric because \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}''\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'' = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}''\psi_{\mathrm{j}}''\). For a column \(\vek c \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek c^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek c = \int_0^L EI\,(\vek c^\T\vek\psi'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\).
  5. If this integral is zero, the continuous nonnegative function \(EI\,(\vek c^\T\vek\psi'')^2\) is zero on \([0, L]\), hence so is \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi''\) (lemma 6.10, item 3). By corollary 1.85 \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi'\) is constant, equal to \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi'(0) = 0\). By the same corollary \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi\) is constant, equal to \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi(0) = 0\). The functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are linearly independent, so \(\vek c = \vek 0\). Hence \(\vek c^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek c > 0\) for every \(\vek c \ne \vek 0\).
  6. The internal forces of an ideally elastic body have the potential \(U\) (definition 4.85, definition 8.53), so the generalized force is \(-\partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\). Since \(U\) does not depend on \(\vek o\) and \(\theta\) (step 1), these derivatives are zero. By the rule for the derivative of a quadratic form with a symmetric matrix, \(\partial U/\partial\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\).

Source: SHABANA (5.113) to (5.117), PDF pp. 225 to 227: the virtual work of the elastic forces is \(-\vek q_{\mathrm{f}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\delta\vek q_{\mathrm{f}}\) with a symmetric positive definite stiffness matrix, because a rigid motion corresponds to a constant strain and the deformation is defined relative to the frame (PDF p. 225). Example 5.4 (PDF p. 226) is the same computation for a beam with an axial and a bending coordinate. The proof in steps is not from the source, because the source does not prove positive definiteness.

We sum up the theorem in words. The elastic energy is a quadratic form of the elastic coordinates in which neither the position nor the rotation of the link appears, so a shift and a rotation of the link without bending do not change the energy. This is exactly the question we asked at figure 28.11: both states have the same \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), hence \(U = \tfrac12\,K_{11}\,q_1^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 436{,}1 \cdot 0{,}010^2 = 0{,}0218\) J in both. For the shapes \(\psi_{\mathrm{r}}\) of the first three cantilever modes, normalized so that \(\psi_{\mathrm{r}}(L) = 1\) (so \(q_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the contribution of mode \(r\) to the tip displacement in metres), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \operatorname{diag}(436{,}1,\ 17\,129,\ 134\,295)\) N/m. The matrix is diagonal because the cantilever modes are orthogonal also with respect to the energy (theorem 13.43), and the computation gives zero off-diagonal entries. The static tip stiffness is \(3EI/L^3 = 423{,}4\) N/m, and \(K_{11}\) is \(3{,}0\) % larger. It is larger because, for a given tip displacement, the shape of the static deflection has the least energy (the principle of minimum potential energy, theorem 4.91, applied to a force at the tip), and the shape of the first mode is another shape.

Now the condition the theorem requires, and a case where it fails. The conditions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\) are not decoration. Take only one condition, \(v(0) = 0\), and the shape \(\psi = x/L\). It satisfies \(\psi(0) = 0\) but not \(\psi'(0) = 0\), and it is a rigid rotation of the link by the angle \(q/L\). Then \(\psi'' = 0\) and \(K_{\mathrm{dd}} = 0\): for \(q = 10\) mm we get \(U = 0\), the matrix is not positive definite and step 5 of the proof stops already at the derivative: \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi' = c/L\) is constant, but equal to \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi'(0) = c/L \ne 0\), so \(\vek c^\T\vek\psi\) need not be constant and \(c = 0\) does not follow. Such a coordinate does not measure bending but a rotation, which \(\theta\) already measures. The same shape gave in section 28.4 a mass matrix with the coordinates \((\theta, q)\) that is singular at \(q = 0\) and nearly singular at \(q = 10\) mm (determinant \(3{,}9 \cdot 10^{-5}\), (28.24)), and here it gives zero stiffness. A coordinate that costs no energy is not elastic, it duplicates \(\theta\).

28.5.2 Generalized forces of the link

We have the elastic forces. The external ones are three: the force at the end of the link, the own weight of the link and the motor moment on the hub. We draw them (figure 28.12). The link lies at the angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal, and at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) it is bent downward from the straight position, the hub is at \(\vek o\) and the frame axes are turned with the link. The weight acts on every point of the link downward, so the arrows of the weight are drawn from a point of the link downward: weight is a pull of the earth, and the arrow of a pulling force starts at the point on which it acts. At the tip acts the force \(\vek F\), \(10\) N downward, in fixed axes. Since the axis of the link is not horizontal, we split it into the components along \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), \(-F\sin\theta\) and \(-F\cos\theta\). The lever arm of the force about the hub is the horizontal distance \(L\cos\theta\) between \(\vek o\) and the tip. On the hub acts the motor moment \(\tau\) in the direction of increasing angle.

Since the link is not a rigid bar, a generalized force for the coordinate \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) has a meaning only if we define it for the link. Definition 8.50 is stated for rigid bodies, but its formula \(\vek F\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) needs only the position of the point of application as a function of the coordinates, and we have that in (28.25).

Lemma 28.19 Generalized forces of the external loads on a link (posplošene sile zunanjih obremenitev člena)

Let the link be as in theorem 28.18 and \(\vek r(x)\) the position (28.25).

  1. A force \(\vek F\) (a column of two numbers in fixed axes) at the point with local coordinate \(a \in [0, L]\) has the generalized forces
    \[\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = \vek F , \qquad Q_\theta = \vek F\cdot\mat R(\theta)\,\mat J\,\big(\bar{\vek r}_0(a) + \mat\Psi(a)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big) , \qquad \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Psi(a)^\T\,\mat R(\theta)^\T\,\vek F , \tag{28.27}\]
    with \(\mat J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (the quarter turn).
  2. A distributed force with continuous density \(\vek f(x)\) per length (in fixed axes) has the generalized forces
    \[\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = \int_0^L \vek f\,\mathrm{d}x , \quad Q_\theta = \int_0^L \vek f\cdot\mat R\,\mat J\,(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\,\mathrm{d}x , \quad \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \int_0^L \mat\Psi^\T\mat R^\T\vek f\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{28.28}\]
    For the own weight, \(\vek f = -\rho A g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\),
    \[\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = -m g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} , \quad Q_\theta = -\rho A g \int_0^L \big(x\cos\theta - v\sin\theta\big)\,\mathrm{d}x , \quad \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = -\rho A g\,\cos\theta\int_0^L \vek\psi\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{28.29}\]
  3. A motor moment \(\tau\) on the hub, which is rigidly fixed to the root of the link, has
    \[\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = \vek 0 , \qquad Q_\theta = \tau , \qquad \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \tau\,\vek\psi'(0) = \vek 0 . \tag{28.30}\]
Proof

We must show that the virtual work of each load is a linear function of the virtual changes of the coordinates, and read off the coefficients. By definition 4.71 the work of the force \(\vek F\) at a virtual change of the position of the point of application \(\delta\vek r\) is \(\vek F\cdot\delta\vek r\).

  1. The position \(\vek r(a)\) from (28.25) is a continuously differentiable function of the coordinates \((\vek o, \theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.29) \(\delta\vek r = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} (\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}})\,\delta q_{\mathrm{s}}\), and as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 8.51 the virtual work is \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} Q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\delta q_{\mathrm{s}}\) with \(Q_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek F\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  2. Derivatives: \(\partial\vek r/\partial\vek o\) is the identity matrix. By theorem 8.12, \(\mat R'(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} -\sin\theta & -\cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \end{pmatrix} = \mat R(\theta)\,\mat J\), so \(\partial\vek r/\partial\theta = \mat R\,\mat J\,(\bar{\vek r}_0 + \mat\Psi\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\). The position is linear in \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), so \(\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat R\,\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) the \(k\)-th column of the matrix \(\mat\Psi\).
  3. We insert into \(Q_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek F\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\). For \(s = \vek o\) we get \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = \vek F\), for \(s = \theta\) we get \(Q_\theta = \vek F\cdot\mat R\mat J(\ldots)\), and for \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) we get \(\vek F\cdot\mat R\,\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}} = (\mat R^\T\vek F)\cdot\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), because \(\mat R\) is orthogonal by lemma 2.40. This is (28.27).
  4. We divide the distributed force into pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) of length \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\). We replace a piece by the point force \(\vek f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h_{\mathrm{i}}\) at a point \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the piece. By definition 4.71 its work is \(\vek f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\delta\vek r(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h_{\mathrm{i}}\). Definition 4.71 covers only point forces, so we define the work of a distributed force as the limit of the work of these substitute forces. The sum over the pieces is a Riemann sum of the continuous function \(\vek f\cdot\delta\vek r\), its limit at \(\max h_{\mathrm{i}} \to 0\) is the integral (definition 3.34), so the work of the distributed force is \(\int_0^L \vek f\cdot\delta\vek r\,\mathrm{d}x\). We insert step 1 and exchange the finite sum over \(s\) with the integral (linearity of the integral): \(Q_{\mathrm{s}} = \int_0^L \vek f\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). By step 3, (28.28) follows.
  5. For the weight, \(\vek f = (0, -\rho A g)\). With \(\mat R\mat J\,(x, v)^\T = (-v\cos\theta - x\sin\theta,\ x\cos\theta - v\sin\theta)\) the second component is \(x\cos\theta - v\sin\theta\), and with \(\mat R\,(0, \psi_{\mathrm{k}})^\T = (-\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\sin\theta,\ \psi_{\mathrm{k}}\cos\theta)\) the second component is \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\cos\theta\). This is (28.29).
  6. The hub is a rigid body rigidly fixed to the root of the link, so its angle of rotation is the angle of rotation of the cross-section at \(x = 0\). By theorem 5.15 the cross-section turns by \(v'\) relative to the axis of the frame, so \(\varphi_{\text{hub}} = \theta + v'(0) = \theta + \vek\psi'(0)^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). By definition 8.50 (the term with moments) the moment \(\tau\) has \(Q_{\mathrm{s}} = \tau\,\partial\varphi_{\text{hub}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), so \(Q_\theta = \tau\), \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \tau\,\vek\psi'(0)\) and \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} = \vek 0\). With the reference condition \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\) the last is \(\vek 0\).

Source: SHABANA (5.118) to (5.119), PDF p. 227, and Example 5.5 (PDF pp. 227 to 228): \(\delta W_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek Q_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\delta\vek q\) split into \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{R}}\), \(\vek Q_\theta\), \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{f}}\), a force at a point written with the shape matrix and the matrix \(\mat B\) of columns of derivatives with respect to the rotation. The distributed force, the weight and the moment on the hub are not from the source.

The lemma tells how each load divides among the three groups of coordinates. The force \(\vek F\) goes whole into \(\vek o\), into the rotation as a moment about \(\vek o\) (\(Q_\theta\) is the scalar product with the position vector turned by a quarter turn) and into \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) as the transverse component of the force, evaluated with the shapes at the point of application. The axial component \(-F\sin\theta\) does not go into \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), because the matrix \(\mat\Psi\) has no axial row: the unstretchable axis carries it, and the hub takes it as a reaction. This holds in the model of this section, which leaves out the shortening of the axis (simplification 2). The effect of the axial force on bending, the geometric stiffness, is brought back in section 28.7.

We test it on an example with the same strip, \(L = 1\) m, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m\(^2\), \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, \(m = 1{,}872\) kg. The plane of motion is now vertical, so the own weight acts in the plane of bending, in which the strip is \(6\) mm wide. The three shapes are the first three cantilever modes, normalized to \(\psi_{\mathrm{r}}(L) = 1\).

Example A: weight at \(\theta = 0\). The link is horizontal, \(\cos\theta = 1\) and \(\sin\theta = 0\). By (28.29), \(Q_\theta = -\rho A g\,L^2/2 = -9{,}182\) N m and \(Q_{\mathrm{d}}\) has components \(-7{,}190\), \(3{,}985\) and \(-2{,}336\) N. At rest the hub is held by the moment \(\tau = 9{,}182\) N m, which is the equilibrium of the hub (\(\tau + Q_\theta = 0\), in the equation for \(\theta\) there are no elastic forces by theorem 28.18, item 3), and equals the root moment of a cantilever under its own weight, \(\rho A g L^2/2\) (equilibrium of the whole link about the hub, chapter 5). The elastic tip displacement from \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the first \(k\) modes:

number of modes tip displacement (mm) ratio to \(-\rho A g L^4/(8EI) = -16{,}267\) mm
1 \(-16{,}484\) \(1{,}0134\)
2 \(-16{,}252\) \(0{,}9991\)
3 \(-16{,}269\) \(1{,}0002\)

With the modes the displacement approaches the static deflection of the cantilever (chapter 5, theorem 5.56). With one mode it is \(1{,}3\) % too large. Theorem 28.18 and lemma 28.19 are thus checked together on a case we know from chapter 5.

Example B: at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) (\(\cos\theta = 0{,}8660\)). By (28.29), \(Q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is \(\cos 30^\circ\) times smaller, \(-6{,}226\), \(3{,}451\) and \(-2{,}023\) N, and the displacement is also \(0{,}8660\) times smaller, \(14{,}09\) mm. The moment \(Q_\theta\) depends on the bending too: for a rigid link it is \(-\rho A g\,L^2\cos\theta/2 = -7{,}952\) N m, with the bending \(\int_0^L v\,\mathrm{d}x = -5{,}635\) mm m it is \(-8{,}004\) N m, which is \(0{,}65\) % more. The force at the tip from figure 28.12: \(\vek F = (0, -10)\) N. By (28.27) the component of \(\vek F\) in the frame is transverse \(-F\cos\theta = -8{,}660\) N and axial \(-F\sin\theta = -5{,}000\) N. So \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \psi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\cdot(-8{,}660) = -8{,}660\) N for every \(r\), and the moment about the hub is \(Q_\theta = -F\,(L\cos\theta - v(L)\sin\theta)\). At \(v(L) = 0\) it is \(-F\,L\cos\theta = -8{,}660\) N m, with the lever arm \(L\cos\theta = 0{,}8660\) m from the figure. At the true displacement \(v(L) = -20{,}4\) mm it is \(-8{,}762\) N m, which is \(1{,}18\) % more, because the tip has dropped and the lever arm is longer. The tip displacement with three modes is \(-20{,}426\) mm, the exact value \(-F\cos\theta\,L^3/(3EI)\) is \(-20{,}456\) mm, the ratio is \(0{,}9985\). Since the bending is \(2\) % of the length, the effect on the lever arm is measurable, and the lemma includes it, while a frozen lever arm \(L\cos\theta\) does not. An effect of the same size is the one the model leaves out: by the beam-column formula the axial component \(-5\) N increases the tip deflection by \(1{,}44\) %, to \(-20{,}750\) mm (simplification 2). Likewise the axial weight component \(\rho A g\sin\theta\,(L - x)\) at \(30^\circ\) softens mode 1 by about \(0{,}8\) % (one-mode estimate \(\dfrac{\rho A g\sin\theta}{K_{11}}\int_0^L (L - x)\,\psi_1'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), with the integral \(0{,}393\) m and \(K_{11} = 436{,}1\) N/m). The model of this section leaves this out too, and section 28.7 returns it as geometric stiffness.

Now a case that shows that the claim of the lemma, item 3 (\(\vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) for a moment on the hub), is a property of the frame and not of the moment. Take the chord frame: the axis \(\bar x\) goes from \(\vek o\) to the tip of the link, and the reference conditions are \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v(L) = 0\) (section 28.2, reference conditions). The shapes are \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \sin(k\pi x/L)\), and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = k\pi/L \ne 0\). Figure 28.13 shows the same link in both frames. Above is the clamped frame: the axis \(\bar x\) lies on the tangent at the root, which is the direction of the hub, and the moment \(\tau\) acts only on the rotation. Below is the chord frame: the axis \(\bar x\) goes through the tip, the tangent at the root, which is the direction of the hub, is turned relative to the axis by the slope \(v'(0)\), the rotation of the axis from the horizontal is \(\theta\), and the angle of the hub is \(\theta + v'(0)\). The moment \(\tau\) acts on the hub, that is on the angle \(\theta + v'(0)\).

In the chord frame \(\tau = 6{,}24\) N m (the moment that accelerates a rigid link with moment of inertia \(0{,}624\) kg m\(^2\) about the hub at \(10\) rad/s\(^2\)) and by (28.30) \(Q_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{k}} = \tau\,k\pi/L\) equals \(19{,}60\), \(39{,}21\) and \(58{,}81\) N for \(k = 1, 2, 3\), while in the clamped frame it is \(0\). For the first mode the chord stiffness is \(K_{11} = EI\,(\pi/L)^4\,L/2 = 6873\) N/m, so the force \(19{,}60\) N alone would give an elastic displacement of \(2{,}85\) mm. This is not an error but bookkeeping: the same physical rotation of the hub is \(\theta\) in the clamped frame and the sum \(\theta + v'(0)\) in the chord frame. For the bent link of the figure (tip \(10\) mm, tangent at the root horizontal) the angle of the chord is \(d/L = 0{,}0100\) rad, the slope of the root against the chord is \(v'(0) = -0{,}0100\) and the angle of the hub is \(0{,}0100 - 0{,}0100 = 0\), equal to the rotation of the clamped frame. The rule "the moment enters only the equation for \(\theta\)" therefore holds only in the clamped frame. If we used it in the chord frame, we would leave out the force \(19{,}60\) N in the first elastic equation, and the model would pass the moment only to the rotation of the frame axis and would not impose the slope of the root on the link, as if the link were joined to the hub by a hinge.

For this reason we shall use the clamped frame from here on (section 28.6). In it the total generalized force of the link on the hub is

\[\vek Q = \begin{pmatrix} \vek Q_{\mathrm{o}} \\ Q_\theta \\ \vek Q_{\mathrm{d}} \end{pmatrix}_{\text{external}} + \begin{pmatrix} \vek 0 \\ 0 \\ -\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} \end{pmatrix}_{\text{elastic}} ,\]

where the external loads have the groups of lemma 28.19. This column will be the right side of Lagrange's equations in section 28.6. The effects of the turning of the link are not in this section. In Lagrange's equations they are given by the terms of the kinetic energy that depend on \(\dot\theta\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(\dot\theta^2\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (section 28.4), and at fast turning also by the axial force at the shortening of the axis (section 28.7).

28.6 Equations of motion of the link

So far we have described the link with two groups of coordinates, the reference coordinates \(o\) and \(\theta\) and the elastic coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (definitions 28.3 and 28.4). We have computed its kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 28.13) and its elastic energy \(U = \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (theorem 28.18). We now ask how the link moves when loads act on it. The answer is the equations of motion (gibalne enačbe), the equations that connect the coordinates, their velocities and accelerations with the loads at every time. This section derives them, then applies them to a link driven by a motor on a hub and shows two things: how the frequencies of such a link interlace with the frequencies of the link held by the hub, and why we must not compute the elastic coordinates separately from the rigid motion.

28.6.1 Equations of motion of a general planar link

Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88) are the road we already know: from the kinetic energy we have and the generalized forces they give the equations of motion without computing the forces in the constraints. The link brings one novelty. It is not finitely many points and rigid bodies but infinitely many points whose positions are determined by the coordinates \(\vek q = (\vek q_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) with \(\vek q_{\mathrm{r}} = (o_{\mathrm{x}}, o_{\mathrm{y}}, \theta)\). The proof of theorem 8.88 uses for each point only that its position is a function of the coordinates (steps 3 and 4), and for the body also that the derivatives with respect to the coordinates go under the integral (step 5), so it holds here too. The elastic forces in the link are internal forces with a potential \(U\). We know that \(U\) depends only on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (theorem 28.18), which is also all the dependence on the position of the frame that we need.

As in theorem 8.120 we separate the derivatives of the mass matrix from Lagrange's equations. The resulting term with squares of velocities is named the quadratic velocity vector (vektor kvadratnih hitrosti) \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{v}}\). For the link these are the forces that no external load causes but that appear because the mass matrix changes with position: centrifugal, Coriolis and gyroscopic forces (SHABANA PDF p. 235, equations 5.142 and 5.144, where it is named this way).

Theorem 28.20 Equations of motion of a planar flexible link (gibalne enačbe ravninskega člena)

Let a planar link have coordinates \(\vek q = (\vek q_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) made of \(n\) numbers, where \(\vek q_{\mathrm{r}} = (o_{\mathrm{x}}, o_{\mathrm{y}}, \theta)\) are the reference coordinates and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) the elastic coordinates under the reference conditions of definition 28.5. Let the kinetic energy be \(T = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M(\vek q)\dot{\vek q}\) with a matrix \(\mat M\) that is symmetric, positive definite and continuously differentiable (theorem 28.13), let the elastic energy be \(U = \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), and let \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the vector of generalized forces of the applied loads (definition 8.50). Then a twice differentiable motion \(\vek q(t)\) satisfies Lagrange's equations of the link if and only if for \(s = 1, \dots, n\)

\[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} M_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q)\,\ddot q_{\mathrm{j}} + (\mat K\vek q)_{\mathrm{s}} = Q_{\mathrm{e},\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{s}} , \qquad Q_{\mathrm{v},\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}}\Big(\partial_{\mathrm{k}} M_{\mathrm{sj}} - \tfrac12\,\partial_{\mathrm{s}} M_{\mathrm{jk}}\Big)\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{k}} , \tag{28.31}\]

where \(\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} \mat 0 & \mat 0 \\ \mat 0 & \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the derivative with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\). In matrix form \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q_{\mathrm{e}} + \vek Q_{\mathrm{v}}\) with \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{v}} = -\dot{\mat M}\dot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\,\big[\partial(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q})/\partial\vek q\big]^\T\).

Proof

We must show that Lagrange's equations of the link read as (28.31). The link has many points, so we first say what theorem 8.88 means here.

  1. The position of the point of the link at \(x\) is \(\vek X(x, \vek q) = \vek o + \mat R(\theta)\,(\bar{\vek r}_0(x) + \mat\Psi(x)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) (definition 28.4). It is a twice continuously differentiable function of the coordinates, because \(\mat R(\theta)\) is built from sine and cosine and \(\vek X\) is linear in \(\vek o\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). So for every point steps 3 and 4 of the proof of theorem 8.88 hold: \(\ddot{\vek X}\cdot\partial\vek X/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) equals the difference between the time derivative of \(\dot{\vek X}\cdot\partial\dot{\vek X}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) and the quantity \(\dot{\vek X}\cdot\partial\dot{\vek X}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), and each of these is a derivative of half the squared velocity.
  2. The summation over points in step 5 of that proof is replaced by the integral over the link, \(T = \tfrac12\int\rho A\,|\dot{\vek X}|^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the derivatives with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) go under the integral (lemma 8.31). The inertial work is therefore \(I_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial T}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \frac{\partial T}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\) for every \(s\).
  3. The elastic forces of the link are internal forces with a potential \(U\) (theorem 28.18, which follows from definition 4.85), so their generalized force is \(-\partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) (definition 8.53). Since \(U\) does not depend on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(-\partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = -(\mat K\vek q)_{\mathrm{s}}\) by theorem 28.18. The applied loads give \(Q_{\mathrm{e},\mathrm{s}}\) (definition 8.50).
  4. D'Alembert's principle gives by step 6 of the proof of theorem 8.88 the equality \(I_{\mathrm{s}} = Q_{\mathrm{e},\mathrm{s}} - (\mat K\vek q)_{\mathrm{s}}\) for every \(s\), because the coordinates are independent.
  5. From \(T = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}}M_{\mathrm{jk}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the same computation as in steps 2 to 4 of the proof of theorem 8.120 (symmetry of the matrix \(\mat M\) and the chain rule, lemma 8.29) we get \(I_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} M_{\mathrm{sj}}\ddot q_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}}(\partial_{\mathrm{k}} M_{\mathrm{sj}} - \tfrac12\partial_{\mathrm{s}} M_{\mathrm{jk}})\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert it into step 4 and move the term with squares of velocities to the right-hand side. This is (28.31).

Source: SHABANA section 5.5, PDF pp. 234-237: equation 5.144 (\(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q + \mat C_{\mathrm{q}}^\T\vek\lambda = \vek Q_{\mathrm{e}} + \vek Q_{\mathrm{v}}\), here without constraints) and 5.142 (the quadratic velocity vector, an expression with \(\dot{\mat M}\) and the derivative with respect to \(\vek q\), which we checked on the image of the equation). The proof is not from the source: it only announces the equation, and the derivation from theorem 8.88 and theorem 8.120 is ours.

The theorem holds for a free link. A link connected to other links by joints gets one more term \(\mat C_{\mathrm{q}}^\T\vek\lambda\) with the multipliers of the constraints, as equation 5.144 in SHABANA, PDF p. 235, says. We have the multipliers of constraints in theorem 8.95. Assembling several links with constraints is outside this chapter (SHABANA sections 5.4 and 5.8 to 5.10, PDF pp. 230-233 and 251-260). The vector \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{v}}\) is the part of the equations that the rigid body of chapter 8 would not have: because \(\mat M\) depends on \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), elastic displacements affect the rotation, and the rotation affects the elastic displacements.

28.6.2 The link on a hub

For the first joint of a robot this theorem is too general, so we narrow it to the case we will keep until the end of the chapter. The link is the steel strip from the section on running examples (length \(L = 1\) m, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m², \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = mL^2/3 = 0{,}624\) kg m²), and a motor turns it about an axis at the point \(O\), which we take as the origin. This case is our choice and not from a source (SHABANA has no link on a hub with numbers), so we vary the inertia of the hub so that the conclusion does not hang on it.

Let us draw it. The motion is in the horizontal plane \(xy\), so weight does no work, since it is perpendicular to every displacement (definition 8.50). First the fixed axes \(x\) and \(y\), measured from the resting ground. About the point \(O\) turns the hub, named after the wheel, where the hub is its central part on which the axle sits. Here it is a rigid body with inertia \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) about the axis, into which the rotor of the motor and the gearbox are converted. For the hub we take radius zero, and the link is attached to the axis (an idealization from the chapter outline: a hub of larger radius would change the forces in the link, which the section on steady rotation says). The frame \(\bar x\bar y\) is the one of definition 28.3, with origin at \(O\), and it is turned by the angle \(\theta\) from the axis \(x\). The reference conditions of definition 28.5 are clamped conditions at \(x = 0\): the axis \(\bar x\) is the tangent of the link at the hub, \(v(0) = v'(0) = 0\). In the frame the link bends by \(v(x)\) perpendicular to the axis \(\bar x\), the tip bending is \(v(L)\). Finally the motor torque \(\tau\) acts on the hub in the direction of increasing \(\theta\). Its work is \(\tau\,\delta\theta\), because the angle of the hub is \(\theta\) and the bending angle does not affect it: by definition 8.50 \(Q_\theta = \tau\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{k}} = 0\). This is why the torque with a clamped frame enters only the equation for \(\theta\).

The simplification of the elastic field is this: a point on the axis at \(x\) moves only transversally, \(\bar{\vek r}_0 = (x, 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek u} = (0, v)\) with \(v(x) = \mat\Psi_2(x)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,q_{\mathrm{k}}\). The displacement along the axis, the shortening of the axis due to bending, we neglect. For a tip of 10 mm in the first mode the shortening is \(\tfrac12\int v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}058\) mm, which is 0,6 % of the tip, so in this section it is negligible. In fast rotation we must not forget it, because there the centrifugal force opposes exactly this shortening. The next section therefore brings this work back. Let the \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) be free of rigid motions, that is \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), and independent, and let \(\vek b = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\,\vek\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\) be the coupling column and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,\vek\psi\vek\psi^\T\mathrm{d}x\) (both as in theorem 28.13 and lemma 28.15).

The motor is an ideal source of torque: its electrical dynamics and the flexibility of the joint itself (a hub that twists under torque) are not taken into account in this chapter. Robots with flexible joints are treated by SPONG in his chapter on the control of such robots (PDF p. 461).

Corollary 28.21 Equations of motion of a link on a hub (gibalne enačbe člena na pestu)

Let a link with a transverse elastic field \(v = \vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) have a clamped frame and let the hub have inertia \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) and torque \(\tau\), as described above. Let \(\vek q = (\theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\). Then the equations of motion are

\[\big(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big)\,\ddot\theta + \vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + 2\,\dot\theta\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \tau , \tag{28.32}\]
\[\vek b\,\ddot\theta + \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} - \dot\theta^2\,\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\big)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0 . \tag{28.33}\]
Proof

We must show what the kinetic energy of the link and the hub is (step 2), and then insert it into theorem 28.20.

  1. The point of the link at \(x\) has in the frame the position \(\bar{\vek u}_{\mathrm{tot}} = (x, v)\), and by lemma 28.8 its velocity in the axes of the frame is \(\dot\theta\,\mat J(x, v)^\T + (0, \dot v)^\T = (-\dot\theta v,\ \dot\theta x + \dot v)\). Because \(\mat R(\theta)\) is an orthogonal matrix (lemma 2.40), \(|\dot{\vek r}|^2 = \dot\theta^2v^2 + (\dot\theta x + \dot v)^2\), that is \(\dot\theta^2(x^2 + v^2) + 2\dot\theta x\dot v + \dot v^2\). The end \(O\) is at rest.
  2. The kinetic energy of the link is \(\tfrac12\int_0^L\rho A\,|\dot{\vek r}|^2\mathrm{d}x\). With \(v = \vek\psi^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), \(\int\rho A x^2\mathrm{d}x = J_{\mathrm{link}}\) (this is \(mL^2/3\) for constant \(\rho A\)), \(\vek b\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) this is
    \[T_{\mathrm{link}} = \tfrac12\big(J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big)\dot\theta^2 + \dot\theta\,\vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} .\]
    The hub contributes \(\tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{h}}\dot\theta^2\). Together \(T\) equals
    \[T = \tfrac12\big(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\big)\dot\theta^2 + \dot\theta\,\vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} . \tag{28.34}\]
  3. The elastic energy is \(U = \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (theorem 28.18). The generalized forces are \(Q_\theta = \tau\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{k}} = 0\) (above). Lagrange's equations of the link (theorem 28.20) are Lagrange's equations with \(T\), \(-\partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  4. The coordinate \(\theta\). \(\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial\dot\theta} = (J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\dot\theta + \vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\). Its time derivative by the product rule is \((J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\ddot\theta + 2\,\dot\theta\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), since \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}) = 2\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) (symmetry of the matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\)). Because \(T\) does not contain \(\theta\), \(\partial T/\partial\theta = 0\), and \(\partial U/\partial\theta = 0\). We get (28.32).
  5. The coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). \(\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}} = \dot\theta\,\vek b + \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), its time derivative is \(\ddot\theta\,\vek b + \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\), because \(\vek b\) is constant. The derivatives are \(\partial T/\partial\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \dot\theta^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(\partial U/\partial\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). Lagrange's equation is \(\vek b\ddot\theta + \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} - \dot\theta^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\), which is (28.33).

Source: The derivation is not from a source: SHABANA has no link on a hub, he has the general equations 5.144 and 5.147 (PDF pp. 235-237). Here they are derived from theorem 28.20 for the transverse field.

Let us see what the equations say. The first, (28.32), is the rotation: the torque \(\tau\) accelerates the total inertia \(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}\), and the term \(\vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) we will turn to below, because it says that the bending of the link itself turns the hub. The second, (28.33), is the bending: \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the elastic force, \(\vek b\ddot\theta\) is the inertial force due to the acceleration of the hub (as a vehicle pulling away pushes us back into the seat, the link lags behind the accelerating hub), and \(-\dot\theta^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the transverse part of the centrifugal force, which pulls the bent link still further from the axis \(\bar x\) and reduces its stiffness. The axial part of the centrifugal force stretches the link and increases its stiffness, but it is not in the equation, because we neglected the shortening of the axis (section 28.7).

How small are the terms we will now drop? The first class are the terms with \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). For a tip of 10 mm in the first mode, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = 4{,}68\cdot10^{-5}\) kg m², which is \(7{,}5\cdot10^{-5}\) of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\). The second class is \(\dot\theta^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) against \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\): the ratio is \(\dot\theta^2/\omega_1^2\) with \(\omega_1 = 30{,}53\) rad/s. At \(\dot\theta = 3\) rad/s it is \(0{,}0097\), at \(\dot\theta = 10\) rad/s it is \(0{,}107\). Linearization is therefore good for rotation around 3 rad/s (1 % in stiffness), at 10 rad/s it is already 11 %.

28.6.3 Linearization and angular momentum

The state in which the link is at rest and straight, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) and \(\dot\theta = 0\), is an equilibrium at every angle \(\theta\): every angle is equally good, because the rotation of the whole link is not resisted. Theorem 8.120 reads the equilibrium at \(\vek q = \vek 0\), and since \(\mat M\) and \(U\) do not contain \(\theta\), we may take \(\theta = 0\).

Corollary 28.22 Linearized equations of a link on a hub (linearizirane enačbe člena na pestu)

Let \(\tau = 0\) (a free joint) and \(\vek q = (\theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) as in corollary 28.21. Let \(\mat M_0\) be the matrix with cells \(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}\), \(\vek b^\T\), \(\vek b\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and \(\mat K = \mathrm{diag}(0, \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}})\). Then \(\mat M_0\) is symmetric and positive definite, \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and every twice differentiable motion of the link satisfies the equation

\[\begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b^\T \\ \vek b & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\ddot\theta \\ \ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \vek 0^\T \\ \vek 0 & \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\theta \\ \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\end{bmatrix} = \vek R , \tag{28.35}\]

where the remainder \(\vek R\) satisfies the estimate (8.108) of theorem 8.120.

Proof

We must show that the assumptions of theorem 8.120 hold, and read off \(\mat M_0\) and \(\mat K\).

  1. Lagrange's equations of the link are Lagrange's equations with the potential \(V = U\) (theorem 8.90), because at \(\tau = 0\) there are no non-elastic forces. \(U\) is a quadratic form, so arbitrarily differentiable, \(\nabla U(\vek 0) = \vek 0\). The elements of \(\mat M(\vek q)\) from (28.34) are polynomials in \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), hence continuously differentiable.
  2. The matrix of second derivatives of \(U\) at \(\vek 0\) is \(\mat K = \mathrm{diag}(0, \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}})\). \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is symmetric and positive definite, because \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \int_0^L EI\,(v'')^2\mathrm{d}x\) (lemma 5.76) and this is zero only for \(v'' \equiv 0\), that is \(v\) linear, and because of \(v(0) = v'(0) = 0\) then \(v \equiv 0\), so \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) (independence of the \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\)). The matrix \(\mat K\) is therefore semidefinite, \(\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q \ge 0\).
  3. \(\mat M_0 = \mat M(\vek 0)\) has the cells written by (28.34). For every column \(\vek\xi = (\xi_\theta, \vek\xi_{\mathrm{d}})\) we have \(\vek\xi^\T\mat M_0\vek\xi = J_{\mathrm{h}}\xi_\theta^2 + \int_0^L\rho A\,(\xi_\theta x + \vek\psi^\T\vek\xi_{\mathrm{d}})^2\mathrm{d}x\), which follows from the definitions of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\), \(\vek b\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\). This is zero only if \(\xi_\theta x + \vek\psi^\T\vek\xi_{\mathrm{d}} \equiv 0\) and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\xi_\theta = 0\). The derivative at \(x = 0\) gives \(\xi_\theta + 0 = 0\), because \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), then \(\vek\psi^\T\vek\xi_{\mathrm{d}} \equiv 0\) and \(\vek\xi_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). So \(\mat M_0\) is positive definite. It is symmetric by construction.
  4. Theorem 8.120 now gives (28.35) with the remainder satisfying (8.108).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The form of \(\mat M_0\) and \(\mat K\) corresponds to the splitting of equation 5.159 in SHABANA, PDF p. 241.

The corollary has behind it a law we know, which is very useful in this system. The coordinate \(\theta\) is cyclic (ciklična), because \(T\) does not contain it (equation (28.34)). By corollary 8.112 the quantity \(p_\theta = \partial T/\partial\dot\theta\) is conserved at \(\tau = 0\).

Lemma 28.23 Conservation of angular momentum of a link on a hub (ohranitev kotne količine člena na pestu)

At \(\tau = 0\) the quantity \(p_\theta = (J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\dot\theta + \vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) in equations (28.32) and (28.33) is constant, and it is the angular momentum of the hub and the link about the axis \(O\). In the linear equations (28.35) \(p_\theta = (J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\dot\theta + \vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) and therefore \((J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\,\ddot\theta = -\vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\).

Proof

We must show that \(p_\theta\) is constant and that it is the angular momentum.

  1. The coordinate \(\theta\) is cyclic and \(Q_\theta = 0\), so by corollary 8.112 \(\mathrm{d}p_\theta/\mathrm{d}t = 0\) with \(p_\theta = \partial T/\partial\dot\theta\).
  2. From step 2 of the proof of corollary 28.21, \(\partial T/\partial\dot\theta = J_{\mathrm{h}}\dot\theta + \int_0^L\rho A\,\big(\dot\theta(x^2 + v^2) + x\dot v\big)\mathrm{d}x\). A point with position \((x, v)\) and velocity \((-\dot\theta v,\ \dot\theta x + \dot v)\) in the axes of the frame has angular momentum per unit mass \(x(\dot\theta x + \dot v) - v(-\dot\theta v) = \dot\theta(x^2 + v^2) + x\dot v\). The integral with \(\rho A\) is the angular momentum of the link, \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\dot\theta\) is the angular momentum of the hub.
  3. In linearization (corollary 28.22) \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\,\dot\theta\) are of higher order, so \(p_\theta = (J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\dot\theta + \vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\). If we differentiate this constant quantity with respect to time, we get \((J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\ddot\theta + \vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\), which is the first row of equation (28.35).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The physical reason we know from school: without an external torque about an axis, the angular momentum about that axis does not change. If the elastic coordinates of the link start to oscillate, \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} \ne \vek 0\), the hub must turn so that the sum stays the same. The hub and the link in a free joint are thus coupled.

28.6.4 Example: free vibration of a link on a hub

Example 28.24 First vibration of the link on a hub with \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m² (prvo nihanje člena na pestu)

We look for the vibration with a free joint, \(\tau = 0\), without rigid motion, at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m². We take one elastic coordinate, the amplitude of the first cantilever mode (chapter 13, theorem 13.37, \(\omega_1' = 30{,}53\) rad/s), mass normalized, \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = 1\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \omega_1'^2\), \(\vek b = b_1 = 0{,}77827\) kg\(^{1/2}\) m, which corresponds to \(\int\rho A\,x\,\varphi_1\,\mathrm{d}x\) for this mode.

We write (28.35) with \(\tau = 0\): \(J_{\mathrm{tot}}\ddot\theta + b_1\ddot q = 0\) and \(b_1\ddot\theta + \ddot q + \omega_1'^2 q = 0\), where \(J_{\mathrm{tot}} = J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}824\) kg m². We solve the first equation for \(\ddot\theta\) (lemma 28.23) and insert it into the second. We get

\[\Big(1 - \frac{b_1^2}{J_{\mathrm{tot}}}\Big)\ddot q + \omega_1'^2\,q = 0 . \tag{28.36}\]

The matrix \(\mat M_0\) is positive definite (corollary 28.22), so \(\det\mat M_0 = J_{\mathrm{tot}} - b_1^2 > 0\) and the factor in the parentheses lies between 0 and 1. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\), \(b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{tot}} = 0{,}7351\), the factor is \(0{,}2649\), and

\[\omega = \frac{\omega_1'}{\sqrt{0{,}2649}} = 59{,}31\ \text{rad/s} .\]

With 20 finite elements (chapter 12) it is \(59{,}147\) rad/s, with two modes \(59{,}150\). A single mode thus hits the frequency to 0,3 %.

Let us draw what this means.

First the link at rest (grey line), lying along the axis \(x\). In the extreme position the hub is turned by the angle \(\theta\), negative in the picture, and the bent link lies in blue in the turned frame, which is shown by a dashed line. The tip is displaced by \(v(L)\) from this line. The hub turns against the bending.
