From \(J_{\mathrm{tot}}\ddot\theta = -b_1\ddot q\) it follows for oscillation about rest that \(\theta = -b_1 q/J_{\mathrm{tot}}\) (the constants of integration are zero, because the hub and the link are on average at rest). With one mode this is \(-b_1/(J_{\mathrm{tot}}\,\varphi_1(L)) = -0{,}646\) rad per metre of tip bending, where \(\varphi_1(L) = 1{,}4618\) kg\(^{-1/2}\) is the tip bending of the mass-normalized mode. The whole model with 20 elements, in which \(\theta = -\vek b^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}/J_{\mathrm{tot}}\) (lemma 28.23), gives \(-0{,}6373\) rad per metre. At a tip of 10 mm the turn of the hub is \(-6{,}4\) mrad (\(-0{,}37^\circ\)).

The example has two more limiting cases. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} \to \infty\) the ratio \(b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{tot}} \to 0\) and \(\omega \to \omega_1'\): a heavy hub does not turn and the link vibrates as a cantilever. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) the factor is \(1 - b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{link}} = 1 - 0{,}9707 = 0{,}0293\) and \(\omega = 178{,}3\) rad/s with one mode, while the exact value is \(133{,}87\) rad/s (20 elements), because one mode is not enough for such strong coupling. The table repeats this for four hubs.

\(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) (kg m²) \(b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{tot}}\) \(\omega\) with one mode (rad/s) \(\omega\), 20 elements (rad/s)
\(0\) \(0{,}9707\) \(178{,}3\) \(133{,}87\)
\(0{,}2\) \(0{,}7351\) \(59{,}31\) \(59{,}15\)
\(2\) \(0{,}2308\) \(34{,}81\) \(34{,}81\)
\(100\) \(0{,}0060\) \(30{,}62\) \(30{,}62\)

28.6.5 Interlacing of frequencies

The hub releases the rotation, and so we cannot get the free vibration simply from the cantilever: at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) the first vibration is at \(59{,}15\) rad/s, the cantilever has \(30{,}53\) rad/s. The question is whether anything holds for all hubs. The answer is a theorem that follows from corollary 10.29: locking the hub is one constraint.

Theorem 28.25 Interlacing of the frequencies of a link (prepletanje frekvenc člena)

Let a link in a free joint be as in corollary 28.22 with \(n_{\mathrm{d}} \ge 1\) elastic coordinates, and let \(0 \le \omega_1 \le \omega_2 \le \dots \le \omega_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{d}+1}\) be the nonnegative roots of the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M_0)\), that is the frequencies of the free joint. Let \(\omega_1' \le \dots \le \omega_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{d}}'\) be the frequencies of the link with the hub locked, \(\theta = 0\), that is the eigenfrequencies of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) (the cantilever). Then \(\omega_1 = 0\) and for \(r = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{d}}\)

\[\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \le \omega_{\mathrm{r}}' \le \omega_{\mathrm{r}+1} . \tag{28.37}\]
Proof

We must show that \(\theta = 0\) matches the constraint of corollary 10.29 with \(\mat G\vek u = (0, \vek u)\), and that the pair \((\mat K', \mat M')\) agrees with \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\).

  1. The pair \((\mat K, \mat M_0)\) has \(\mat K\) symmetric and \(\mat M_0\) symmetric and positive definite (corollary 28.22), so by theorem 10.13 the eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) exist and theorem 10.26 holds. The column \(\vek e_\theta = (1, \vek 0)\) satisfies \(\mat K\vek e_\theta = \vek 0\), so \(R(\vek e_\theta) = 0\). Since \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite, \(R \ge 0\) everywhere, and by theorem 10.26 \(\lambda_1 \le R(\vek e_\theta) = 0\), hence \(\lambda_1 = 0\) and \(\omega_1 = 0\). This is the rigid rotation of definition 10.22.
  2. The lock \(\theta = 0\) is a constraint \(\vek b_{\mathrm{c}}^\T\vek q = 0\) with the column \(\vek b_{\mathrm{c}} = \vek e_\theta\) and \(b_{\mathrm{c},\mathrm{p}} = 1\) for the index \(p\) that corresponds to \(\theta\). The matrix \(\mat G\) of corollary 10.29 assigns to every column \(\vek u\) of \(n_{\mathrm{d}}\) numbers the column \((0, \vek u)\), because \(v_{\mathrm{p}} = -\frac{1}{b_{\mathrm{p}}}\sum_{\mathrm{i} \ne \mathrm{p}}b_{\mathrm{i}}u_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), since all \(b_{\mathrm{i}}\) with \(i \ne p\) are zero.
  3. Then \(\mat K' = \mat G^\T\mat K\mat G = \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and \(\mat M' = \mat G^\T\mat M_0\mat G = \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\), as block multiplication shows. The eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}'\) are therefore the squares of the cantilever frequencies, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}' = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\).
  4. Corollary 10.29 gives \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}' \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}+1}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{d}}\). Since the frequencies are nonnegative roots (all \(\lambda \ge 0\)), (28.37) follows.

Source: The theorem is ours. GR section 2.10.6, equations 2.230-2.240 (PDF pp. 135-136) has the theorem on constraints that we use (corollary 10.29). Nothing in the sources is about a link on a hub.

Now let us test it on four hubs.

Four axes, one for each hub inertia: \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), \(0{,}2\), \(2\) and \(100\) kg m² (the axis \(\omega\) is shown by the scale in rad/s). First on each axis the orange circles: these are the cantilever frequencies, which are the same for every \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\), since the hub is at rest when locked. Then the blue dots: the free joint has one path more, so the first dot is at \(0\), the rigid rotation, and the next ones depend on \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\). At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) the first nonzero blue dot is at \(133{,}87\) rad/s, between the circles \(30{,}53\) and \(191{,}31\). Inequality (28.37) with \(r = 1\) is \(\omega_1 = 0 \le \omega_1' = 30{,}53 \le \omega_2 = 133{,}87\), and with \(r = 2\) it is \(\omega_2 = 133{,}87 \le \omega_2' = 191{,}31 \le \omega_3 = 433{,}82\). For larger \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) the dots move toward the circles, at \(100\) kg m² the difference is \(0{,}09\) rad/s. The same follows from the example: \(\omega_2 \to \omega_1'\) as \(J_{\mathrm{h}} \to \infty\).

The theorem says two things about the first vibration frequency of a link with a free joint. First, the cantilever frequency \(\omega_1' = 30{,}53\) rad/s is a lower bound for it: \(\omega_2 \ge \omega_1'\). Second, it does not exceed the second cantilever frequency: \(\omega_2 \le \omega_2' = 191{,}31\) rad/s. A reader might expect that a lock, which is a constraint, raises all frequencies, so \(\omega_1' \ge \omega_2\). At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m² this does not hold: \(\omega_2 = 59{,}15 > \omega_1' = 30{,}53\) rad/s. The constraint does raise the frequencies, but each cantilever frequency is compared with the free-joint number with the same index: \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \le \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'\), which at \(r = 1\) means \(0 \le 30{,}53\). The first free-joint frequency is the rigid rotation with frequency zero, so the first nonzero free-joint frequency has the index 2, and (28.37) compares it with \(\omega_1'\) and \(\omega_2'\): \(\omega_1' \le \omega_2 \le \omega_2'\).

28.6.6 What linear elastodynamics says

SHABANA describes a road that was used for a long time: first we compute the link as rigid, from the rigid motion we get the inertial and reaction forces, and these we put into a problem of linear elasticity, which gives the deformations. It is called the linear theory of elastodynamics (linearna teorija elastodinamike) and says: in the equation for the reference coordinates we neglect the coupling \(\mat m_{\mathrm{rf}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{f}}\), and the matrix \(\mat m_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and the vector \(\bar{\vek Q}_{\mathrm{r}}\) must not depend on the deformation (equations 5.160 and 5.161, PDF p. 241). The elastic equation is then solved with the known acceleration of the reference motion. The author warns that this assumption does not hold for fast, light systems (PDF p. 240). The example of the link on a hub shows how good it is.

Example 28.26 Linear elastodynamics of a link on a hub (linearna elastodinamika člena na pestu)

At \(\tau = 0\) let us write equations 5.161 for our link in the notation of this section. We neglect \(\vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) in the first equation of (28.35).

  1. After neglecting, the first equation is \((J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\ddot\theta = 0\), so the hub does not turn (\(\ddot\theta = 0\), and at rest \(\theta = 0\)).
  2. In the second equation \(\vek b\ddot\theta\) therefore cancels: \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). This is the cantilever, its first frequency is \(\omega_1' = 30{,}53\) rad/s regardless of \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\).
  3. The coupled model (corollary 28.22) has for the same link the frequency \(\omega_2\) from the table: \(133{,}87\), \(59{,}15\), \(34{,}81\) and \(30{,}62\) rad/s at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), \(0{,}2\), \(2\) and \(100\) kg m².
  4. The error of the linear theory, relative to the coupled model, is \(77{,}2\ \%\), \(48{,}4\ \%\), \(12{,}3\ \%\) and \(0{,}3\ \%\).

The figure shows the error by the inertia of the hub.

First we draw the axes: horizontally \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) on a logarithmic scale, because it changes over several orders of magnitude, vertically \(\omega\) in rad/s. The orange line is the answer of the linear theory, the same for all hubs, \(30{,}53\) rad/s. The blue curve is the coupled model: it falls from \(133{,}87\) rad/s at a small hub toward the orange line. On the curve are three points from the table, and the dashed segments show the difference to the orange line.

Why does the theory fail? The term \(\vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) that it dropped is the moment that the vibrating link gives to the hub. By lemma 28.23 the vibration of a link without torque must turn the hub. By how much, figure 28.15 says: \(0{,}6373\) rad per metre of tip bending at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m². The theory stays exact when the motion of the hub is prescribed in advance (a fast servo that fulfils \(\theta(t)\) exactly): then \(\ddot\theta\) is not an unknown but a known function, and equation (28.33) with the given \(\ddot\theta\) is precisely linear elastodynamics. Section 28.9 shows that the linearized equation (28.33) in the cantilever modes splits into one equation for each mode, driven by the force \(-b_{\mathrm{r}}\ddot\theta\), proportional to the acceleration of the hub. If the motor gives a torque and the link decides where the hub turns, the error remains. With a heavy hub the two models are equal, because \(\vek b^\T\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}/(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}) \to 0\).

28.6.7 What we have shown

The equations of motion of the link (theorem 28.20) are Lagrange's equations with the kinetic energy \(T\) and the elastic energy \(U\). For a link on a hub they are equations (28.32) and (28.33), linearized in (28.35). The frequencies of a link with a free joint interlace with the frequencies of the cantilever (theorem 28.25, (28.37)) and differ from them by the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 - b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{tot}}}\) for one mode. Linear elastodynamics, which drops the coupling, computes the cantilever, and its error at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m² is 48 %. The next section returns to the term \(-\dot\theta^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) in (28.33): at constant rotation rate it gives a falling frequency and a predicted instability at \(\dot\theta = \omega_1'\), which is false, because we dropped the shortening of the axis.

28.7 Centrifugal stiffening (sredobežna ojačitev)

We linearized the link on the hub of section 28.6 at rest (corollary 28.22): the hub with inertia \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) stood still and the link vibrated only transversely. Now let a driver turn the hub at a constant angular velocity \(\Omega\), as it is in an arm that follows a circular arc, or in a turbine blade. What happens to the first transverse frequency of the link? For the steel strip of example A (\(L = 1\) m, cross-section \(40 \times 6\) mm, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m\(^2\), \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, first cantilever frequency \(\omega_1 = 30{,}53\) rad/s, that is \(4{,}86\) Hz) the speed \(\Omega = 10\) rad/s is about \(95\) revolutions per minute, which a joint reaches easily. The answer we shall get is short, and the model of section 28.6 misses it: under spin the frequency rises, it does not fall. The result is drawn in figure 28.20.

The name of the section has two parts. Centrifugal (sredobežna) is the force that seems to a driver to pull him away from the centre of a bend: the word is built from the Latin for centre and fleeing, and in turning axes every piece of matter "flees" from the centre. In non-turning axes there is no such force, the piece only needs a real force that holds it on its circle, and we shall compute that force. Stiffening (ojačitev) means that the link becomes stiffer: the tensile force in the link that this effect causes raises the bending frequency, just as a taut string gives a higher note. The piece of the link that this force holds is shown in figure 28.18.

The path is this. First we look at what the model of section 28.6 says at constant spin and why we cannot accept it. Then we compute the axial force of a spinning link. Then we compute the work of this force on the shortening of the axis in bending, and so obtain the missing term in the energy. At the end we test the theorem on example A and on cases where its condition fails.

Notation. The angular velocity of the hub is \(\Omega\), but in chapter 9 \(\Omega\) is the frequency of excitation, another quantity with the same symbol. The angle of the hub is \(\theta\) as in chapter 8 (not the Timoshenko rotation of the cross-section of chapter 5, which we do not use here). The axial force \(N(x)\) is the one of definition 2.5 (tension positive). We have already met the matrix \(\mat G\) of section 28.7.3 in chapter 12 as the geometric stiffness matrix (lemma 12.50), there for a constant axial force, here for a force that varies along the link.

28.7.1 What the model of the equations of motion of the link says

The link is as in section 28.2: the transverse elastic displacement is \(v(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \psi_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,q_{\mathrm{k}}\) in a floating frame (plavajoči koordinatni sistem) with its origin at the hub and the axis \(x\) along the link in the direction of the tangent at the joint (clamped reference conditions, definition 28.5). The model is Euler-Bernoulli, the axis is inextensible and the hub radius is zero. The last two assumptions are idealizations: in a real joint the axis of rotation lies a hub radius before the start of the strip, which we also compute in section 28.7.4. The equations of the link on the hub from corollary 28.21 have a row for the angle \(\theta\) and rows for the elastic coordinates. The driver now prescribes \(\theta(t) = \Omega t\), so we do not look for the moment \(\tau\), which is the moment that holds the speed. Such a link is shown in figure 28.19.

Lemma 28.27 A link at constant spin in the model of the equations of motion (člen pri stalnem vrtenju v modelu gibalnih enačb)

Let the link be as in corollary 28.21 (figure 28.19) with clamped reference conditions and \(\theta(t) = \Omega t\) with constant \(\Omega\). Let \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the circular frequency of the link at \(\Omega = 0\) with a clamped end (for modal shapes the cantilever frequency of theorem 13.37). Then the elastic coordinates move by the equation

\[\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} - \Omega^2\,\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\big)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0 , \tag{28.38}\]

and every harmonic solution of it, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \hat{\vek q}\cos\omega t\) with \(\omega > 0\), has a circular frequency \(\omega\) with \(\omega^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2\) for some \(r\) with \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} > \Omega\).

Proof

We must show that the row of equations for the elastic coordinates turns into (28.38) and that the relation between the frequencies follows from it.

  1. From \(\theta = \Omega t\) we have \(\dot\theta = \Omega\) and \(\ddot\theta = 0\).
  2. In the row for \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) of corollary 28.21 the term with the angular acceleration \(\vek b\,\ddot\theta\) is therefore zero and \(\dot\theta^2 = \Omega^2\). Equation (28.38) remains. The row for \(\theta\) gives the moment \(\tau\) that holds the speed, and we do not need it.
  3. Let \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \hat{\vek q}\cos\omega t\) with \(\hat{\vek q} \ne \vek 0\). Substitution gives \(\big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} - (\omega^2 + \Omega^2)\,\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\big)\hat{\vek q} = \vek 0\), so \(\omega^2 + \Omega^2\) is an eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) (theorem 10.13, \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite by theorem 28.13). The eigenvalues of this pair are \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), the squares of the frequencies of the link with a clamped end.

Source: The proof is not from the source. The equation is a consequence of the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{f}} + \mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{f}} = \ldots\) of SHABANA (5.144), PDF p. 237, with the Coriolis terms neglected, section 28.6.

The lemma says that in this model spin only lowers the frequency. For the link of example A at \(\Omega = 10\) rad/s the first frequency is \(\sqrt{30{,}528^2 - 10^2} = 28{,}843\) rad/s, for \(\Omega = 20\) rad/s it is \(23{,}064\) rad/s, and at \(\Omega = \omega_1 = 30{,}53\) rad/s the first frequency is zero (NumPy, num-07.out), the orange curve in figure 28.20. At larger \(\Omega\) the model predicts even more:

Corollary 28.28 The predicted instability at \(\Omega \ge \omega_1\) (napoved nestabilnosti pri \(\Omega \ge \omega_1\))

Let \(\omega_1\) be the smallest of the frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) of lemma 28.27 and \(\Omega > \omega_1\). Then equation (28.38) has the solution \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}(t) = \vek\varphi_1\big(a\,\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t} + c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma t}\big)\) with \(\sigma = \sqrt{\Omega^2 - \omega_1^2} > 0\), which for \(a \ne 0\) grows beyond all bounds. At \(\Omega = \omega_1\) the solution is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek\varphi_1\,(a + c\,t)\), which grows linearly.

Proof

We must show that the given formula solves (28.38).

  1. Let \(\vek\varphi_1\) be the mode with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_1 = \omega_1^2\,\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_1\) (theorem 10.13) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = f(t)\,\vek\varphi_1\). Substitution into (28.38) gives \(\big(\ddot f + (\omega_1^2 - \Omega^2) f\big)\,\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_1 = \vek 0\), so \(\ddot f = \sigma^2 f\) with \(\sigma^2 = \Omega^2 - \omega_1^2\).
  2. For \(\sigma > 0\) this equation is solved by \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\sigma t}\), for \(\sigma = 0\) (\(\ddot f = 0\)) by \(1\) and \(t\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

Is this prediction true? No. By it the steel strip of length \(1\) m would at \(30{,}53\) rad/s (about \(292\) revolutions per minute) begin to vibrate with a growing amplitude. FPGL in section 10.8 (PDF p. 471) reports for a blade on a turning hub the opposite: the natural frequencies rise with spin. In this section we derive that and prove (corollary 28.32) that the frequency of a straight link at no \(\Omega\) is below \(\omega_1\). At \(\Omega = 10\) rad/s the model of section 28.6 predicts \(28{,}843\) rad/s, that is \(-5{,}5\) % from \(30{,}528\), and the true answer is \(+1{,}0\) % in the plane of rotation. Not only the size is wrong, the sign is wrong. The curves are in figure 28.20.

What is wrong in the model? The model moves a point of the link with material coordinate \(x\) only transversely, from \((x, 0)\) to \((x, v(x))\) (figure 28.19 below). Then the point would be farther from the centre \(\mathrm{O}\) than \(x\), but the axis is inextensible and the piece \([0, x]\) stays of length \(x\). In reality the end of the piece moves transversely and at the same time toward the hub by the shortening (skrček) \(s(x)\). The centrifugal force points away from the centre, but the points of the link move toward the centre in bending: the work is against the force and the energy grows. This work is missing from the model. We compute it with the force and the shortening.

28.7.2 Axial force of a spinning link

We begin with the straight link, before it bends. This spinning link is a straight bar with mass \(\rho A\) per length, of length \(L\), and turns about its end \(\mathrm{O}\) with constant angular velocity \(\Omega\). Every cross-section of it is on a circle about \(\mathrm{O}\), so a force must act on the cross-section that holds it on the circle: just as a stone on a string that we whirl needs the pull of the string toward the hand. The pull in the cross-section \(x\) is the axial force \(N(x)\) of definition 2.5. To compute it we cut the link at \(x\) and take the piece \([x, L]\) out as a free body. On the piece acts the rest of the link with the axial force \(N(x)\), which starts in the cut and points toward the hub, the other end of the piece is free. Newton's second law for the piece says that the sum of forces on it equals the sum of the products of mass and acceleration of its parts. A point at distance \(\xi\) from \(\mathrm{O}\) has at constant angular velocity an acceleration of size \(\Omega^2\xi\) toward \(\mathrm{O}\), like a point we know from circular motion. The force on the piece is therefore the sum of these accelerations multiplied by the mass, and the graph below shows it as a function of \(x\).

Lemma 28.29 Axial force of a spinning link (osna sila vrtečega se člena)

Let a straight prismatic bar of length \(L\) (figure 28.18) with mass \(\rho A\) per length turn about one end \(\mathrm{O}\) with constant angular velocity \(\Omega\) without bending, the hub radius being zero. Then the axial force (definition 2.5) in the cross-section \(x \in [0, L]\) is

\[N(x) = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,\frac{L^2 - x^2}{2} . \tag{28.39}\]

It is tension (\(N \ge 0\)), largest at \(\mathrm{O}\), where \(N(0) = \rho A\,\Omega^2 L^2/2\), and zero at the free end.

Proof

We must show that \(N(x)\) is the sum of the forces that hold the piece \([x, L]\) on circles.

  1. A point of the axis at distance \(\xi\) from \(\mathrm{O}\) has at time \(t\) the position \(\xi\,(\cos\Omega t, \sin\Omega t)\). The second derivative with respect to time is \(-\Omega^2\,\xi\,(\cos\Omega t, \sin\Omega t)\): the acceleration of size \(\Omega^2\xi\) points toward \(\mathrm{O}\) (the velocity \(\Omega\xi\) is perpendicular to the axis, as in lemma 8.78). The acceleration is shown by the grey arrow.
  2. On the piece \([x, L]\) act the forces of the rest of the link in the cross-section \(x\). The free end at \(L\) has no force. The acceleration has a component only along the axis, so the transverse force is zero and the axial force \(N(x)\) remains, directed toward \(\mathrm{O}\) (tension is positive, definition 2.5). The force is the orange arrow on the piece.
  3. Newton's second law projected on the axis toward \(\mathrm{O}\): \(N(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L \rho A\,\Omega^2\,\xi\,\mathrm{d}\xi\). The acceleration and the force are in figure 28.18.
  4. By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40) the integral is \(\rho A\,\Omega^2\,(L^2 - x^2)/2\).

Source: GR (4.267) and (4.268), PDF p. 294, at hub radius \(e = 0\): there the axial force in this same cross-section is the integral of \(m\Omega^2(e + \xi)\) over the piece from \(x\) to the end. The proof with the free body is ours, the source gives only the formula.

For example A at \(\Omega = 10\) rad/s we have \(N(0) = 1{,}872 \cdot 100 \cdot 1/2 = 93{,}6\) N, and at \(\Omega = \omega_1 = 30{,}528\) rad/s it is \(872{,}3\) N (NumPy). At \(x = L/2\) at this speed it is \(654{,}2\) N, which is \(0{,}75\) of the value at the hub, and at the end zero. We check also the piece \([0{,}4, 1]\) m: it has mass \(1{,}1232\) kg and its centre of mass at \(0{,}70\) m, so mass times acceleration is \(1{,}1232 \cdot 30{,}528^2 \cdot 0{,}70 = 732{,}7\) N, and formula (28.39) gives \(1{,}872 \cdot 30{,}528^2 \cdot (1 - 0{,}16)/2 = 732{,}7\) N. The graph of the axial force is in figure 28.18.

The force of \(872\) N is large, but the extension is small: at cross-section \(240\) mm\(^2\) and \(E = 196\) GPa we have \(N(0)/(EA) = 1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-5}\). An inextensible axis is therefore a good idealization. The force is large, however, when we multiply it by the displacement that bending will cause, and that is the energy term we are looking for. The only displacement along the axis is the shortening of figure 28.19.

28.7.3 Shortening of the axis and the energy of the force

We draw the link in the plane of rotation, which we watch in turning axes. First the axis \(x\), the transverse axis \(v\) and the dashed link before bending, the origin \(\mathrm{O}\) is in the hub. Then the bent link, which has the shape of the first cantilever mode. We choose the point with material coordinate \(x\) at \(x = 0{,}6\,L\) and mark the piece of the axis \([0, x]\), which because of the inextensible axis has length \(x\) also after bending. Its end is the point \(\mathrm{P}\). The model of the equations of motion would leave the same point on the vertical above \(x\), in the empty dot \((x, v(x))\). The tilted piece has a horizontal projection shorter than \(x\) and the difference is the shortening \(s(x)\), at the end of the link the shortening \(s(L)\). Such geometry was already computed by lemma 12.48 of chapter 12.

Lemma 12.48 is proved for an element on which \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\) are continuously differentiable, the axis is inextensible and \(q = \max|v'|\) with \(q^2 \le 10^{-2}\). Its steps 1 to 3 hold for every upper limit \(x \in [0, h]\) and here we have \(u(0) = 0\) (the hub is at \(\mathrm{O}\)). Therefore the point \(\mathrm{P}\) with coordinate \(x\) is in the floating frame at

\[\big(x - s(x, t),\ v(x, t)\big) , \qquad s(x, t) = \int_0^x \Big(1 - \sqrt{1 - v'^2}\Big)\mathrm{d}\xi , \quad \tfrac12\int_0^x v'^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi \le s \le 1{,}0026\cdot\tfrac12\int_0^x v'^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi , \tag{28.40}\]

where the upper bound is from equation (12.53) at \(q^2 = 10^{-2}\). For example A with tip displacement \(10\) mm in the first mode we have \(\max|v'| = 0{,}0138\), so \(q^2 = 1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and the factor is \(1{,}00005\), the shortening at the end is \(s(L) = 0{,}0581\) mm, at \(x = L/2\) it is \(0{,}0144\) mm and at \(x = L/4\) it is \(0{,}0025\) mm (NumPy). The shortening is zero at the clamp and grows fast toward the end.

The shortening is small, but the axial force at \(\Omega = \omega_1\) is up to \(872\) N: the product is of the order \(872 \cdot 0{,}0581 \cdot 10^{-3} = 0{,}05\) J, the same order as the elastic energy \(0{,}0218\) J at the same displacement. The work of the force on the shortening must therefore be taken into account. The shortening is shown in figure 28.19.

Theorem 28.30 Centrifugal stiffening of a link (sredobežna ojačitev člena)

Let the link be that of section 28.2 (figure 28.19) with clamped reference conditions, \(v(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^n \psi_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,q_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\) with independent \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}'(0) = 0\), constant \(\rho A\) and \(EI\), an inextensible axis, hub radius zero and \(\theta(t) = \Omega t\) with constant \(\Omega\), and let \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) on the link. Let \((\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})_{\mathrm{kl}} = \int_0^L \rho A\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\psi_{\mathrm{l}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}})_{\mathrm{kl}} = \int_0^L EI\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}}''\psi_{\mathrm{l}}''\,\mathrm{d}x\) and

\[\mat G_{\mathrm{kl}} = \int_0^L \rho A\,\frac{L^2 - x^2}{2}\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}}'\psi_{\mathrm{l}}'\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{28.41}\]

Then the elastic coordinates satisfy the following two equations, where terms of third and higher order in \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) are left out of the energy (steps 3 and 4). If the elastic displacement lies in the plane of rotation, then

\[\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2\,(\mat G - \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\big)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0 , \tag{28.42}\]

and if the displacement \(w\) is perpendicular to the plane of rotation, along the axis of the joint, which here is the axis of rotation, then

\[\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2\,\mat G\big)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0 . \tag{28.43}\]
Proof

We must show that the kinetic energy of the link in turning axes is to second order \(T = \text{constant} + \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \tfrac12\Omega^2\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} - \mat G)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) plus a total time derivative, and then apply Lagrange's equations.

  1. In non-turning axes the point of the axis with coordinate \(x\) has the position \(\vek r = \mat R(\Omega t)\,\bar{\vek r}\) with \(\bar{\vek r} = (x - s,\ v)\) by equation (28.40) and the rotation matrix \(\mat R\) (lemma 8.40). The time derivative of the matrix is \(\dot{\mat R} = \Omega\,\mat R\,\mat J\) with \(\mat J = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (lemma 8.76, as in lemma 28.8), so the velocity is \(\dot{\vek r} = \mat R\,\big(\dot{\bar{\vek r}} + \Omega\,\mat J\bar{\vek r}\big)\). The point is \(\mathrm{P}\) in figure 28.19.
  2. The matrix \(\mat R\) preserves lengths (lemma 2.40), so \(|\dot{\vek r}|^2 = |\dot{\bar{\vek r}}|^2 + 2\Omega\,\dot{\bar{\vek r}}\cdot\mat J\bar{\vek r} + \Omega^2|\bar{\vek r}|^2\). With \(\dot{\bar{\vek r}} = (-\dot s, \dot v)\) and \(\mat J\bar{\vek r} = (-v, x - s)\) the three terms are \(\dot s^2 + \dot v^2\), \(2\Omega\,\big(\dot s\,v + \dot v\,(x - s)\big)\) and \(\Omega^2\big((x - s)^2 + v^2\big)\). The kinetic energy is \(T = \tfrac12\int_0^L\rho A\,|\dot{\vek r}|^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (definition 8.79) and by theorem 8.86 it splits into parts \(T_2 + T_1 + T_0\) by the degree in the velocities.
  3. Since \(s\) is of second order in \(v\) (equation (28.40)), to second order \(T_2 = \tfrac12\int\rho A\,\dot v^2 = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(T_1 = \Omega\int\rho A\,x\,\dot v\,\mathrm{d}x = \Omega\,\vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) with \(b_{\mathrm{k}} = \int\rho A\,x\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The terms \(\dot s\,v\) and \(-s\,\dot v\) of \(T_1\) are of third order and we leave them out, and so \(\dot s^2\) and \(s^2\) (fourth order). The term \(\Omega\,\vek b^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the total time derivative \(\mathrm{d}(\Omega\,\vek b^\T\vek q_{\mathrm{d}})/\mathrm{d}t\) at constant \(\Omega\) and drops out of Lagrange's equation: \(\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}t\,(\partial T_1/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}) = \mathrm{d}(\Omega b_{\mathrm{k}})/\mathrm{d}t = 0\) and \(\partial T_1/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). The shortening in figure 28.19 is small.
  4. What remains is \(T_0 = \tfrac12\Omega^2\int\rho A\,\big((x - s)^2 + v^2\big)\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\Omega^2\int\rho A\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \Omega^2\int\rho A\,x\,s\,\mathrm{d}x + \tfrac12\Omega^2\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), where the term \(\tfrac12\Omega^2\int\rho A\,s^2\) (fourth order) is left out. The first term is a constant.
  5. The integral \(\int_0^L\rho A\,x\,s\,\mathrm{d}x\) we compute by parts (corollary 3.41) with \(P(x) = \rho A\,(L^2 - x^2)/2\): \(P' = -\rho A\,x\), \(P(L) = 0\), \(s(0) = 0\), so \(\int\rho A\,x\,s = -[P\,s]_0^L + \int P\,s' = \int_0^L P\,s'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40) \(s' = 1 - \sqrt{1 - v'^2}\), and by equation (28.40) \(s'\) lies between \(\tfrac12 v'^2\) and \(1{,}0026\cdot\tfrac12 v'^2\), so with a relative error of at most \(0{,}26\) %. Therefore \(\int\rho A\,x\,s\,\mathrm{d}x \approx \tfrac12\int_0^L P\,v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat G\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\).
  6. Altogether \(T_0 = \text{constant} + \tfrac12\Omega^2\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} - \mat G)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). The potential energy of the elastic forces is \(U = \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (theorem 28.18). The constraint \(\theta = \Omega t\) contains time (definition 8.42), so Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88, \(Q_{\mathrm{k}} = -\partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}\)) give \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} - \Omega^2(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} - \mat G)\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\). This is (28.42).
  7. A displacement \(w\) perpendicular to the plane: \(\bar{\vek r} = (x - s, 0)\) and \(w\) in the direction of the axis of the joint. The velocity is \(\mat R\,(-\dot s, \Omega(x - s))\) in the plane and \(\dot w\) perpendicular to it, so \(|\dot{\vek r}|^2 = \dot s^2 + \dot w^2 + \Omega^2(x - s)^2\) without a cross term. The term \(\Omega^2 v^2\) drops out and \(T_0 = \text{constant} - \tfrac12\Omega^2\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat G\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) remains, from the same steps 4 and 5 with \(w\) instead of \(v\). Lagrange's equations give (28.43).

Source: The proof is not from the source. GR (4.269), PDF p. 294, writes equation (28.43) for a beam clamped at distance \(e\) from the axis of rotation, with gyroscopic forces neglected (in our computation these are the terms with \(\dot s\), step 3). FPGL (10.41), PDF p. 471: \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + (\mat K + \Omega^2(\mat K_{\mathrm{c}} - \mat M_{\mathrm{t}}\sin^2\alpha))\vek q = \vek 0\) with \(\alpha = 0\) for a displacement out of the plane and \(\alpha = \pi/2\) for a displacement in the plane, where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{c}}\) plays the role of our \(\mat G\). FPGL PDF p. 470: Coriolis effects are neglected.

The theorem is derived with two approximations that we name. The first is the shortening \(s\) replaced by \(\tfrac12\int v'^2\) (step 5): the error is at most \(0{,}26\) % at \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) and \(0{,}005\) % at the displacement \(10\) mm in example A. The second are the left-out terms of third order \(\dot s\,v - s\,\dot v\) of \(T_1\), that is the Coriolis term between the transverse motion and the motion of the point along the axis, which the shortening causes. For one shape (\(n = 1\), \(v = q_1\psi_1\), \(s = q_1^2 S\) with \(S(x) = \tfrac12\int_0^x\psi_1'^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi\)) we have \(\int\rho A\,(\dot s\,v - s\,\dot v)\,\mathrm{d}x = c\,q_1^2\dot q_1 = (c/3)\,\mathrm{d}(q_1^3)/\mathrm{d}t\) with \(c = \int\rho A\,S\,\psi_1\,\mathrm{d}x\) (for the shape with \(\psi_1(L) = 1\), \(c = 0{,}250\) kg/m), a total time derivative, so it drops out of the equation. For several shapes it is not a total derivative. An estimate that is not a bound: at tip displacement \(10\) mm and \(\Omega = \omega_1\) the first shape excites the second with an amplitude of the order \(6 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of the amplitude of the first (a factor \(3\) for the number of terms, NumPy). FPGL says that for blades the Coriolis influence on bending is negligible because of the large radial stiffness (PDF pp. 470 and 472). We measure both approximations by the smallness of the shortening in figure 28.19.

What the theorem says. The force \(N(x)\) is tension and pulls the link toward the hub, like a taut string (section 12.10.1, figure 12.31: a taut bar resists transverse displacement). Bending does not lengthen the axis but shortens it, and the shortening works against the centrifugal force and raises the energy by \(\tfrac12\Omega^2\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat G\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). The softening \(-\tfrac12\Omega^2\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the work of the centrifugal force on the transverse displacement, and the model of the equations of motion of the link has only this. In the first mode of example A at \(\Omega = \omega_1\) and tip displacement \(10\) mm the elastic energy is \(\tfrac12\omega_1^2 q_1^2 = 0{,}0218\) J, the softening is \(-0{,}0218\) J and the stiffening \(+0{,}0260\) J (num-07.out). The stiffening exceeds the softening by \(0{,}0042\) J, so the sum of the energies is positive and there is no instability.

28.7.4 A test on example A and cases where the condition fails

Example 28.31 The steel strip spinning (jekleni trak pri vrtenju)

The link of example A: \(L = 1\) m, \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m\(^2\), hub radius zero. The first cantilever frequency is \(\omega_1 = 30{,}528\) rad/s. Three cantilever shapes (theorem 13.37), mass normalized (\(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \mat I\)), give \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\) with \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = 30{,}528,\ 191{,}313,\ 535{,}682\) rad/s and the matrix \(\mat G\) with diagonal \(1{,}1933,\ 6{,}4782,\ 17{,}8595\) and off-diagonal entries \(G_{12} = -0{,}6859\) and \(G_{13} = -0{,}7924\) (NumPy). For \(n = 1\) it follows from (28.42) and (28.43) that \(\omega^2 = \omega_1^2 + 0{,}19334\,\Omega^2\) and \(\omega^2 = \omega_1^2 + 1{,}19334\,\Omega^2\). The results are in figure 28.20.

The table gives the first frequency of the link in rad/s at speeds \(\Omega\) (rad/s), in the model of section 28.6 (equation (28.38)), in the plane by equation (28.42) with three shapes and out of the plane by equation (28.43) with three shapes (the same \(EI\), the strip is turned by \(90^\circ\) about its axis so that it is in the soft direction). The same data are drawn in figure 28.20.

\(10\) \(28{,}843\) \(30{,}840\) \(32{,}421\)

Source: Computations in NumPy (outlines/ch-podajni-cleni/num-07.py, num-07.out). Comparison with \(20\) elements of the Hermite element of chapter 12 with the exact \(N(x)\) per element (c28.out, part D): \(33{,}164\) and \(45{,}076\) at \(\Omega = \omega_1\), \(38{,}563\) and \(71{,}324\) at \(60\) rad/s. FPGL PDF p. 471, figure 10.37: for a blade the first frequencies rise with spin, less in the plane than out of the plane.

We draw the diagram as follows. Horizontal is the angular velocity \(\Omega\), vertical the frequency \(\omega\). At \(\Omega = 0\) all three curves are at \(30{,}53\) rad/s. The linear model falls toward zero, where \(\omega_1\) is, and ends there because there is no longer a real frequency (corollary 28.28). The displacement in the plane raises the frequency slowly by the theorem, at \(\Omega = 60\) rad/s to \(38{,}6\) rad/s. The displacement out of the plane raises it faster, to \(71{,}4\) rad/s. The dashed line \(\omega = \Omega\) shows when the frequency coincides with the spin: in the plane this is at \(\Omega = 33{,}67\) rad/s, out of the plane never: with one shape \(\omega^2 = \omega_1^2 + 1{,}19\,\Omega^2 > \Omega^2\), and with any number of shapes \(\omega^2 \ge \omega_1^2 + \Omega^2 > \Omega^2\) (corollary 28.32 below). Three shapes are enough: at \(\Omega = 60\) rad/s the value \(38{,}648\) in the plane agrees with the \(20\)-element value \(38{,}563\) to \(0{,}22\) %, and with five shapes it is \(38{,}573\) (NumPy).

Now we prove that the prediction of instability is wrong.

Corollary 28.32 A spinning link does not fall below the cantilever frequency (frekvenca vrtečega se člena ni pod frekvenco konzole)

Let the link be as in theorem 28.30. For every column \(\vek q\) we have \(\vek q^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q \le \vek q^\T\mat G\,\vek q\). Therefore the matrices \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2(\mat G - \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2\mat G\) are positive definite at every \(\Omega\), all frequencies are real and the first frequency is at every \(\Omega\) at least \(\omega_1\). For the displacement out of the plane the square of the first frequency is at least \(\omega_1^2 + \Omega^2\).

Proof

We must show the estimate \(\int\rho A\,v^2 \le \int P\,v'^2\) with \(P = \rho A(L^2 - x^2)/2\) and then estimate the Rayleigh quotient.

  1. For \(v = \sum\psi_{\mathrm{k}} q_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(v(0) = 0\) we have \(v(x) = \int_0^x v'\,\mathrm{d}\xi\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (lemma 6.19, the functions \(1\) and \(v'\) on \([0, x]\)) we have \(v(x)^2 \le x\int_0^x v'^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi\).
  2. We multiply by \(\rho A\) and integrate over \(x\). By parts (corollary 3.41) with \(F(x) = \int_0^x v'^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) we have \(\int_0^L x\,F\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{L^2}{2}F(L) - \int_0^L\tfrac{x^2}{2}\,v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L\tfrac{L^2 - x^2}{2}\,v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), so \(\int\rho A\,v^2 \le \int P\,v'^2\), that is \(\vek q^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q \le \vek q^\T\mat G\,\vek q\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite: from \(\vek q^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q = \int EI\,v''^2 = 0\) it follows that \(v'' = 0\), so \(v = a + bx\), and \(v(0) = v'(0) = 0\) gives \(v = 0\), that is \(\vek q = \vek 0\) for independent \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\). By step 2 we have \(\vek q^\T\big(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2(\mat G - \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\big)\vek q \ge \vek q^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q > 0\) for \(\vek q \ne \vek 0\), and even more for \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2\mat G\).
  4. The Rayleigh quotient of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2(\mat G - \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}),\ \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) is by step 2 at every \(\vek q\) at least the quotient of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\), and this is at least \(\omega_1^2\) (theorem 10.26). The smallest eigenvalue of the first pair is its smallest quotient (the same theorem), so \(\omega_1(\Omega)^2 \ge \omega_1^2\). The quotient of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} + \Omega^2\mat G,\ \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) is by step 2 at least the quotient of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) plus \(\Omega^2\), so the square of the first frequency out of the plane is at least \(\omega_1^2 + \Omega^2\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

We test the inequality on the first shape of example A: \(G_{11} = 1{,}19334 \ge 1 = M_{11}\). The linear model is therefore not only quantitatively but in principle wrong: it predicts an instability that does not exist. The ratio is visible in figure 28.20 as the difference between the blue and the orange curve.

We test the theorem also on two cases where its condition fails.

The first case is the hub radius. In a real arm the axis of the joint can lie a hub radius \(e\) before the start of the strip. At hub radius \(e > 0\) the position of the point is \((e + x - s,\ v)\), the same steps 4 and 5 of the proof give the weight \(\big((L + e)^2 - (x + e)^2\big)/2\) instead of \((L^2 - x^2)/2\) in equation (28.41) and \(N(x) = \rho A\,\Omega^2\,\big((L + e)^2 - (x + e)^2\big)/2\), which is GR (4.268), PDF p. 294. For example A at \(e = 0\), \(0{,}1\), \(0{,}2\) m we have \(G_{11} = 1{,}19334\), \(1{,}35042\), \(1{,}50751\) and the first frequency in the plane at \(\Omega = 60\) rad/s is \(38{,}648\), \(45{,}224\), \(50{,}954\) rad/s (out of the plane \(71{,}370\), \(75{,}135\), \(78{,}717\)). The theorem therefore holds for \(e = 0\), at \(e > 0\) the stiffening is larger and formula (28.41) is no longer exact. At \(e > 0\) the graph in figure 28.18 would be higher: at \(\Omega = 20\) rad/s and \(e = 0{,}1\) m we have \(N(0) = 449{,}3\) N instead of \(374{,}4\) N (num-07.out).

A test with a rigid blade: the straight link of figure 28.18 is hinged at \(\mathrm{O}\) and tilts out of the plane or in the plane. GR (4.274), PDF p. 295, for a rigid blade hinged at radius \(e\) gives \(\omega^2 = \Omega^2\,(1 + 3e/(2L))\). Our formula with the function \(\psi = x\) and the weight for \(e\) gives the ratio \(\int\rho A\big((L + e)^2 - (x + e)^2\big)/2\,\mathrm{d}x\,/\int\rho A\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is \(1{,}15000\) at \(e = 0{,}1\,L\) and \(1{,}75\) at \(0{,}5\,L\), equal to \(1 + 3e/(2L)\). At \(e = 0\) the ratio is \(1\), so \(\omega = \Omega\) out of the plane, and in the plane the ratio is \((G - M)/M = 0\): a rigid blade hinged at the axis of rotation is left neutral by the spin in the plane. The linear model would give \(-\Omega^2\), an instability at every speed. The shape \(\psi = x\) is not admissible under clamped reference conditions (\(\psi'(0) = 0\)), but steps 1 to 5 of the proof require only \(\psi(0) = 0\), so the test holds. It is also a case where the inequality of corollary 28.32 is an equality, since \(v'\) is constant.

The second case is the linear model itself at \(\Omega = \omega_1\). The linear model of section 28.7.1 predicts \(0\) rad/s, the theorem \(33{,}170\) rad/s and \(20\) elements \(33{,}164\) rad/s. When the work of the axial force is missing, the model agrees neither with the theorem nor with the elements. The difference is the difference between the orange and the blue curve in figure 28.20.

What have we shown? A link that spins has, besides the softening \(-\Omega^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) that the model of section 28.6 already knows, a stiffening \(+\Omega^2\mat G\): the matrix \(\mat G\) is the work of the axial force \(N(x)\) of lemma 28.29 on the shortening of the axis of equation (28.40). In the plane of rotation the stiffening beats the softening at every \(\Omega\) (corollary 28.32), out of the plane there is no softening. The same computation with an axial force that varies along the element gives nearly the same frequencies on \(20\) Hermite elements (example 28.31). For turbine blades FPGL uses the same term in section 10.8 (PDF p. 471). What stays neglected are the Coriolis term with the displacement along the axis (third order, estimate \(6 \cdot 10^{-4}\)), spatial terms and joints with several links, which chapter 27 treats. The result is shown in figure 28.20.

28.8 The flexible link from finite elements

In the previous sections we described the flexible link with a floating frame and a field \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat\Psi\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) with arbitrary shapes \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) (definition 28.4). The equations of motion contained three quantities: the stiffness matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\), the mass matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and the column \(\vek b\) that couples the rotation of the joint to the bending (theorem 28.13). For numbers we used the cantilever shapes of chapter 13, which exist only for a uniform straight beam, and the completeness of these shapes is not proved there. How do we get the three quantities for a link for which we have no closed forms? The answer is the same as for the beam in chapter 12: we divide the link into elements, and the shapes \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the Hermite node functions. In doing so we keep the promise of chapter 7: an element without a support has a rigid motion, which something must remove. For a link the reference conditions do it (definition 28.5).

The link is a straight beam of length \(L\) with constant bending stiffness \(EI\) and mass per unit length \(\rho A\), Euler-Bernoulli (definition 5.14), with an elastic displacement only perpendicular to the axis and an axis that does not lengthen, as in section 28.2. The last assumption is an idealization. An axial extension would add coordinates, and we leave it out because the axial stiffness \(EA/L\) of our link is larger by the factor \(1{,}1\cdot 10^5\) than the bending stiffness of the tip \(3EI/L^3\) (c28.py). A piece of the link of finite length \(h\), which we do not get as a limit, we call a finite element (končni element), hence the word "finite".

We build the figure as on a board. First we draw the fixed axes \(X\) and \(Y\), in which we measure the position of the hub. At the point \(o\) the link is attached to the hub, this is the origin of the floating frame, and the small bar beside it shows that the displacement and the slope of the link are prescribed there. The floating frame has the axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), turned by the angle \(\theta\) against \(X\) and \(Y\) (definition 28.3). Because the hub turns the link as a whole, the angle \(\theta\) may be large, while the bending of the link in this frame is small. The link is in the frame \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) a bent line with the deflection \(v(x)\), measured from the axis \(\bar x\). We divide it into three elements \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), and between them are the nodes \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), \(3\). At the node \(N\) we measure two numbers, the deflection \(v_{\mathrm{N}}\) and the slope \(\varphi_{\mathrm{N}}\), as for the beam in definition 12.3. The slope is the tangent of the angle between the tangent line and the axis \(\bar x\) and has no unit, the deflection has the unit metre.

We collect all numbers in a column \(\vek d = (v_0, \varphi_0, v_1, \varphi_1, \dots, v_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})^\T\) with \(2(n+1)\) numbers, and the field of the link is \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\) with the node functions \(H_{\mathrm{I}}\) of lemma 12.8. The column \(\vek d\) has more than the link needs. Already a single element has a field that is a polynomial of degree three, and among the polynomials of degree three are the straight lines. A straight line means that the element is displaced or tilted as a whole without bending, as figure 12.3 shows. Such a motion costs no energy, but for a link the floating frame already describes it. If we had it also among the elastic coordinates, we would describe the same position in several ways. So we first compute which columns \(\vek d\) the straight lines give at all.

Lemma 28.33 Energy-free rigid motions of an element and of the link (toga gibanja elementa in člena brez energije)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite beam element of length \(h\) and constant bending stiffness \(EI > 0\) (definition 12.3), and let \(\vek r_1 = (1, 0, 1, 0)^\T\), \(\vek r_2 = (0, 1, h, 1)^\T\). Then:

  1. For a column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) if and only if \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = a\,\vek r_1 + b\,\vek r_2\) with real numbers \(a\), \(b\), that is, if and only if the field of the element \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the straight line \(a + b\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})\). The condition \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) is the same, so the kernel of the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is exactly two-dimensional.
  2. Let the link be divided into \(n\) elements, and let \(\mat K\) be the full matrix of all \(2(n+1)\) unknowns without supports (theorem 12.9). Then \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = 0\) if and only if there are real numbers \(a\), \(b\) such that \(d_{2\mathrm{N}} = a + b\,x_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(d_{2\mathrm{N}+1} = b\) for every node \(N\), that is, when \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is one straight line \(a + b\,x\) along the whole link.
Proof

We must show that zero energy means a zero second derivative of the field, that such fields are straight lines, and that by lemma 12.2 a straight line indeed corresponds to the column \(a\,\vek r_1 + b\,\vek r_2\). Item 1 is already lemma 12.5 (items 2 and 3). We repeat the steps because we need steps 1 and 2 for item 2.

  1. By lemma 12.4, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). The field \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = c_0 + c_1 s + c_2 s^2 + c_3 s^3\) with \(s = x - x_{\mathrm{a}}\) has \(v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 2c_2 + 6c_3 s\), and the integrand is continuous and nonnegative.
  2. If the integral is zero, the integrand is zero everywhere (lemma 6.10, item 3). Because \(EI > 0\), we have \(2c_2 + 6c_3 s = 0\) for every \(s \in [0, h]\), hence \(c_3 = 0\) (the value at two different \(s\)) and \(c_2 = 0\). The field \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = c_0 + c_1 s\) is a straight line.
  3. By lemma 12.2 (item 2) the straight line \(a + b\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})\) corresponds to the column \((a,\ b,\ a + bh,\ b)^\T = a\,\vek r_1 + b\,\vek r_2\). Conversely, by item 1 of the same lemma the polynomial of degree three with the values and slopes of the column \(a\,\vek r_1 + b\,\vek r_2\) is unique, and the straight line \(a + b\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})\) has \(v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\), hence zero energy.
  4. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) (lemma 12.5), so by lemma 7.16 \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) if and only if \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\). The kernel is thus \(\{a\,\vek r_1 + b\,\vek r_2\}\), the columns \(\vek r_1\), \(\vek r_2\) are independent (\(\vek r_1\) has second entry \(0\), \(\vek r_2\) has \(1\)), and the dimension is two. This is item 1.
  5. Item 2. By item 3 of theorem 12.9, \(\tfrac12\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \tfrac12\int_0^L EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). This integral is a sum over the elements (lemma 6.10, item 1), each term is nonnegative, so at zero each is zero. By steps 1 and 2, \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a straight line on every element.
  6. The field \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is continuously differentiable (lemma 12.8), so the straight lines of neighbouring elements have the same value and the same slope at the common node. A straight line is determined by the value and the slope at one point, so the lines are equal and \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = a + b\,x\) along the whole link. By item 2 of lemma 12.8, \(d_{2\mathrm{N}} = v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_{\mathrm{N}}) = a + b\,x_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(d_{2\mathrm{N}+1} = v_{\mathrm{h}}'(x_{\mathrm{N}}) = b\).
  7. Conversely: for such \(d_{\mathrm{I}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\) equals \(a + b\,x\) by the same item of the lemma (a straight line is continuously differentiable and on every element a polynomial of degree three), it has a zero second derivative and zero energy.

Source: The proof is not from the source. SHABANA (PDF p. 280-281): the field of an element with nodal coordinates and slope describes an arbitrary rigid displacement in both axis directions, but nodal coordinates with small rotations do not describe a rigid rotation arbitrarily (chapter 7 of SHABANA). So the rotation is carried by the reference frame (SHABANA, PDF p. 286), here the frame \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\).

The lemma showed that the element and the whole link each have exactly two energy-free rigid motions: a displacement \(a\) perpendicular to the axis and a tilt \(b\). For an element the tilt is a line that rises by \(bh\) over the length \(h\), as the right half of figure 12.3 shows. The tilt \(b\) is a tangent of an angle, while a rigid rotation keeps the length of a rod, so the line \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = b\,x\) rotates only approximately. A point of the axis at distance \(x\) from the pivot comes to the distance \(x\sqrt{1 + b^2}\), so the relative error of the length is \(\sqrt{1 + b^2} - 1\). For \(b = 0{,}01\) this is \(5{,}0\cdot 10^{-5}\), for \(b = 0{,}0354\) (the slope of the end of our cantilever under a force of \(10\) N, \(FL^2/(2EI)\)) \(6{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\), for \(b = 0{,}1\) already \(5{,}0\cdot 10^{-3}\) and for \(b = 0{,}3\) as much as \(4{,}4\cdot 10^{-2}\) (num-08.out). The field of the elements therefore describes a rotation only to first order in \(b\). For the elastic coordinates the slope is small and this suffices, while the finite rotation of the link is carried by the floating frame with the angle \(\theta\). This is the way in which SHABANA removed the rotation from the element coordinates.

Now we choose what to remove. The reference conditions for the frame at the joint (definition 28.5) prescribe the displacement and the slope of the link at \(x = 0\), \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\), that is \(d_0 = d_1 = 0\). Two conditions remove the two rigid motions of lemma 28.33: the line \(a + b\,x\) with value zero and slope zero at \(x = 0\) is \(a = b = 0\), the zero line. SHABANA requires at least as many conditions as rigid modes (PDF p. 287), and for a link there are two modes and two conditions. The elastic coordinates are the remaining \(2n\) numbers \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = (d_2, \dots, d_{2\mathrm{n}+1})^\T = (v_1, \varphi_1, \dots, v_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})^\T\) and the field is \(\bar{\vek u}(x) = (0,\ v_{\mathrm{h}}(x))^\T = \mat\Psi(x)\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the rows of \(\mat\Psi\) being the node functions \(H_{\mathrm{I}}\), \(I \ge 2\). Figure 28.21 shows exactly this: at node \(0\) there are no unknowns, at nodes \(1\) to \(3\) there are two each.

We need three quantities: the bending energy \(U = \tfrac12\int_0^L EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (lemma 5.76), the mass matrix \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int_0^L \rho A\,\mat\psi^\T\mat\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\) and the coupling column \(\vek b = \int_0^L \rho A\,x\,\mat\psi^\T\,\mathrm{d}x\) (section 28.4), where \(\mat\psi = (H_2, \dots, H_{2\mathrm{n}+1})\) is the row of functions. The first and the second we know from chapter 12, the third is new. For one element with start \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and length \(h\), after integrating the polynomials (SymPy),

\[\vek b_{\mathrm{e}} = \rho A\,h\,\Big(\tfrac{3h + 10\,x_{\mathrm{a}}}{20},\ \tfrac{h\,(2h + 5\,x_{\mathrm{a}})}{60},\ \tfrac{7h + 10\,x_{\mathrm{a}}}{20},\ -\tfrac{h\,(3h + 5\,x_{\mathrm{a}})}{60}\Big)^\T , \tag{28.44}\]

that is \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}} = \big(\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\rho A\,x\,H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}x\big)_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{4}\) with units kg m for the deflection and kg m\(^2\) for the slope.

Theorem 28.34 Flexible link from elements (podajni člen iz elementov)

Let the link be a straight beam of length \(L\) with constant \(EI > 0\) and \(\rho A > 0\), divided into \(n\) elements with nodes \(0 = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{n}} = L\) (definition 12.3), with node functions \(H_0, \dots, H_{2\mathrm{n}+1}\) (lemma 12.8), full matrices \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) of order \(2(n+1)\) (theorem 12.9 and equation (12.50)) and the full column \(\vek b = (b_0, \dots, b_{2\mathrm{n}+1})^\T\), \(b_{\mathrm{I}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\,H_{\mathrm{I}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). Let the reference conditions be \(d_0 = d_1 = 0\) (frame attached at the joint, tangent to the link), the elastic coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = (d_2, \dots, d_{2\mathrm{n}+1})^\T\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) the submatrices of rows and columns \(2, \dots, 2n+1\) of the matrices \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\), \(\vek b_{\mathrm{d}} = (b_2, \dots, b_{2\mathrm{n}+1})^\T\) and \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). Then:

  1. The elastic energy is \(U = \tfrac12\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) and the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
  2. \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,\mat\psi^\T\mat\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\vek b_{\mathrm{d}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\,\mat\psi^\T\mathrm{d}x\) are sums over the elements, \(\vek b = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}\) from equation (28.44) and selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  3. For every \(n\), \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}=0}^{2n+1} b_{\mathrm{I}}\,(\vek d_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{I}}\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, x_1, 1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}, 1)^\T\), with no mesh error.
  4. The symmetric matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b_{\mathrm{d}}^\T \\ \vek b_{\mathrm{d}} & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{pmatrix}\) of order \(2n + 1\) is positive definite, and so is \(\begin{pmatrix} J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} & \vek b_{\mathrm{d}}^\T \\ \vek b_{\mathrm{d}} & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{pmatrix}\) for every \(J_{\mathrm{h}} \ge 0\) and every \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\).
Proof

We must show that the energy and the matrices follow from the assembly, that the column \(\vek b\) splits over the elements, that the line \(x\) belongs to the field of the elements, and that the kinetic energy at zero velocity of the field is zero only at zero velocity of the joint and of the elastic coordinates.

  1. By item 3 of theorem 12.9, \(\tfrac12\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \tfrac12\int_0^L EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x = U\) (lemma 5.76). With \(d_0 = d_1 = 0\) only the block of rows and columns \(2, \dots, 2n+1\) remains in the quadratic form, so \(U = \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric, and so is its block.
  2. The support at node \(0\) prescribes the displacement and the slope. The only line \(a + b\,x\) with value \(0\) and slope \(0\) at \(x = 0\) is \(a = b = 0\), the zero line. By corollary 12.11 (item 1) the block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite. This is item 1.
  3. By lemma 12.43 and equation (12.50), for \(\vek d\) with \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\) the value is \(\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d = \int_0^L\rho A\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), so \(M_{\mathrm{IJ}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,H_{\mathrm{I}}H_{\mathrm{J}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) (by bilinearity and symmetry). For \(I, J \ge 2\) these are the entries of the block \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\).
  4. The integral \(b_{\mathrm{I}}\) is a sum over the elements (lemma 6.10, item 1). By item 1 of lemma 12.8, on the element \(e\) the function \(H_{\mathrm{I}}\) equals \(H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\) for \(I = g_{\mathrm{ei}}\) and is zero elsewhere, so \(b_{\mathrm{I}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek b_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{I}}\) with \((\vek b_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\rho A\,x\,H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}x\) (lemma 7.12).
  5. With \(s = x - x_{\mathrm{a}}\) we have \(x = x_{\mathrm{a}} + s\) and \((\vek b_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} = \rho A\,\big(x_{\mathrm{a}}\int_0^h H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_0^h s\,H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\). Integrals of polynomials (SymPy): \(\int H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}s = (h/2,\ h^2/12,\ h/2,\ -h^2/12)\) and \(\int s\,H_{\mathrm{i}}^e\,\mathrm{d}s = (3h^2/20,\ h^3/30,\ 7h^2/20,\ -h^3/20)\). The sum gives equation (28.44). This is item 2.
  6. Item 3. The line \(x\) is continuously differentiable and on every element a polynomial of degree three, so by item 2 of lemma 12.8 \(x = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} (\vek d_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{I}}\,H_{\mathrm{I}}\) with the values \(x_{\mathrm{N}}\) and the slope \(1\) at node \(N\). By linearity of the integral, \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\cdot x\,\mathrm{d}x = \sum_{\mathrm{I}}(\vek d_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{I}}\int_0^L\rho A\,x\,H_{\mathrm{I}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \sum_{\mathrm{I}}(\vek d_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{I}}\,b_{\mathrm{I}}\). There is no mesh approximation in this.
  7. Item 4. Let \((\dot\theta, \dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}})\) be a vector at which the quadratic form of the matrix is zero. The form is \(\int_0^L\rho A\,(x\,\dot\theta + \dot v_{\mathrm{h}})^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) with \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}\ge2}\dot q_{\mathrm{I}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\), because squaring gives \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\dot\theta^2 + 2\dot\theta\,\vek b_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} + \dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}\) by steps 3 to 5 and the definition of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\). The integrand is continuous and nonnegative and \(\rho A > 0\), so by lemma 6.10 (item 3) \(x\,\dot\theta + \dot v_{\mathrm{h}}(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L]\).
  8. The derivative at \(x = 0\): \(\dot\theta + \dot v_{\mathrm{h}}'(0) = 0\). The reference condition \(d_1 = 0\) means \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}'(0) = 0\), so \(\dot\theta = 0\). Then \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), and by item 2 of lemma 12.8 all \(\dot q_{\mathrm{I}} = 0\). The matrix is positive definite. The diagonal addition \(J_{\mathrm{h}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} \ge 0\) (item 3 for \(\vek d = (0, 0, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\)) does not decrease the quadratic form.

Source: The proof is not from the source. SHABANA (PDF pp. 288-289, 298-300) assembles the mass matrix of a body from element matrices and separates the rigid and the elastic motion, and here it is derived directly for the joint and the transverse field with the lemmas of chapter 12.

The proof showed that \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) are the matrices that we already have from chapter 12 for the cantilever, and that only the row \(\vek b\) is new, which we assemble from elements with equation (28.44). All three quantities are integrals over the undeformed link and do not depend on \(\theta\) or \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), so we compute them once. Item 3 says something that the modal model of the next section cannot do: we get \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\) exactly, because the line \(x\) belongs to the field of the elements, while for the modal model the sum of squares of the couplings will be smaller than \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\).

Example 28.35 Steel strip with one element and with several (jekleni trak iz enega elementa in iz več)

The link is a steel strip of length \(L = 1\) m with cross-section \(40 \times 6\) mm, the thickness \(6\) mm lying in the plane of motion. We take \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\), so \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m\(^2\), \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m, \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = \rho A L^3/3 = 0{,}624\) kg m\(^2\), and a hub with \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m\(^2\).

With one element (\(n = 1\), \(h = L\), \(x_{\mathrm{a}} = 0\)), in the coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = (v_1, \varphi_1)\), by lemma 12.4 and lemma 12.43,

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \frac{EI}{L^3}\begin{pmatrix}12 & -6L\\ -6L & 4L^2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1693{,}44 & -846{,}72\\ -846{,}72 & 564{,}48\end{pmatrix} , \quad \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} = \frac{\rho A L}{420}\begin{pmatrix}156 & -22L\\ -22L & 4L^2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0{,}69531 & -0{,}09806\\ -0{,}09806 & 0{,}01783\end{pmatrix} ,\]

and by equation (28.44) \(\vek b_{\mathrm{d}} = (7\rho A L^2/20,\ -3\rho A L^3/60)^\T = (0{,}6552,\ -0{,}0936)^\T\). The node \(0\) contributes \(b_0 = 0{,}2808\) and \(b_1 = 0{,}0624\). We check item 3 of theorem 28.34: \(\vek d_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, 1, 1)^\T\) and \(b_1\cdot 1 + b_2\cdot 1 + b_3\cdot 1 = 0{,}0624 + 0{,}6552 - 0{,}0936 = 0{,}6240\) kg m\(^2\), exactly \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\). The mass of the whole element, \(\vek d = (1, 0, 1, 0)^\T\), is \(\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d = 1{,}872\) kg, exactly \(\rho A L\) (lemma 12.43).

For more elements we compute the same way (num-08.py). The table shows the lowest frequencies of the model with a locked joint (\(\theta = 0\), the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\)) and of the model with a free joint (the matrices \(\begin{pmatrix}J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\\ \vek b_{\mathrm{d}} & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathrm{diag}(0, \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}})\)) in rad/s:

\(n\) locked \(\omega_1\) free, \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), \(\omega_2\) free, \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\), \(\omega_2\) free, \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\), \(\omega_3\)
1 30,673 152,328 59,224 312,854
2 30,542 134,701 59,178 200,533
4 30,529 133,946 59,149 199,211
8 30,528 133,873 59,147 198,997
20 133,868 59,147 198,982
exact 30,53 133,868

For the free joint \(\omega_1 = 0\), which is the rigid rotation of the link with the hub, and the other frequencies we count from \(\omega_2\). The exact value at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) is the pinned-free beam: from the general solution \(v = B\sin\beta x + D\sinh\beta x\) (conditions \(v(0) = v''(0) = 0\)) and the conditions \(v''(L) = v'''(L) = 0\) it follows that \(\tan\beta L = \tanh\beta L\) with roots \(3{,}9266\) and \(7{,}0686\) (the general solution is the same as in the proof of theorem 13.37), that is \(\omega = 133{,}868\) and \(433{,}816\) rad/s. For \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) we have no exact value, but two independent computations (four cantilever modes, c28.out, and twenty elements) give \(59{,}147\) and \(198{,}98\) rad/s.

Figure 28.22 shows the error as a function of the number of elements.

In the figure the axes show the number of elements \(n\) and the relative error \(\varepsilon = \omega_{\mathrm{h}}/\omega - 1\), where \(\omega_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the frequency from the elements and \(\omega\) the exact one. Line \(1\) is the first frequency of the locked link, \(0{,}48\) % at one element and \(2{,}1\cdot 10^{-6}\) at eight. All points lie above the exact value: for the locked link this is guaranteed by corollary 13.56 (cantilever, under the assumption of completeness, which chapter 13 states without proof). Line \(2\) is the first nonzero frequency of the link with \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) and line \(3\) the second. For the second and higher frequencies the error is larger, because a higher mode gets one half-wave fewer elements. For the free joint the results are likewise above the exact ones, but we have no proof for the pair with the coupling \(\vek b\), because corollary 13.56 speaks of a beam with a locked joint and not of a pair with a coupling: this is an observation from the numbers. After every doubling of the number of elements from \(n = 4\) onwards the errors fall by a factor from \(13\) to \(16\) (num-08.out), which is an observation, not a theorem.

Now we show why both reference conditions are needed. If we prescribe only the displacement \(v(0) = 0\) and leave the slope at the joint free (one condition), the field of the elements still contains the rigid tilt \(x\). The same bent position of the link would then be written in two ways.

We draw the same blackwhite curve twice. On the left the frame \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) is directed along the tangent of the link at the joint, which is the angle \(\theta_1\) against the horizontal, and the slope at the joint is zero, as the choice of theorem 28.34 prescribes. On the right the curve stays the same, but the frame is turned by a larger angle \(\theta_2\), for example to the direction of the chord from the joint to the end. The curve now has a slope at the joint, the angle \(\beta\) against the new axis \(\bar x\), and the two descriptions give the same position if \(\theta\) and the elastic slope change against each other. A simple consequence is the following lemma.

Lemma 28.36 One reference condition is not enough (en referenčni pogoj ne zadošča)

Let the link be as in theorem 28.34, but with only the displacement \(d_0 = 0\) prescribed, and the slope \(d_1\) remains an elastic coordinate: \(\vek q'_{\mathrm{d}} = (d_1, \dots, d_{2\mathrm{n}+1})^\T\) with submatrices \(\mat K'\), \(\mat M'\) and the column \(\vek b'\). Let \(J_{\mathrm{h}} > 0\) be the moment of inertia of the hub. Then:

  1. The column \(\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, x_1, 1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}, 1)^\T\) has \(\vek d'^\T_{\mathrm{x}}\mat K'\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so \(\mat K'\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\). The pair of matrices for \((\theta, \vek q'_{\mathrm{d}})\) thus has two zero frequencies instead of the one for a link with both conditions (the rigid rotation of the link with the hub).
  2. In the undeformed position \(\vek q'_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) the velocity vector \((\dot\theta, \dot{\vek q}'_{\mathrm{d}}) = (1, -\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}})\) has kinetic energy \(\tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{h}}\), that is only the energy of the hub. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) the mass matrix is singular in this position.
Proof

We must show that the line \(x\) belongs to the chosen field, that it has no energy, and that its kinetic energy, when we cancel it with the rotation of the frame, is only the energy of the hub.

  1. By lemma 28.33 (item 2) the line \(x\) has the column \((0, 1, x_1, 1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}, 1)^\T\). At \(x = 0\) it has the value zero, so it fulfils the prescribed \(d_0 = 0\), and its column without the first entry is \(\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}}\). Its energy is zero (item 2 of the same lemma), so \(\mat K'\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\) by lemma 7.16. There are no other columns in the kernel: by item 2 of the same lemma only the line \(a + b\,x\) has zero energy, the condition \(d_0 = 0\) gives \(a = 0\), so the kernel of the matrix \(\mat K'\) is the set of columns \(b\,\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. The mass matrix of \((\theta, \vek q'_{\mathrm{d}})\) is positive definite for \(J_{\mathrm{h}} > 0\) (a zero quadratic form gives from \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\dot\theta^2\) first \(\dot\theta = 0\), then from \(\int\rho A\,\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}^2 = 0\) the field \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), and by lemma 12.8 all \(\dot q'_{\mathrm{I}} = 0\)), so the eigenproblem \(\mat K\vek x = \omega^2\mat M\vek x\) with \(\mat K = \mathrm{diag}(0, \mat K')\) counts the zero frequencies as the dimension of the kernel. The kernel of the matrix \(\mat K\) consists of the columns \((t,\ b\,\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}})\) with arbitrary real \(t\) and \(b\), so it is two-dimensional and there are exactly two zero frequencies.
  3. In the position \(\vek q'_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) the term \(\vek q'^\T_{\mathrm{d}}\mat M'\vek q'_{\mathrm{d}}\) in the upper left entry of the mass matrix (item 4 of theorem 28.34) is zero, so the kinetic energy is, as in step 7 of the same theorem, \(\tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{h}}\dot\theta^2 + \tfrac12\int_0^L\rho A\,(x\,\dot\theta + \dot v_{\mathrm{h}})^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). At \(\dot\theta = 1\) and \(\dot v_{\mathrm{h}} = -x\) (the column \(-\vek d'_{\mathrm{x}}\)) the integrand is zero, \(\tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{h}}\) remains, and at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) zero.

Source: The proof is not from the source. SHABANA (PDF p. 287): the number of reference conditions must be greater than or equal to the number of rigid modes in the field, a link has two rigid modes and one condition is too few.

The lemma says that one condition does not merely leave the matter undetermined, but that the model predicts something else. We check it on the link of example 28.35 with \(n = 4\) elements and \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m\(^2\) (num-08.out). With both conditions the lowest frequencies are \(0\), \(59{,}149\) and \(199{,}211\) rad/s. With one condition they are \(0\), \(0\) and \(133{,}946\). The second zero is false, and the third value equals the first nonzero frequency at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) (the table of the example). The reason is the false rigid rotation: the link can turn against the hub without energy, as if it were attached by a hinge, so the hub does not influence the frequencies of the link. In figure 28.23 this is the exchange of the rotation of the frame with the slope at the joint. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) and in the undeformed position the smallest eigenvalue of the mass matrix with one condition is below \(10^{-15}\) kg m\(^2\) in magnitude, which is a zero due to rounding, while with both conditions it is \(2{,}0\cdot 10^{-5}\) kg m\(^2\) against the largest \(1{,}02\) kg m\(^2\). The second value is positive, as item 4 of theorem 28.34 demands, and the first is zero. The choice of both conditions at the joint follows from the fact that the hub holds the position and the tangent of the link. For other links the choice follows from other joints, and SHABANA (PDF p. 286) for the connecting rod (ojnica), hinged at both ends, chooses the conditions of a simply supported beam.

With theorem 28.34 we have, for a link with any number of elements, all three quantities that the equations of motion of section 28.6 need. What remains is to reduce the elastic coordinates: the number \(2n\) is large for a fine mesh, but we are interested only in the lowest modes. This is done by the next section on modal reduction. How we connect the joints of several links and what else a whole manipulator needs is the subject of chapter 27.

28.9 Modal reduction of the link (modalna redukcija člena)

In section 28.8 we built the link of a steel strip (\(L = 1\) m, \(EI = 141{,}12\) N m², \(\rho A = 1{,}872\) kg/m) from 20 Hermite elements. After the reference conditions of section 28.2 there remain \(n_{\mathrm{d}} = 40\) elastic coordinates \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), and together with the hub angle \(\theta\) there are 41 unknowns. Linearized at rest (corollary 28.22, with the matrix \(\mat M_0\) there) the equation of motion is

\[\begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b^{\mathsf T} \\ \vek b & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \ddot\theta \\ \ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \vek 0^{\mathsf T} \\ \vek 0 & \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \theta \\ \vek q_{\mathrm{d}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tau \\ \vek 0 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{28.45}\]

where \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the moment of inertia of the hub, \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}624\) kg m² the moment of inertia of the link about the joint, \(\vek b\) a column of 40 numbers that ties the rotation of the hub to the elastic coordinates (in section 28.8 \(\vek b_{\mathrm{d}}\)), \(\tau\) the motor torque (lemma 28.19), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) the mass matrix and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) the stiffness matrix of the link with the joint clamped (theorem 28.34). Now we ask whether we really need all 41 numbers. The highest natural frequency of the clamped link is \(2{,}08 \cdot 10^5\) rad/s for these 20 elements and the first is \(30{,}5\) rad/s, so the ratio is about \(6800\). The mesh describes the high frequencies worse (chapter 12: with a consistent mass all of them lie above the true ones), and each of them is one more unknown in every step of the computation.

The answer from chapter 10 is the Ritz one: we write the wanted shape as a combination of a few chosen shapes and compute only their coefficients instead of 40 coordinates (definition 10.41). What remains is the question which shapes to take. For a link the answer is natural. We have already computed the link as a cantilever in chapter 13, and the eigenvectors of the pair of matrices are those that decoupling (theorem 10.20) separates from each other. So we take the natural modes of the link with the joint clamped, that is under the same reference conditions under which \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) was assembled. SHABANA calls this step the modal transformation (SHABANA, section 6.7, PDF pp. 309-312) and writes about the choice that the shapes should be chosen so that they describe the displaced shape well (PDF p. 311).

The words have an origin. Mode (način, Latin modus, "manner") is here the manner in which the link vibrates, and the modal coordinates say how much of each mode the present shape contains. Reduction (redukcija, Latin reducere, "to bring back, to lessen") means that we lessen the number of coordinates and return to a smaller model.

We build figure 28.24 from left to right. First the clamp: the link is fixed in the hub and the axis of the floating frame points along the axis of the link at the joint, which is the reference condition of definition 28.5 (\(v = v' = 0\) at \(x = 0\)). From this line we draw the length of the link \(L\) as the distance between the end marks. The first mode is an arc without a node that moves farthest at the tip. The second mode has one node, the third two and the fourth three, as the computed shapes in the figure show. Beside each mode stand its frequency and the numbers that we introduce below. We mark the frequencies with the joint clamped with a prime, \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'\), because we shall need \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) without a prime for the free joint. They grow quickly: \(\omega_2'/\omega_1' = 6{,}27\) and \(\omega_3'/\omega_1' = 17{,}5\), because the frequency of a cantilever is proportional to the square of the root of equation (13.40) (chapter 13).

Let us write what we replace. In equation (28.45) the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}})\) is the one of chapter 10: by theorem 28.34 \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is symmetric and positive definite (the two reference conditions of definition 28.5 remove both zero-energy fields of the element, \(a + b x\)) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is symmetric and positive definite. SHABANA says of his matrix in words that it is positive definite because the reference conditions determine the displacement field uniquely (PDF p. 310).

Definition 28.37 Modal coordinates of the link (modalne koordinate člena)
