Let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n_{\mathrm{d}}\) of the elastic coordinates of the link under the reference conditions (definition 28.5), \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (\(r = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{d}}\), \(\omega_1' \le \omega_2' \le \dots\)) their eigenpairs by theorem 10.13, \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\)-orthonormal, and \(\mat\Phi\) their modal matrix (definition 10.15). For \(1 \le m \le n_{\mathrm{d}}\) let \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the matrix with \(n_{\mathrm{d}}\) rows and the first \(m\) columns of \(\mat\Phi\). The modal coordinates of the link (modal coordinates of the link) are the numbers \(\eta_1, \dots, \eta_{\mathrm{m}}\) in the column \(\boldsymbol\eta\) that satisfy

\[\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\,\boldsymbol\eta = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} . \tag{28.46}\]

For \(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\) we have \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) (definition 10.19), and for \(m < n_{\mathrm{d}}\) equation (28.46) is the assumption that the elastic shape lies in the space of the first \(m\) modes. The coupling of mode \(r\) (coupling of mode \(r\)) is the number

\[b_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\vek b \tag{28.47}\]

(the column \(\vek b\) of theorem 28.13 has the elements \(\int_0^L \rho A\,x\,\psi_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) for the shape functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the mesh). When the shape functions are already the modes of a cantilever (theorem 13.37), normalized with \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) as above, \(\mat\Phi\) is the identity matrix.

Source: SHABANA (6.167)-(6.172) PDF pp. 310-311: "The nm mode shapes should be selected such that a good approximation for the displaced shape can be obtained." The notation and the name "coupling" are ours.

Why "coupling"? In the theorem below every mode will satisfy \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -b_{\mathrm{r}}\ddot\theta\): the number \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the coefficient with which the acceleration of the hub drives mode \(r\), so it couples the rotation of the hub and the vibration. The sign of a mode is arbitrary (\(-\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is also an eigencolumn), so we choose it so that the displacement of the tip is positive. With this choice the couplings are \(b_1 = 0{,}778\), \(b_2 = -0{,}124\), \(b_3 = 0{,}044\) and \(b_4 = -0{,}023\) kg\(^{1/2}\) m (beside the modes in the figure). The unit is not kg m, because the modes are normalized by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\) and have the unit kg\(^{-1/2}\).

Before we state the theorem, let us draw it with matrices.

In figure 28.25 the mass matrix of equation (28.45) stands at top left, with \(1 + n_{\mathrm{d}}\) rows and columns. The angle block is the number \(J = J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}\), which would be everything if the link were rigid. The column and row of coupling are beside it, because the rotation of the hub drives the elastic coordinates. The block \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is the mass of the elastic coordinates themselves. At bottom left is the stiffness matrix: the angle block is \(0\), because the link does not deform when the hub turns and so has no elastic energy, and the block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) carries all the elasticity. The arrow replaces \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) by \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\boldsymbol\eta\) and multiplies from the left by \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\). On the right is the result with \(1 + m\) rows and columns: the elastic blocks have become small, and because the modes are \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\)-orthonormal, the mass block is the identity matrix \(\mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\) and the stiffness block a diagonal matrix with \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\). The row of coupling is now \(\vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = (b_1, \dots, b_{\mathrm{m}})\), \(m\) numbers instead of \(n_{\mathrm{d}}\). The angle block has not changed.

Theorem 28.38 Reduced model of the link (reducirani model člena)

Let the equation of motion (28.45) hold for a link on a hub with \(J_{\mathrm{h}} \ge 0\), let \(\mat M_0 = \begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b^{\mathsf T} \\ \vek b & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{bmatrix}\) be symmetric positive definite (corollary 28.22), \(\mat K = \operatorname{diag}(0, \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}})\), and \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(\boldsymbol\eta\), \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in definition 28.37. Let \(\omega_1 \le \dots \le \omega_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{d} + 1}\) denote the frequencies of the full model with the joint free (the roots of the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M_0)\)). If in (28.45) we insert \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\boldsymbol\eta\) and multiply from the left by \(\operatorname{diag}(1, \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T})\), we get

\[\begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} & b_1 & \dots & b_{\mathrm{m}} \\ b_1 & 1 & & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \\ b_{\mathrm{m}} & & & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \ddot\theta \\ \ddot\eta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \ddot\eta_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} + \operatorname{diag}\big(0,\ \omega_1'^2, \dots, \omega_{\mathrm{m}}'^2\big)\begin{bmatrix} \theta \\ \eta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \eta_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tau \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{28.48}\]

that is \((J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})\,\ddot\theta + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \tau\) and \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -b_{\mathrm{r}}\,\ddot\theta\) for \(r = 1, \dots, m\). The matrices of this equation are symmetric, and the mass matrix is positive definite. Its frequencies \(0 = \tilde\omega_1 \le \tilde\omega_2 \le \dots \le \tilde\omega_{\mathrm{m}+1}\) with the joint free satisfy:

  1. \(\tilde\omega_1 = \omega_1 = 0\): the reduced model describes the rigid rotation of the hub exactly.
  2. \(\tilde\omega_{\mathrm{k}} \ge \omega_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k = 1, \dots, m + 1\).
  3. For \(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\) we have \(\tilde\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \omega_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(k\), the reduced model is only written in other coordinates.
Proof

We must show that the reduced model is a Ritz approximation of the full one, that its matrices are those that equation (28.48) gives, and that theorem 10.42 then gives points 2 and 3.

  1. Let \(\tilde{\mat\Psi} = \operatorname{diag}(1, \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}})\), a matrix with \(n_{\mathrm{d}} + 1\) rows and \(m + 1\) columns. Its columns are independent: if \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}\,\vek c = \vek 0\) and \(\vek c = (c_0, \vek c_1)\), then \(c_0 = 0\) and \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek c_1 = \vek 0\). Since \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\) (theorem 10.13), it follows that \(\vek c_1 = \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek c_1 = \vek 0\).
  2. The substitution \(\vek x = \tilde{\mat\Psi}\,\vek y\) with \(\vek x = (\theta, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) and \(\vek y = (\theta, \boldsymbol\eta)\) is equation (28.46). The matrices \(\mat M_0\) and \(\mat K\) are constant, so \(\dot{\vek x} = \tilde{\mat\Psi}\,\dot{\vek y}\), the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek x}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_0\dot{\vek x} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek y}^{\mathsf T}(\tilde{\mat\Psi}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_0\tilde{\mat\Psi})\dot{\vek y}\) and the elastic energy is \(\tfrac12\vek x^{\mathsf T}\mat K\vek x = \tfrac12\vek y^{\mathsf T}(\tilde{\mat\Psi}^{\mathsf T}\mat K\tilde{\mat\Psi})\vek y\). The generalized force at the coordinates \(\vek y\) is by definition 8.50 equal to \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}^{\mathsf T}(\tau, \vek 0) = (\tau, \vek 0)\), because the first column of \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}\) is a unit vector. Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88) give \(\tilde{\mat M}\ddot{\vek y} + \tilde{\mat K}\vek y = (\tau, \vek 0)\) with \(\tilde{\mat M} = \tilde{\mat\Psi}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_0\tilde{\mat\Psi}\) and \(\tilde{\mat K} = \tilde{\mat\Psi}^{\mathsf T}\mat K\tilde{\mat\Psi}\).
  3. We multiply the blocks in turn: \(\tilde{\mat M}\) has \(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}\) in the corner, \(\vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = (b_1, \dots, b_{\mathrm{m}})\) in the first row, \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\vek b\) in the first column and \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\) in the elastic block.
  4. In \(\tilde{\mat K}\) the first row and the first column are all zeros. From \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{s}}'^2\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) by multiplying with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\) it follows that \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{s}}'^2\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), which is \(\omega_{\mathrm{s}}'^2\) for \(r = s\) and zero otherwise. With steps 2 and 3 equation (28.48) is proved.
  5. By lemma 10.40 with the independent columns of step 1, \(\tilde{\mat K}\) is symmetric and \(\tilde{\mat M}\) is symmetric positive definite.
  6. Point 1. Because \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite, \(\vek x^{\mathsf T}\mat K\vek x \ge 0\) for every \(\vek x\), and \(\vek y^{\mathsf T}\tilde{\mat K}\vek y \ge 0\) for every \(\vek y\). By theorem 10.13 \(\lambda_1\) and \(\tilde\lambda_1\) are the smallest values of these expressions at \(\vek x^{\mathsf T}\mat M_0\vek x = 1\), so they are not negative. The first column of the identity matrix, \(\vek e_1\), gives \(\mat K\vek e_1 = \vek 0\) and \(\tilde{\mat K}\vek e_1 = \vek 0\), so \(\vek e_1/\sqrt{J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}}\) is a column with \(\vek x^{\mathsf T}\mat K\vek x = 0\) and \(\vek x^{\mathsf T}\mat M_0\vek x = 1\). Hence \(\lambda_1 = \tilde\lambda_1 = 0\).
  7. Point 2. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric, \(\mat M_0\) symmetric positive definite and \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}\) has independent columns (step 1). By theorem 10.42 \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{k}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k \le m + 1\), and the root is an increasing function.
  8. Point 3. For \(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\) the matrix \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}\) is square with independent columns. By point 2 of theorem 10.42 the eigenvalues of the two problems are equal.

Source: SHABANA (6.169)-(6.173) PDF p. 311, which multiplies the full equations of the link by \(\bar{\mat B}_{\mathrm{m}}^i\) and obtains a coupled system of reference and modal coordinates. The Ritz explanation, points 1 to 3 and the proof in eight steps are not from the source.

What the theorem says, as it would be said at the board. The reduced model is the full model in which we have restricted the elastic shape to the first \(m\) modes. So the link in it is somewhat too stiff and the error of the frequencies has one sign (theorem 10.42). The rigid rotation (frequency zero) is not spoiled by the reduction, because the first column of the matrix \(\tilde{\mat\Psi}\) is the unit vector \(\vek e_1\) and the rotation of the hub at \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) lies in the space of the kept shapes.

We get the frequencies of the reduced model from equation (28.48) with an ansatz in which all columns vary as \(\cos\tilde\omega t\). For \(\lambda = \tilde\omega^2 \ne 0\) and \(J = J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}\) the computation is short.

  1. Row \(r\) of equation (28.48) at \(\tau = 0\) is \((\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2 - \lambda)\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda\,b_{\mathrm{r}}\,\theta = 0\), so \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\,b_{\mathrm{r}}\,\theta/(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2 - \lambda)\).
  2. The first row is \(-\lambda J\,\theta - \lambda\sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\). We insert step 1 and divide by \(-\lambda\theta\) (\(\theta \ne 0\), otherwise all \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) by step 1).
  3. The result is the frequency equation
    \[J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m}\frac{b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\lambda}{\lambda - \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2} . \tag{28.49}\]

For the full model (\(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\)) the same equation holds with all terms. For \(m = 1\) it can be solved by hand: \(J(\lambda - \omega_1'^2) = b_1^2\lambda\), which is equation (28.36) of section 28.6,

\[\tilde\omega_2^2 = \frac{\omega_1'^2}{1 - b_1^2/(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}})} . \tag{28.50}\]

In the denominator there is a number smaller than \(1\), so \(\tilde\omega_2 > \omega_1'\), in agreement with the interlacing \(\omega_1' \le \omega_2\) of theorem 28.25 (locking the joint is one constraint). The cause lies in the hub: when the joint is free, the rotation of the hub takes over part of the motion (the share \(b_1^2/J\)), so the effective mass of the mode is smaller and the frequency higher. For \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m² we have \(\tilde\omega_2 = 59{,}31\) rad/s (section 28.6, example 28.24). For \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) we have \(b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}9707\), the denominator is only \(0{,}0293\) and \(\tilde\omega_2 = 178{,}3\) rad/s. For \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 2\) we have \(b_1^2/(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}}) = 0{,}231\), the denominator \(0{,}769\) and \(\tilde\omega_2 = 34{,}81\) rad/s.

The number \(b_1^2/J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}9707\) is the ratio from figure 28.24: the first mode carries 97,07 % of the inertia of the link. Why a sum of such shares cannot exceed \(100\ \%\) is told by the next lemma. By point 4 of theorem 28.34 the mass matrix of the link alone is \(\mat M_{\mathrm{link}} = \begin{bmatrix} J_{\mathrm{link}} & \vek b^{\mathsf T} \\ \vek b & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{bmatrix}\) (without the hub), positive definite, which is the only property that the lemma needs. For all the modes together the same inequality is already given by equation (28.23) of lemma 28.15, here we write it for any number of kept modes.

Lemma 28.39 Sum of the coupling shares (vsota deležev sklopitve)

Let \(\mat M_{\mathrm{link}}\) (the mass matrix of the link without the hub, positive definite by point 4 of theorem 28.34), \(\vek b\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\), \(\mat\Phi\) and \(b_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\vek b\) be as in theorem 28.38. For every \(m = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{d}}\)

\[\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2 < J_{\mathrm{link}} , \tag{28.51}\]

and the sum grows with \(m\). For \(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\) the sum is \(\vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b\).

Proof

We must show that the kinetic energy of the link at a chosen velocity is positive, and compute it as a difference.

  1. Choose the velocities \(\dot\theta = 1\) and \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{m}} b_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = -\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek\beta\) with \(\vek\beta = (b_1, \dots, b_{\mathrm{m}})\), so \(\dot{\vek x} = (1, -\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek\beta)\). This vector is not zero (its first component is \(1\)).
  2. Twice the kinetic energy of the link at \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) is \(2T = \dot{\vek x}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{link}}\dot{\vek x}\) and by theorem 28.13 (lemma 28.15) has three parts: \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\dot\theta^2 = J_{\mathrm{link}}\), the mixed term \(2\,\dot\theta\,\vek b^{\mathsf T}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = -2\,\vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek\beta = -2\sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) and \(\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek\beta^{\mathsf T}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\vek\beta = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\).
  3. Together \(2T = J_{\mathrm{link}} - 2\sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = J_{\mathrm{link}} - \sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{m}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\).
  4. Because \(\mat M_{\mathrm{link}}\) is positive definite, \(2T > 0\) for a nonzero \(\dot{\vek x}\) (step 1). This is inequality (28.51). The sum grows because the terms \(b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) are nonnegative.
  5. For \(m = n_{\mathrm{d}}\) we have \(\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\mathsf T} = \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\) (lemma 10.16), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = \vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\mathsf T}\vek b = \vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b\).

Source: The inequality is Bessel's inequality for the \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) scalar product, in which \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the scalar product of the rigid rotation with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). The proof is not from the source.

The lemma also has a geometric meaning. A rotation of the link about the joint by a small angle \(\delta\) moves the point \(x\) in the transverse direction by about \(x\,\delta\), so by \(x\) per unit angle. This is the field \(x\) along the link, and \(b_{\mathrm{r}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the scalar product of this field with mode \(r\) (with the mass as weight). The sum of squares is the square of the length of the projection of the field \(x\) onto the kept modes, and this cannot be longer than the length of the field itself, \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\). The difference \(J_{\mathrm{link}} - \sum b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) is the square of the length of the part of the rigid rotation that the kept modes cannot show. For link A: after one, two, three, four and five modes there is missing \(2{,}93\), \(0{,}46\), \(0{,}144\), \(0{,}062\) and \(0{,}032\ \%\), and all the modes of the mesh of 20 elements together give \(\vek b^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek b = 0{,}6239988\) kg m² against \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}6240000\) kg m². The field \(x\) has slope \(1\) at \(x = 0\) and does not satisfy \(v'(0) = 0\), so it is not exactly in the space of the mesh, but it is very near: the deficit is \(2 \cdot 10^{-6}\) relative. For a continuous link with the functions \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) of chapter 13 the same proof with integrals instead of sums gives \(\sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{m}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2 < J_{\mathrm{link}}\), and equality as \(m \to \infty\) is the completeness of the cantilever modes. The book does not prove this completeness, it cites it from sources (the remark to theorem 13.45).

When is such a reduced model good? Let us try it on example 28.24 of section 28.6, which we computed there with one mode, this time with the full model and several reduced ones.

Example 28.40

Link A on a hub, the full model of 20 elements (\(n_{\mathrm{d}} = 40\)), reduced models with \(1, 2, 3, 4\) modes, hubs \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), \(0{,}2\), \(2\) kg m². The table shows the first nonzero frequency with the joint free \(\tilde\omega_2\) in rad/s (NumPy). For \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) the values of the full model from section 28.6 are \(59{,}147\), \(198{,}982\) and \(538{,}36\) rad/s.

\(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) (kg m²) full model \(m = 1\) \(m = 2\) \(m = 3\) \(m = 4\)
\(0\) \(133{,}868\) \(178{,}308\) \(134{,}015\) \(133{,}878\) \(133{,}869\)
\(0{,}2\) \(59{,}147\) \(59{,}311\) \(59{,}150\) \(59{,}147\) \(59{,}147\)
\(2\) \(34{,}807\) \(34{,}808\) \(34{,}807\) \(34{,}807\) \(34{,}807\)

The second nonzero frequency \(\tilde\omega_3\) at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) is \(198{,}995\) with \(m = 2\) and \(198{,}983\) with \(m = 3\) (full \(198{,}982\)), and at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) it is \(642{,}83\), \(435{,}23\), \(434{,}01\) with \(m = 2, 3, 4\) (full \(433{,}82\)). All the reduced results lie above the full ones, as point 2 of theorem 28.38 requires.

We read figure 28.26 along the axis \(m\). The vertical axis shows the relative error on a logarithmic scale. For each hub we draw the line of errors in turn and see that all three fall. The heavy hub \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 2\) (blackwhite) has an error of \(3 \cdot 10^{-5}\) already with one mode, the middle one (blue) \(2{,}8 \cdot 10^{-3}\), and no hub (orange) \(0{,}33\). The middle hub gets under the limit \(1\ \%\) with one mode, no hub with two (\(1{,}1 \cdot 10^{-3}\)). The reason is in the frequency equation (28.49). A dropped mode \(r\) would add to the left side the term \(b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\lambda/(\lambda - \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2)\), which is small only if \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\) is much larger than \(\lambda = \tilde\omega^2\). For the second mode (\(b_2^2 = 0{,}0154\) kg m²) at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) the ratio is \(\omega_2'^2/\lambda = 2{,}04\) and the term is \(-0{,}0148\) kg m², which is \(2{,}4\ \%\) of \(J = 0{,}624\) kg m². At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) the ratio is \(10{,}5\) and the term \(0{,}20\ \%\) of \(J\), at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 2\) the ratio is \(30{,}2\) and the term \(0{,}02\ \%\). A light hub puts the free frequency near the frequencies of the link, so it needs more modes. The full model (20 elements) at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) is near the values of the equation \(\tan x = \tanh x\) for a pinned-free beam (prostoležeč-prosti nosilec) (\(133{,}868\) and \(433{,}816\) rad/s, full model \(133{,}868\) and \(433{,}821\)), which we use only as a check and the book does not prove, so the error in the table comes from the reduction.

The frequency test is light, but it does not tell us everything. Under load the reduced model can mislead, and we show this as a test of the theorem that fails if we choose the modes by frequency alone.

The task is static: the tip of the link carries a load \(F = 10\) N, the joint is locked. The static result can be compared with a known one: by theorem 5.56 (equation (5.54)) the tip deflects by \(FL^3/(3EI) = 23{,}62\) mm. How does the reduced model get this result? The static equation is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek Q\) with \(\vek Q = F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{tip}}\) (the unit vector at the tip coordinate). After inserting \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}\boldsymbol\eta\) and multiplying by \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\) as in step 2 of theorem 28.38 we have \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\vek Q = F\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\), so

\[u_{\mathrm{m}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m}\frac{F\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2} . \tag{28.52}\]

Each term of the sum is nonnegative, so \(u_{\mathrm{m}}\) grows with \(m\) and is always below the true value (the reduced model is too stiff, as we predicted). The work of the load at the tip is \(F\,u_{\mathrm{m}}\), so this is the same phenomenon as in theorem 28.38. The numbers for link A, in mm: \(22{,}93\), \(0{,}584\), \(0{,}0745\), \(0{,}0194\), \(0{,}0071\), \(0{,}0032\) for \(r = 1, \dots, 6\), the sum of all 40 terms \(23{,}62\). With one mode the deflection is too small by \(2{,}93\ \%\), with two by \(0{,}46\ \%\), with three by \(0{,}14\ \%\). The terms fall as \(1/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\), because \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)| = 1{,}4618\) kg\(^{-1/2}\) is the same for the first four modes (the ratio of the second term to the first is \(0{,}0255 = (30{,}53/191{,}3)^2\)). The fast fall is good news, but it holds for the deflection, not for everything that interests us.

For a robot link the stress at the clamp matters besides the deflection. The stress in the most loaded fibre is proportional to the bending moment \(EI\,v''(0)\) (chapter 5). How much moment at the root does one mode give? The lemma answers.

Lemma 28.41 Root moment of a mode (moment načina ob korenu)

Let \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be a mode of a cantilever of length \(L\) with frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'\) and \(b_{\mathrm{r}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,x\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) its coupling. Then the bending moment of the mode at the root is

\[EI\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}''(0) = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\,b_{\mathrm{r}} . \tag{28.53}\]
Proof

We must show the balance of the piece \([x, L]\) of the link vibrating in the mode and take it at \(x = 0\).

  1. By theorem 13.31 \(EI\,\varphi'''' = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\rho A\,\varphi\) on \([0, L]\) (equation (13.36)), and the free end at \(x = L\) means \(\varphi''(L) = \varphi'''(L) = 0\) (definition 13.30).
  2. The integral \(\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L EI\,\varphi''''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = EI\,\varphi'''(L) - EI\,\varphi'''(x) = -EI\,\varphi'''(x)\). One more integral with a weight: \(\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L (s - x)\,EI\,\varphi''''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \big[(s - x)\,EI\,\varphi'''(s)\big]_{\mathrm{x}}^L - \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L EI\,\varphi'''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = 0 - EI\,\big(\varphi''(L) - \varphi''(x)\big) = EI\,\varphi''(x)\), by integration by parts (lemma 6.13) and step 1.
  3. By step 1 the left part in step 2 equals \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L(s - x)\,\rho A\,\varphi(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). This is the balance of moments of the piece \([x, L]\): the moment of the inertial load \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\rho A\,\varphi\) about the point \(x\) is carried by the bending moment in the section \(x\).
  4. At \(x = 0\) we have \(\int_0^L s\,\rho A\,\varphi(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = b_{\mathrm{r}}\), so (28.53).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

The lemma says what we wanted. With the statics fulfilled, mode \(r\) at a tip force has the root moment \(EI\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}''(0)\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2 b_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot F\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2 = F\,b_{\mathrm{r}}\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\). The weight \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\) has dropped out, so the terms do not fall as \(1/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\) but as the couplings \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\), and these fall slowly (\(0{,}778\), \(0{,}124\), \(0{,}044\), \(0{,}023\), \(0{,}014\)). Because \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\) is positive by choice, the terms have the signs of the couplings \(+, -, +, -\), as the computed values give (the reason for the alternation is not proved in the book). The numbers for \(F = 10\) N, in N m: \(11{,}377\), \(-1{,}815\), \(0{,}648\), \(-0{,}331\), \(0{,}200\), \(-0{,}134\), the sum of all \(10{,}000 = FL\), as it must be by the balance of the link (the piece \([0, L]\) carries the moment \(FL\)).

In figure 28.27 the vertical axis shows the ratio to the true value, the horizontal one the number of modes \(m\). The blue line shows the ratio of the tip deflection \(u_{\mathrm{m}}/u_{40}\): \(0{,}9707\), \(0{,}9954\), \(0{,}9986\), \(0{,}9994\), \(0{,}9997\) for \(m = 1, \dots, 5\), always below one and growing, fast. The orange line shows the root moment at the same force: \(1{,}138\), \(0{,}956\), \(1{,}021\), \(0{,}988\), \(1{,}008\). With one mode the moment is \(13{,}8\ \%\) too high, because the first term (\(11{,}377\) N m) exceeds the true \(10\) N m, and the other terms correct it with alternating signs, so the line oscillates about the true value and approaches it slowly. The stress at the root is proportional to the moment, so after one mode we would predict a stress \(13{,}8\ \%\) too large and a deflection \(2{,}9\ \%\) too small, with the same model and the same force. Yet the first nonzero frequency of the reduced model at \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 2\) differs from the full one by only \(3 \cdot 10^{-5}\) relative with one mode (example 28.40).

The same case is the acceleration of the hub, which is the load of the robot itself. An angular acceleration \(\ddot\theta = \alpha = 10\) rad/s² loads the link with inertial forces that by equation (28.48) give mode \(r\) the modal force \(-b_{\mathrm{r}}\alpha\). At slow acceleration (statically) we have \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -b_{\mathrm{r}}\alpha/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}'^2\) and the root moment by lemma 28.41 is in magnitude the sum \(\alpha\sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{m}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\). The true value is \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\alpha = 6{,}24\) N m, because by the balance of the piece \([0, L]\) about the joint the moment of the inertial load \(\rho A\,\alpha\,x\) is \(\alpha\int_0^L\rho A\,x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). By lemma 28.39 the sum is always below the true value, and the grey dashed line shows the ratio \(\sum b_{\mathrm{r}}^2/J_{\mathrm{link}}\): with \(m = 1\) the moment is \(6{,}057\) N m, \(2{,}9\ \%\) too small, with \(m = 3\) it is \(6{,}231\) N m. The tip moves by \(12{,}208\) mm with one mode in this load (true value \(12{,}160\) mm, \(0{,}4\ \%\) too high). So the deflection is too high, the moment too low, and the errors have different signs. The quantity that always grows with \(m\) is the work of the load (a sum of nonnegative terms), and the tip deflection is the work only for the tip force. The grey line lies on the same curve as the blue one: the ratios agree to six digits (\(0{,}970688\) at \(m = 1\)). We found this by computation for a uniform cantilever and do not use it in this section.

Why are two computations of the same moment in the reduced model different? The first, from the bending at the root, is \(\alpha\sum b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\). The second, from the equation of motion for \(\theta\) in equation (28.48), is \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\alpha\): at \(\ddot{\eta}_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 0\) we have \(\tau - J_{\mathrm{h}}\ddot\theta = J_{\mathrm{link}}\ddot\theta + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} \approx J_{\mathrm{link}}\alpha\), which is the moment that the link receives from the hub. In the full model they agree (for the mesh of 20 elements up to the deficit \(2 \cdot 10^{-6}\) relative that we found for lemma 28.39), in the reduced one they differ by \((J_{\mathrm{link}} - \sum b_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\,\alpha\), which is the deficit of lemma 28.39. What the kept modes cannot show as bending is passed through the joint all the same, so the stress at the root must not be read from the reduced model without a correction.

The conclusion of the example is a rule of choice. The modes are not chosen by frequency alone: we must keep all that the chosen load excites (\(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathsf T}\vek Q\) in statics, \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\) in hub acceleration), and each mode by the measure of the quantity we seek. The tip deflection needs 2 to 3 modes, the stress at the root 5 or more. CK (section 11.4, PDF p. 367) says the same for a general system: a solution by modal displacements may be inexact even under a static load, because the convergence is often slow and many modes are needed. The mode-acceleration method (metoda modalnega pospeška) improves it, because it computes the pseudostatic response from the full stiffness matrix and takes only a correction from the modes. This method and the related method of Craig and Bampton (CK, section 17.6, PDF p. 575) are treated in chapter 21, here we only name them.

Two things remain open. First, the nonlinear term in the equation for \(\theta\): by lemma 28.15 \(m_{\theta\theta} = J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{d}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\), and in modal coordinates, because of \(\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathsf T}\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\mat\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\), simply \(J_{\mathrm{h}} + J_{\mathrm{link}} + \boldsymbol\eta^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\eta\). For a tip displaced by \(10\) mm in the first mode we have \(\eta_1 = 0{,}00684\) kg\(^{1/2}\) m and \(\eta_1^2 = 4{,}68 \cdot 10^{-5}\) kg m², which is \(7{,}5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of \(J_{\mathrm{link}}\), so we dropped it in the linear equation. SHABANA (PDF p. 312) says that the structure of the equations of motion does not change if the inertia integrals are written in the corresponding modal form, which is done once in advance. Second, for rotation with constant speed (section 28.7) the stiffness matrix changes, so the modes computed at rest are no longer eigenmodes but only the shape functions of the Ritz method. The upper bound of theorem 10.42 still holds, because the matrices are again symmetric and the mass matrix positive definite, which is all the theorem needs.

How far have we come. The model of the link on a hub, which has 41 unknowns, we reduced to \(m + 1\) unknowns with a proved guarantee (the frequencies above the full ones, the rigid rotation exact) and with two tests. The frequency test is light and depends on the hub, the load test is harder, because it requires choosing the modes by the load and by the quantity we seek. Chapter 21 develops the choice of modes further, the damping of the modes is treated in chapter 20.

28.10 Connections

The ideas of this chapter return in the chapters on robots, on modal reduction, on damping, on rotors and on modelling. For each we say where it is needed next and what stays open there. The abbreviations of subjects are the same as in section 1.19.

We build the figure as we built the model of the chapter. The hub is the turning part of the joint into which the link is fixed, as the spokes of a wheel are fixed in its hub. Its moment of inertia about the joint axis is \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\). The torque \(\tau\) of the motor turns the hub, and the angle \(\theta\) is the angle between the axis \(\bar x\) of the floating frame from section 28.2 and the horizontal axis of the fixed frame. The link is clamped in the hub, so it bends when the hub turns, and the tip deflection \(v\) is the elastic coordinate that the model of the chapter computes. If the hub turns at a constant angular velocity \(\Omega\), a centrifugal axial force appears, which section 28.7 treats. Dashed is everything the model does not have: the next joint and link at the end and the damper that removes energy. Each of the following points relies on one part of the figure.

  • A robot with several links (next joint and link): chapter 27 (DSK) assembles rigid links into a chain and derives its mass matrix from theorem 8.86 (VD, DSK). Our link is one link of that chain. Corollary 28.14 shows that at \(\boldsymbol q_{\mathrm{d}} = \boldsymbol 0\) and \(\dot{\boldsymbol q}_{\mathrm{d}} = \boldsymbol 0\) the kinetic energy of the link reduces to the kinetic energy of a rigid body from theorem 8.82, so the rigid robot is a special case. Flexibility adds to each link a coupling column \(\boldsymbol b\) and the elastic coordinates (lemma 28.15). Several links joined by joints need constraints with multipliers by theorem 8.95 and a split of the coordinates into independent and dependent ones (SHABANA, §5.4, PDF pp. 230 to 233, §5.8 to §5.10, PDF pp. 251 to 260). We do not prove this in the chapter, because one link does not need it. The equations of a link on a hub from corollary 28.21 are our own derivation from the general equations (SHABANA, §5.5, PDF pp. 234 to 238), because no source in the book treats a flexible robot link with a joint by Lagrange equations, and SPONG has only flexible joints (PDF pp. 314 and 461).
  • A controlled joint (hub and torque): locking the joint (\(\theta = 0\)) is one constraint, so by theorem 28.25 the frequencies of the locked link lie between those of the link with a free joint. At \(J_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}2\) kg m² the order is \(0 \le 30{,}53 \le 59{,}15 \le 191{,}31 \le 198{,}98\) rad/s, so the first elastic frequency with a free joint is \(1{,}94\) times that of the locked link. Which of the two models applies depends on whether the controller holds the joint or leaves it to the torque. That is a question of control, which lies outside the book (SPONG, from chapter 8 on).
  • Spin and blades (angular velocity \(\Omega\)): theorem 28.30 for constant spin is the same derivation as for a turbine or fan blade, where the centrifugal axial force raises the bending stiffness and the frequency rises (FPGL, §10.8, PDF pp. 469 to 472). Here, at \(\Omega = \omega_1 = 30{,}53\) rad/s the first in-plane frequency rises to \(33{,}17\) rad/s, which is \(8{,}7\) %, while the linear model without this axial force falls to zero, a false instability (corollary 28.28). Rotating blades are treated in chapter 24 (DSK). A hub radius larger than zero changes the axial force \(N(x)\) and the in-plane coefficient, and turning combined with axial motion of the link brings a Coriolis coupling that our model leaves out, as FPGL also neglects it (PDF p. 470).
  • Model reduction (bent link): theorem 28.38 replaces \(n\) elastic coordinates by a few modal ones, and the frequencies of the model stay above those of the full model by theorem 10.42. By lemma 28.39 the sum of squared couplings \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} b_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) is less than \(J_{\mathrm{link}} = 0{,}624\) kg m², and with five modes it is \(0{,}62380\). The static deflection of the end under a force of \(10\) N, \(23{,}62\) mm, is underestimated by \(2{,}9\) % with a single mode, so we choose modes by the loading and not only by frequency. The static modes that correct this (Craig-Bampton) and the mode acceleration correction are treated in chapter 21 (CK, §17.6, PDF p. 575).
  • Damping (damper): the equations of the chapter have no damping. The steel link has a small internal damping and the joint has friction, which the model does not contain. How damping is added to equations in modes and how it is measured is treated in chapter 20 (DSK).
  • Limits of the model (tip deflection \(v\)): the elastic field is Euler-Bernoulli (definition 5.14) with an inextensible axis. The axial stiffness \(E A / L\) is \(1{,}11 \cdot 10^5\) times the bending stiffness of the tip \(3 E I / L^3\) in the example, so axial stretching is not needed. We neglect shear and rotary inertia: for a thin strip of thickness \(h = 6\) mm the radius of gyration of the section is \(r = h/\sqrt{12} = 1{,}73\) mm and \(r/L = 1{,}73 \cdot 10^{-3}\), so the first rule of corollary 13.64 (\(n r / L \le 0{,}022\), frequency correction below \(1\) %) holds up to \(n = 12\). The corollary is for a simply supported beam, so for the cantilever this is an estimate and not a proof. When the beam model is no longer enough (thicker links, plates and shells, nonlinear models, large deformation) is a question for chapters 17, 18 and 22 (AK, MK). SHABANA treats large deformation in the floating frame in §6.8 (PDF pp. 313 to 315).

What is proved in this chapter and what is only cited: the planar floating frame, the kinetic energy, the elastic energy, the equations of the link, the interlacing of frequencies, the centrifugal stiffening and the reduction are proved from chapters 1, 2, 5, 8, 10, 12 and 13. Cited without proof are the completeness of the cantilever modes (from chapter 13), the spatial floating frame (SHABANA, §5.1, PDF pp. 207 and 208, §6.6, PDF pp. 303 to 308), several links with joints, constraints and multipliers, the slider-crank with a flexible rod (SHABANA, §5.7, PDF pp. 242 to 250, and chapter 23, DSK), numerical integration of the equations (SHABANA, §5.12, PDF pp. 264 to 272) and flexible joints (SPONG, PDF pp. 314 and 461).
